\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{MWC cost (Match Winning Chance cost)}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Cumulative match winning probability lost due to errors, over the full filtered dataset. Computed using the database’s current MET, by default the Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2 embedded in blunderDB. A match\sphinxhyphen{}score analysis computed with another table is “different MET” and stays out of the statistics.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{caution}{Caution:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
MWC cost \sphinxstylestrong{does not apply} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{money\sphinxhyphen{}game} positions (with no match stake). Those positions are excluded from the MWC computation. MWC values depend on the MET used; they are not directly comparable across software using different METs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:perte-mwc-7pts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{MWC loss (7\sphinxhyphen{}pt eq.)}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The probability of winning the match that a player lost across all their decisions — checker plays, cube, take or pass, with cube — scaled to a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match. For an \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}\sphinxhyphen{}point match in which the player lost \sphinxstyleemphasis{L} of MWC:
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
L₇ = L × √(7 / N)
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match, this is the match’s MWC loss, the one eXtreme Gammon displays. The square root comes from the FIBS formula’s model: at equal strength, a player’s loss grows as the square root of the match length. 7 points is the reference length because it is the most common in tournaments.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It reads as the share of the match lost against a perfect player: 12.3\% means that instead of 50\% winning chances against the engine, the player had only 37.7\% in a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match. The tooltip gives the reading as Elo against the engine, by inverting the FIBS formula: D = (2000 / √7) × log₁₀(q / (1 − q)), with q = 0.5 − L₇. Beyond a loss of 49\%, the formula has no finite value: the displayed Elo is then a ceiling (”≤”). The two figures rank players in the same order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It complements the PR without replacing it: the PR divides errors by a number of decisions, and that number depends on what is counted as a decision (forced moves, obvious cube decisions). The MWC loss counts no decisions: each error weighs what it cost at the score where it was made.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Over several matches (a player’s or a tournament’s statistics), the losses and the square roots of the lengths are added before taking the ratio: L₇ = √7 × ΣL / Σ√N. A 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match therefore weighs more than a 1\sphinxhyphen{}point match, and a single match gives its own value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A single match is very noisy: a few big errors are enough to make it vary by a factor of two. The badge and the match summary ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_matchs:bilan-match}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{match summary}}}}}) give the 95\% interval by resampling its games; an aggregate (a player’s or a tournament’s statistics) gives it by resampling its matches; without a player filter, the two seats of a match form a single unit, since they play the same positions. At least three games, or three matches, are needed, and they must not all give the same loss: otherwise there is no interval. A per\sphinxhyphen{}match row of the statistics therefore has none: it is a single unit. Do not rank players on a single match.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{caution}{Caution:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{money\sphinxhyphen{}game} has no match length: the MWC loss (7\sphinxhyphen{}pt eq.) is not defined there and the panel says so instead of displaying a number. Like the MWC cost, it depends on the MET.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The button’s third choice, \sphinxstylestrong{MWC 7 pts}, plots this loss in the Progression tab, and shows it on the dashboard cards and in the checker/cube comparison of the Errors tab, split into checker and cube on the same matches (the two parts add up). The player ranking has its column. Charts with no 7\sphinxhyphen{}point equivalent (per cube action) keep the MWC cost.
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The PR ↔ MWC toggle is instant: no backend recalculation is performed.


\subsubsection{The HTML report}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:le-rapport-html}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:rapport-html}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{HTML report} button in the panel’s header produces a \sphinxstylestrong{self\sphinxhyphen{}contained} document: a single file, with no external image, no remote stylesheet, no script. The diagrams are inline SVG, drawn by the same renderer as the board on screen, with your palette. It opens in any browser, travels by e\sphinxhyphen{}mail, and \sphinxstylestrong{prints to PDF from the browser itself} — which avoids embedding a PDF generator to produce what everybody already has.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It carries the current scope’s figures (positions, matches, counted decisions, global, checker and cube PR), then the \sphinxstylestrong{ten most expensive decisions}, each with its diagram, its cost, the match it comes from and the best move when an analysis gives one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The document is built by the engine, not by the screen: the command line (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats report \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}html}}, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}) and the HTTP daemon (route \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats.report}}) produce the same report, in any of the nine interface languages. Only the graphical application draws the diagrams with the board palette; the other two use the default palette.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The report carries the Stats panel’s \sphinxstylestrong{current filter}. A report that does not state its scope is a report whose figures mean nothing: set the filter — a tournament, a date range, a player — before producing it.


\subsubsection{Dashboard tab}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:onglet-tableau-de-bord}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Dashboard} tab gives a synthetic view of the key indicators. It reads from top to bottom: the level cards, then what is worked on (study plan, top blunders), then the readings (rolling PR, before/after study, signed biases). The explanation of each card is in the tooltip of its title.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=1.000\linewidth]{{panel_stats_dashboard}.png}
\caption{The Dashboard tab: global PR, checker PR, cube PR.}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:id2}}\end{figure}


\paragraph{Level cards}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:cartes-de-niveau}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Three cards display the PR (or MWC) for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{PR Global} — all decisions (checker + cube);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Checker PR} — checker decisions only;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{PR Cube} — cube decisions only.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a card loads the positions in the corresponding subset into the analysis panel (drill\sphinxhyphen{}down). A fourth card, \sphinxstylestrong{MWC loss (7\sphinxhyphen{}pt eq.)}, gives this loss whatever the PR / MWC button is set to, with its interval; it loads nothing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below the cards, the totals line counts the filter’s tournaments, matches and decisions. The tournament count opens those tournaments in the Tournaments panel: a single tournament opens directly; several restrict the list, which then carries the button « N tournaments opened from Stats × »: it restores the full list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of decisions opens their positions; the number of matches opens those matches in the Matches panel, except when a decision type or a provenance filter is active: it then counts fewer matches than the list would open and stays a plain number.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The total number of decisions is shown at the bottom of each card on hover.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Study plan}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:plan-d-etude}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:plan-etude}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Study plan} card answers “what should I work on now?”. Recurring mistakes (Errors tab) say where the filter lost the most; they do not say where study pays off the most. A family of truly hard positions costs everyone dearly, and three mistakes do not make a trend. The plan corrects both.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{family} is a group of recurring mistakes: a game plan, a kind of decision (checkers or cube) and a theme. Mistakes without a theme form none: they point to nothing to study.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each mistake is priced in \sphinxstylestrong{MWC}, as in the Match panel: its loss ℓ, and its \sphinxstyleemphasis{difficulty} d, the loss a reference player would have suffered in the same position (see the per\sphinxhyphen{}decision difficulty in the Match panel). A mistake in a free game has no MWC: it is only counted, “unpriced”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{recoverable MWC} of a family is the sum of ℓ − d over its mistakes: the family’s frequency times its average loss beyond the difficulty. It is what you would regain by playing these positions like the reference player. A family of avoidable mistakes rises, a family of positions where everyone errs falls.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{95\% interval} accompanies every figure. A family enters the plan from \sphinxstylestrong{5 mistakes} and an interval entirely above zero; the plan is ranked by the lower bound of the interval, so that at equal recoverable the best\sphinxhyphen{}established family comes first. The others are named under the list, \sphinxstylestrong{to be confirmed}, without a rank: the plan does not push you toward noise. The same line counts the mistakes \sphinxstylestrong{outside the plan} (without a theme, not quantified).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each row of the plan shows its rank, the family, a bar whose length is its recoverable MWC relative to that of the first, this MWC with its interval, and the number of mistakes. Every count of positions in the plan (per family, to confirm, outside the plan) is clickable: it loads exactly those positions into the list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each family offers three actions: \sphinxstylestrong{Study} opens the study queue on its positions, the largest gap to the reference player first; \sphinxstylestrong{Quiz} starts the Decision exercise of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-entrainement}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Training}}}}} panel on twenty of them; \sphinxstylestrong{Anki} turns them into a deck of cards. At the top of the card, \sphinxstylestrong{Quiz on the top three families} draws twenty positions from those of the three leading families. The plan follows the panel’s filter: set the player to get \sphinxstyleemphasis{your} plan. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb stats plan}} (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}).


\paragraph{Before/after study}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:avant-apres-l-etude}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:avant-apres-etude}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Before/after study} card closes the plan’s loop: does what you worked on cost you less in real matches? Without it, study is judged by feel; with it, a family that does not move despite the work says you should change method, and a family that improves can give up its place in the plan.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A family (the plan’s family) is \sphinxstylestrong{studied} on the date of the first study action on one of its positions: the “studied” mark in the study queue, an Anki review, a quiz answer. Creating a card or filing a position in a collection does not count.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For each studied family, the card compares two \sphinxstylestrong{windows}: the matches played before that day and those played after it (the day itself is left out). In each, the \sphinxstylestrong{loss rate} is the MWC lost by the family’s mistakes, relative to all decisions of the same game plan and the same kind, and shown in MWC points per 100 decisions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{gain} is the before rate minus the after rate, with its 95\% interval. The verdict is “improved” (or “worse”) only if each window has at least \sphinxstylestrong{30 decisions} and the interval excludes zero; otherwise it stays “undetermined” or “too few decisions”.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Next to each window, the \sphinxstylestrong{Positions} column counts the distinct positions of its decisions and opens them with a click; the number in brackets remains the number of decisions, the rate’s denominator.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a change, not an effect: a family is studied because it was costing you, and part of the gain is regression to the mean; nothing controls for opponents, format or dice. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb stats effect}} (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}).


\paragraph{Signed biases}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:biais-signes}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Signed biases} card tells you in which direction you go wrong, not just how much. “You take too much” is easier to fix than a PR: the rule to review is named. Each bias is the share of faulty decisions in one direction minus the share of faulty decisions in the other, with its 95\% interval; a tendency is named only from \sphinxstylestrong{20 decisions} and an interval that excludes zero.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Take / pass} — on cube responses: faulty takes (the bot passes) minus faulty passes (the bot takes). This is exactly your take rate minus the bot’s on the same positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Doubles} — on doubling decisions: premature doubles (the bot does not double, or the position is too good to double) minus missed doubles. The same bias is given \sphinxstylestrong{by score} (your away, your opponent’s, a post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford score counted as 1 point; money play in its own cell), for the scores with enough decisions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Blots} — on checker plays with contact: plays that leave more blots than the best play minus those that leave fewer. A play is recognized by the board it leaves, whatever its notation (“13/7(2)”, “8/5*/4”); a play the move generator still cannot replay is discarded, and the share of discarded plays is given under the table. The bias counts blots without weighing their exposure: a blot out of reach counts as much as an exposed one.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Next to each count, its cost in millipoints tells you whether the tendency costs you; a position played in several matches counts there with the move played in each. The biases follow the panel’s filter. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb stats biases}} (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each count of decisions (all, one way, the other way) is followed by a \sphinxstylestrong{Positions} column: the distinct positions of those decisions, which a click opens. A position played in several matches counts one decision per match, but a single position.


\paragraph{Rolling PR over last N decisions}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:pr-glissant-sur-n-dernieres-decisions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A row of PR (or MWC) values computed over the last \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} decisions (N = 5, 10, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000) lets you measure the recent trend. Greyed values correspond to an N larger than the number of available decisions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a value loads the corresponding last \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} positions.


\paragraph{Top blunders}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:top-blunders}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of the 10 worst errors (or MWC cost), sorted by descending magnitude. Clicking a row loads the relevant position in the analysis panel.


\subsubsection{Progression tab}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:onglet-progression}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Progression} tab shows how your level evolves over time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the top of the tab, a \sphinxstylestrong{goal}: “PR < 5 within twelve weeks”. A target, a deadline, and a trend that says where you are heading — nothing more. A goal that started grading, congratulating or reminding would be a different feature, not this one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Suggest} button proposes a target from your current level: the lower bound of the band you are in, that is, the entry into the next one. Proposing “a bit better” would be anchored to nothing; proposing a band says something — going from intermediate to advanced can be seen and told.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{trend} is a least\sphinxhyphen{}squares fit over your matches’ PR, projected to the deadline. It refuses to speak below three matches: drawing a line between two points would be a claim that cannot be held. And the sentence says so every time — \sphinxstyleemphasis{a trend is not a prediction}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The goal is stored in the \sphinxstylestrong{database’s metadata}, not in the configuration: it is about that library, so it follows the file rather than the machine. No schema change: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{metadata}} is already a key/value table, readable by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb info}} as by the daemon.


\paragraph{Tournament line chart}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:courbe-par-tournoi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A line chart shows the PR (or MWC) of each tournament: one point per tournament, labelled with its name, in the chronological order of its date — failing that, the date of its oldest match (Y axis: the metric’s value). Coloured bands mark the level thresholds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a point on the chart opens a context menu with two options:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open tournament} — opens the tournament in the Tournaments panel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open positions} — loads all positions from the tournament into the analysis panel.

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Match scatter plot}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:scatter-plot-par-match}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A scatter plot shows each match (X axis: date, Y axis: PR or MWC). The size of each point is proportional to the number of decisions in the match. A match without a date does not appear.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a point opens a context menu:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open match} — opens the match in the Matches panel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open positions} — loads all positions from the match into the analysis panel.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Errors tab}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:onglet-erreurs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Errors} tab breaks down error sources.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[width=1.000\linewidth]{{panel_stats_errors}.png}
\caption{The Errors tab: PR breakdown by cube action.}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:id3}}\end{figure}


\paragraph{Recurring errors}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:erreurs-recurrentes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At the top of the tab, a table groups the errors of the current filter — so those of a single player when a player is filtered — by \sphinxstylestrong{game plan} and by \sphinxstylestrong{theme}, the most costly first. It answers the question “where am I losing the most?”: for example, “holding · too many blots”.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{error} is a counted decision whose cost reaches the library’s \sphinxstyleemphasis{Error} threshold.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{game plan} is that of the player on roll, as the Breakdowns tab presents it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{theme} of a checker play is the one named by the rules of the explanation sentence in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-analyse}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Analysis panel}}}}}: gammon underestimated, too many blots, point not made, too passive. That of a cube decision is the direction of the error, as in the cube error direction below: missed double, premature double, wrong pass, wrong take.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
An error that no rule names with confidence is not guessed: it leaves the ranking and appears apart, under the table, as one line per game plan (“no theme identified: N errors, cost X”), clickable too. This remainder is often the heaviest, because the explanation only speaks from 60 mp, above the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Error} threshold: ranked with the others, it would top a table that said nothing.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{cost} is the share of the filter’s PR that the group represents: the PR formula applied to the group’s errors, divided by all counted decisions. The costs of the groups therefore never exceed the PR.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a group, or its error count, loads its positions, from the most costly to the least costly. The theme is recomputed at every display, never stored: like the game plan, it is a derived label that cannot be edited. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb stats recurring}} (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each row offers three ways to go from the error to study: \sphinxstylestrong{Quiz this group} starts the Decision exercise of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-entrainement}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Training}}}}} panel on the group’s positions, \sphinxstylestrong{Anki deck} makes a deck of cards from them, \sphinxstylestrong{Collection} files them in a new collection. Above the table, \sphinxstylestrong{Quiz my three worst groups} draws twenty positions at random from those of the three costliest groups. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats recurring \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}quiz}} draws these positions and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}deck}} creates the deck.


\paragraph{Breakdown by cube action}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:repartition-par-action-de-videau}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A bar chart displays the PR (or MWC) for each type of cube decision: \sphinxstyleemphasis{NoDouble}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DoubleTake}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DoublePass}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{TooGood}. Each bar also shows the number of decisions and the blunder rate in a tooltip.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking a bar loads the positions matching that cube action, \sphinxstylestrong{only those with an error} (drill\sphinxhyphen{}down).


\paragraph{Direction of cube errors}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:direction-des-erreurs-de-videau}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The breakdown above says \sphinxstyleemphasis{how much} cube decisions cost; this table says in \sphinxstyleemphasis{which direction} they go wrong.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A cube position carries two decisions taken by two different players, presented here as two rows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Offer} — the player holding the cube doubles or does not. Their errors are the \sphinxstylestrong{missed doubles} (a double was called for) and the \sphinxstylestrong{premature doubles} (it was not).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Answer} — the player being offered the cube takes or passes. Their errors are the \sphinxstylestrong{wrong passes} (a correct take was passed) and the \sphinxstylestrong{wrong takes} (a correct pass was taken).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two rows are deliberately kept apart: a player can perfectly well double late \sphinxstyleemphasis{and} take loosely, and a single figure would call that “balanced” while losing both halves of the information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each cell shows the number of decisions; the tooltip gives the cumulated equity lost. Clicking a cell loads the matching positions. A cell at zero is not clickable.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This table counts decisions, it passes no judgement. At what gap a tendency deserves to be named depends on the sample size and on a point of reference, neither of which the engine holds.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Checker / Cube comparison}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:repartition-checker-cube}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A comparison chart places checker plays and cube decisions side by side. Clicking a bar loads the positions in the subset with an error.


\paragraph{Error magnitude histogram}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:histogramme-des-magnitudes-d-erreur}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A histogram distributes errors by magnitude in millipoints (mpt, buckets: 0–5, 5–10, 10–25, 25–50, 50–100, ≥ 100). Clicking a bar loads the positions in the bucket.


\subsubsection{Training over time}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:entrainement-dans-le-temps}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:stats-entrainement}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Training} tab sets side by side, over the same calendar windows — the \sphinxstylestrong{week} or the \sphinxstylestrong{month}, as you choose — three series that measure progress in three ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{quiz PR}: that of the Decision exercise sessions in the Training panel, weighted by the number of decisions judged. It is computed on the real PR scale, so it is comparable to it;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{match PR} of the current filter, weighted by the number of decisions;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{Anki retention}: the share of reviews of already learned cards graded \sphinxstyleemphasis{Hard} or better, read on the right axis (in \%).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below the chart, the \sphinxstylestrong{quiz PR by plan of play} lists the quiz decisions drawn from library positions, the worst plans first, with the PR of the last window in which the plan was played.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In parentheses, the number of decisions or reviews behind each value: a window without samples has no value — a dash, not a zero. A window’s number of match decisions opens their positions. The filter restricts the matches only; the quiz and Anki journals are yours and carry no player. Nothing more is recorded: the three series are read back from the existing journals. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb stats training}} (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}).


\subsubsection{Breakdowns tab}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:onglet-ventilations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Breakdowns} tab slices the same decisions the global figures count along four axes. None of them redefines what counts as a decision: that would be a second PR wearing the same name.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{By game phase} — opening, middlegame, race, bearoff. This is what answers “my PR in the race versus my PR in contact”. The label is computed from the board (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-recherche}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Search Panel}}}}}); a database whose phases were never computed files everything under \sphinxstyleemphasis{Unclassified}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb repair}} fills it in.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{By plan of play} — race, blitz, holding, backgame, prime vs prime… This is the breakdown the classifier exists for: “where do I lose the most?”, plan by plan. The same derived label as the phase, the same caveats, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb repair}} fills it the same way.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{By tag} — the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#word}} written in the comments. A position may carry several: \sphinxstylestrong{these rows do not sum to the total}, and the panel says so under the table. A tag labels; it does not partition.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{By score} — both sides’ away score, read from the side of the player on roll, that is from the side of whoever is deciding. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Money} row is money play. A cell with fewer than ten decisions is \sphinxstylestrong{greyed with its count still visible} rather than hidden: too few to read, but the omission stays auditable.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Positions} and \sphinxstylestrong{Blunders} columns count distinct positions, and every figure is a link: a click loads exactly these positions into the analysis panel, like the counters of the status bar. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Blunders} counts the positions where at least one decision is a blunder. A position played in several matches (an opening, for example) counts only once there; the \sphinxstylestrong{Decisions} column counts it each time, because it is the denominator of the PR.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each row carries its \sphinxstylestrong{95 \% confidence interval} (column \sphinxstyleemphasis{95 \% CI}), which replaces the fixed ten\sphinxhyphen{}decision threshold: it says what a PR is worth, not only how many decisions carry it. It resamples the \sphinxstylestrong{matches} of the selection, not the decisions or the games: the games of a match share opponent, session and fatigue, and counting them as independent would give too narrow an interval; with no player filter, the two seats of a match form a single unit. A row that rests on fewer than three matches, or whose matches all give the same PR, has no interval and is greyed out, even with many decisions: two matches say nothing about the dispersion, and identical matches say they agree, not that the PR is exact. For study: a family of positions whose interval stays above your overall PR is an established weakness; a row with a wide interval does not yet justify a study plan. The dashboard’s overall PR carries the same interval, under its card.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the breakdown by score, a post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford score is read as 1\sphinxhyphen{}away: the Crawford game and the post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford games at the same score fall into the same cell.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Study and real play}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:etude-et-jeu-reel}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb list \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}type study \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}days 30}} puts three numbers side by side, plan of play by plan of play: how many \sphinxstylestrong{distinct positions} were revised over the period, what the PR was \sphinxstylestrong{before} it, what the PR is \sphinxstylestrong{since}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Three numbers, and no fourth. There is \sphinxstylestrong{no gain column and no arrow}, because nothing here controls for anything: the player may have met stronger opponents, changed format, or simply played more races this month. The rapprochement is the reader’s; a column announcing an effect would claim a causality these data do not carry. The numbers themselves are exact.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reviews are counted as \sphinxstylestrong{distinct positions}: a card revised four times in the month is one position studied, and counting the repetitions would make a month of cramming look like a month of coverage. The PR’s decisions, on the other hand, are all counted — each was taken once. A PR resting on fewer than ten decisions shows \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{—}}, with its sample visible beside it.

&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average luck per roll, in millipoints (mpt), signed: positive if the dice were favourable.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
