\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sort} — click a column header. The table opens sorted by ascending PR, best player first, and remembers the last sort chosen from one session to the next. Players for whom nothing was measured stay at the bottom whichever way the sort goes: a zero for lack of data is not a perfect performance.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Filter by column} — the row of fields under the headers filters each column: a piece of a name for text, a bound for numbers (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{>=500}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{>500}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{<2.5}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{<=2}}), a range (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3\sphinxhyphen{}7}}) or an exact value (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5}}). An unreadable field is outlined in red and filters nothing; a value never measured passes no bound. Column filters last for the session. The player \sphinxstylestrong{ranking} reads like this: sort by PR, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decisions} column filtered by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{>=500}}. All the tables of the Stats panel — breakdowns, corpus, recurring errors, thinking time, training, bias, study effect — are sorted and filtered the same way.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open a player’s detail} — click a row. The player is selected in the filter bar and the display switches to the Dashboard tab.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open one’s decisions} — the number of decisions opens their positions, under the table’s filters. The number of matches and the W–L record remain plain numbers: they also count matches without any analysed decision, which no match list reproduces.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Narrow the period} — the date, tournament and match\sphinxhyphen{}length filters apply as usual, which makes it possible to bound the table to the dates of a competition.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compare two players} — tick the box in the first column on two rows. A block appears above the table and sets their figures face to face; ticking a third player replaces the older of the two. The box does not select the row: ticking compares, clicking opens the detail.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{See the positions where one played better} — the button of the comparison block lists the positions both players had to play and where one played well (below the library’s Error threshold) and the other did not, widest gap first; a player is judged on their worst play of the position. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Open these positions} loads them into the analysis view. The command line and the server give the same list (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats contrast}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unpriced plays} — a play that no candidate of the analysis names has no error: the list leaves it out, and the block gives their number.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In that block, \sphinxstylestrong{only the rates get a verdict}, and the better of the two is set in bold. Three figures never get one, and it is worth saying why. \sphinxstylestrong{Luck} is not a quality: a luckier player is not a better one. \sphinxstylestrong{Matches, record and decisions} say what the rates are worth, but putting them in competition would let whoever simply played more win. The \sphinxstylestrong{blunder count} does not compare raw — twelve out of a thousand decisions beat ten out of a hundred — so the block adds a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Blunders / 100 dec.} line, which does compare, and leaves the count beside it as context.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A tie is not a win: it is set in bold on neither side. A rate with nothing behind it shows as “—” and decides nothing.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this tab, the \sphinxstylestrong{decision type} choice is disabled: the table already breaks checker and cube decisions down into separate columns. The player of the filter bar stays active: the table always shows all the players, and this player’s row is highlighted and scrolled into view.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two corpus views are in the panel’s \sphinxstylestrong{Corpus} tab, on the command line and through the daemon API (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_stats:cli-stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{stats — Recurring errors}}}}}): the \sphinxstylestrong{head\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}head} of two players (common matches, each one’s PR, record) and the rolling \sphinxstylestrong{PR per calendar window} (1, 3, 6 or 12 months). The Corpus tab computes each view on demand, under the current filter. The PR \sphinxstylestrong{ranking} is read in the Players tab, sorted by PR and filtered on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decisions} column; the command line and the API also give it (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats ranking}}). A \sphinxstylestrong{provenance filter} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Engine} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Min. depth} fields of the filter bar) restricts the statistics to decisions analysed that way; it applies to each decision, and the figures it affects are then recomputed from the decisions. The head\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}head and the PR per window do not accept it: while it is active, they refuse to compute. Like the rest of the bar, it is kept from one session to the next.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the Corpus tab, each row opens what it summarises. The head\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}head record opens its matches in the Matches panel, which then carries the button “N matches opened from Stats ×”: it restores the full list; a head\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}head row opens its match. The first player of the head\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}head is by default the one of the filter bar. A window row and its decision count open its positions, its match count opens the matches. A position count in the Stats panel, in whichever tab, first leaves the current match before opening its list; the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} command then reopens the match at the saved move.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A dash (”—”) marks a value that was \sphinxstylestrong{never measured}, not to be confused with zero. That is notably the case of the Luck column for any match imported before schema version 2.15.0: luck was not stored then, and nothing allows it to be reconstructed afterwards. Re\sphinxhyphen{}importing the source file is not enough: the import recognises a duplicate and applies only the study marks newly raised (the report gives their number). The match must be deleted, then imported again. Formats that do not carry it (BGF, Jellyfish \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.mat}}) never will.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Aggregation rule}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:regle-d-agregation}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The PR of a tournament (or any subset) is computed using the \sphinxstylestrong{sum/sum} rule — never as an average of individual match PRs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Formula:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}PR_{tournament} = 500 \times \frac{\sum_{i} \text{error}_i}{\text{total number of decisions}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example:} a player plays two matches in a tournament —
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Match A: 10 decisions, 0.100 of lost equity → PR = 5.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Match B: 90 decisions, 0.540 of lost equity → PR = 3.0

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Naive average of PRs: (5.0 + 3.0) / 2 = \sphinxstylestrong{4.0} \sphinxstyleemphasis{(incorrect)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sum/sum rule: 500 × 0.640 / (10 + 90) = \sphinxstylestrong{3.2} \sphinxstyleemphasis{(correct)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum/sum rule is the only one that handles varying match lengths correctly (a 21\sphinxhyphen{}point match carries more weight than a 1\sphinxhyphen{}point match).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{MWC: limitations}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_stats:mwc-limitations}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, MWC cost is computed from the \sphinxstylestrong{Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2 MET}, the de facto reference table in competitive backgammon. Results are not directly comparable with software using other METs. It is the same table, read through the same entry point, that the embedded evaluator uses for its cube decisions at a match score: the statistics and the engine cannot diverge on this. It gives its own values up to 25 points to go on each side; beyond that, it is extended by a Zadeh table computed the same way as GNUbg’s, up to 64.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Money\sphinxhyphen{}game} positions (with no match score) are \sphinxstylestrong{excluded} from the MWC computation. If your database contains many money\sphinxhyphen{}game positions, the MWC cost may be underestimated or unavailable.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The MWC cost is cumulative over the full filtered dataset — not a per\sphinxhyphen{}decision indicator. It measures the total impact of your errors on your winning chances.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Evaluation}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:evaluation}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:manuel-eval}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval::doc}}

\subsection{Eval Panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-eval}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-epc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Eval} panel (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}E}) evaluates live whatever position sits on the board; on a bearoff position it specialises and additionally computes the EPC (Effective Pip Count). It is opened by pressing \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}E}, by clicking the Eval tab in the lower panel, or by running the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{eval}} command; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{epc}}, its former name, opens it too. The panel was called \sphinxstyleemphasis{EPC}, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff}, before becoming \sphinxstyleemphasis{Eval} — so this is where to look for what an earlier version called the Bearoff panel, the name now only naming the tab that configures the bearoff tables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The panel always shows the \sphinxstylestrong{single decision} the position on the board calls for — never two at once — and the facts that go with it. Each quantity is read in the axis that suits it rather than in a single imposed axis: the winning, gammon and backgammon probabilities and the cubeless equity of each player, computed \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll}, are read \sphinxstylestrong{per player} (bottom, top, then Δ), to the left of the cube decision, when no dice are showing. Facts and decision stay side by side: the cube decision never drops below the figures that justify it, whatever the interface language and the position on the board. As soon as dice are showing, these same \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} values change axis: they are read \sphinxstylestrong{on roll}, at the head of the candidate\sphinxhyphen{}move list, as an italic \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} row — not one more candidate move, a reference against which to read each move. The gap between that row and a move contains the luck of the roll, never the merit of the move, and so it carries no error column. On a pure bearoff position, a second table, still \sphinxstylestrong{per player} and always present, dice showing or not, carries the EPC, the pip count, the wastage, the average number of rolls and the standard deviation; these five columns never migrate. The two tables are stacked and share the same column grid: same edges, same column guides, a single column of dots — they read as one two\sphinxhyphen{}storey object. Above the tables, the header band carries the title, the regime badge and the engine attribution (the depth of the last evaluation appears there too), then, on the right, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Challenge} box and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add to database} button. As long as gammonNet has returned nothing, the panel says so in one line: “Evaluating…”, or “Set up a position” on an empty board.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only the candidate\sphinxhyphen{}move list scrolls — the \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} row, too, stays pinned above it; the rest of the panel (facts, badge, cube decision) always remains visible, with no particular adjustment of the panel size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The facts table and the decision are computed by gammonNet, embedded, without XG or gnubg. The computation follows the position without ever freezing the interface: a 0\sphinxhyphen{}ply depth is displayed immediately on every gesture, then, after half a second of stillness, a deeper evaluation (2 plies by default, adjustable in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gammonNet} tab of the settings) replaces it in the background — any new gesture cancels that background computation. The depth shown in the badge strip, or inside the regime badge on a race position, is always the one that actually produced the figure shown, never the one requested; it is not repeated on every row, since a live evaluation shares the same depth for all moves. The equity of the candidate moves and of the cube decision follows the score of the position: in money game it is expressed in points, at a match score in \sphinxstylestrong{normalised equity} — the same scale as XG and GNU Backgammon, where winning the value of the current cube is worth +1 and losing it −1 — never mixed in the same table. The column header states it explicitly rather than leaving the scale to guess: “Equity (money)” in money game, “Equity (match)” at a match score. It accounts for the \sphinxstylestrong{live cube}: the search values every terminal position through the cube model (Janowski, measured efficiency) in the position’s cube state, the way XG and GNU Backgammon do in \sphinxstyleemphasis{cubeful} evaluation. This is what makes the gammon\sphinxhyphen{}go and gammon\sphinxhyphen{}save effects visible at the score — at 4\sphinxhyphen{}away/2\sphinxhyphen{}away, the player behind plays 8/2 6/2 on an opening 6\sphinxhyphen{}4 because an early double will give the gammon the value of the match, something a cubeless evaluation cannot see. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} row, by contrast, stays a \sphinxstylestrong{cubeless} equity: it is a fact about the position, not a decision. The evaluation is never stored: it is a computation, not an analysis. Clicking a candidate move shows it on the board as arrows, exactly as in the Analysis panel. The discreet \sphinxstylestrong{?} button, in the badge strip, leads to the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/gammonNet}{gammonNet} engine repository; the full attribution (Strehl network, gammonNet configuration) appears in the Acknowledgments of the help.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The panel \sphinxstylestrong{rolls out} the position like the Analysis panel (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:rollouts}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Rollouts}}}}}): \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ctrl+click} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Shift+click} select moves, the right\sphinxhyphen{}click opens the same menu — rollout, copy of the position and the evaluation, or of the position and the selected moves —, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Shift+R} starts or stops the rollout and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Esc} cancels it; a thin bar follows the games played, and each rolled\sphinxhyphen{}out move carries its result in the \sphinxstylestrong{Rollout} column (without dice, under the cube decision). Since the board is a scratch board, the rollout is never saved: it is played in memory, with no open database as on a read\sphinxhyphen{}only database, and its result is shown only as long as the board stays the same. A rollout started before a change to the board is not shown on the new position.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Add to database} button, at the end of the badge strip, after the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Challenge} checkbox, stores the position on the board in the database; \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}S}, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{w}} command and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Save Position} toolbar button do the same. The gammonNet evaluation shown for this board (the moves when the dice are set, the cube otherwise, with its depth) is saved with the position, as the batch analysis would have written it: the search \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s i ad:gammonnet}} finds these positions (on the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}individual}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}analysis gammonnet}}). If the position was already in the database with an analysis (imported, gammonNet at another depth, rollout), that analysis is kept as is and the status bar says the evaluation shown was not saved; with no evaluation shown (engine still running or position declined), only the position is written, as it is when the match equity table changed since the computation, which the status bar reports. If gammonNet automatic analysis is enabled, its batch starts afterwards, as after an import. The status bar announces the position’s number, including when it was already in the database: it is then marked as individually imported, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Individually Imported} filter (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s i}}) finds it. The panel stays open on the same board, which remains a scratch board: you can move a checker and add the variation, and leaving the panel brings you back to what you were studying. The button is disabled while no database is open, or while the position cannot be saved (for example the panel’s starting position, where the top player has borne off all their checkers); its tooltip gives the reason.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The user edits the checker position over the whole board, exactly as in edit mode: left click places a checker of the bottom player, right click a checker of the top player. The second table, the race one, only appears when the resulting position is a pure bearoff (all checkers of both players in their home board); on any other position, only the table of the four common columns (win, gammon, backgammon, cubeless) responds, and the decision bears on the checkers or on a generic cube depending on whether dice are showing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In each facts table, one row per player — identified by its coloured dot, the black player always at the bottom. The first carries, as long as no dice are showing, the player’s win, gammon and backgammon (probabilities, without the \% sign) and cubeless equity; the second, on a bearoff position and dice showing or not, the EPC, the pip count, the wastage (difference between the EPC and the pip count), the average number of rolls and the standard deviation. When both players have values to compare, a \sphinxstylestrong{Δ} row gives the \sphinxstyleemphasis{signed} differences (bottom − top: negative when the black player is ahead). Outside a race position, showing dice therefore makes the facts tables themselves disappear: the four columns they carried have just changed axis, on roll, at the head of the move list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cube decision always has the same shape, whatever the origin of the figures — exact table, evaluated regime or ordinary gammonNet evaluation: \sphinxstylestrong{one row per option}, in the order \sphinxstyleemphasis{no double}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double/take}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double/pass}, with its equity in the position’s frame of reference and its gap to the best option. The order never changes, unlike the move list: the three options have names, so it is the name one reads, not the rank. The best one is recognised by its highlighting and by its gap cell left empty. When the cube has already been turned, the options read \sphinxstyleemphasis{no redouble}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{redouble/take}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{redouble/pass}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A last row gives the \sphinxstylestrong{verdict}. It takes four values: \sphinxstyleemphasis{no double}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double, take}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double, pass} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{too good to double}, the last when playing the position on is worth more than cashing the point: doubling would then be a mistake for the opposite reason to that of a plain \sphinxstyleemphasis{no double}. It is also the only place where the panel says there is \sphinxstylestrong{no} verdict, rather than suggesting a computation in progress:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{no decision} — the regime is not entitled to one; the cube verdict is never estimated (see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{estimated} badge);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{not evaluable at this score} — the engine refuses the position, typically a score beyond the horizon of the match equity table, i.e. a side with more than 64 points to go;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{opponent owns the cube} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cube dead (Crawford)} — the cube cannot be turned. The equities remain displayed, for information, but no option carries a gap: an error is what a choice costs, and there is no choice.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In money game, the \sphinxstylestrong{Jacoby} and \sphinxstylestrong{Beaver} rules active on the position appear under the cube table, in small badges next to the verdict they change: the \sphinxstyleemphasis{no double} verdict of a position under the Jacoby rule is not the same computation as without it, and nothing else on screen said so.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the \sphinxstylestrong{Beaver} rule, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{double, take} row is worth the opponent’s best answer other than passing: taking, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{beavering} — redoubling at once while keeping the cube, the game then being played for four times the stake — with the doubler then answering with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{raccoon} (eight times the stake, cube on his side) when it pays him. The verdict and the errors are read on this row, as without the rule; at a match score, the rule does not apply.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A third badge, \sphinxstylestrong{Max cube}, appears when the source identifier caps the cube — at a match score as well as in a money game. That one does not describe the computation shown above it: the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator does not model a ceiling, so the verdict is the one for a free cube. That is precisely why the badge is there: a capped cube is the one visible reason blunderDB and eXtreme Gammon can announce two different verdicts on the same position.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{player on roll} and the \sphinxstylestrong{cube position} are edited directly on the board, as in edit mode: clicking a player’s bearoff/score rectangle gives that player the roll; clicking the cube cycles centred → owned bottom → owned top (right click cycles the other way). The cube value stays pinned — in money game the equities are expressed in units of the current cube, only its owner matters. The analysis is recomputed immediately. In the estimated regime, the badge itself is clickable and opens the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab of the settings directly; its tooltip explains why (cube verdict not estimable, \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-race-win-chances-are-read-or-convolved-cube-verdicts-are-never-estimated.md}{ADR\sphinxhyphen{}0009}) and how to widen the exact domain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{score} is also edited directly on the board, as in edit mode: left click on a player’s score rectangle decrements their number of points to go, right click increments it. Leaving the \sphinxstyleemphasis{money} score (\sphinxhyphen{}1, \sphinxhyphen{}1) by editing one side alone automatically aligns the other side on the same value rather than leaving an inconsistent score. On a bearoff position in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{exact} regime, moving from a money score to a match score leaves the winning probability as it is (a database lookup, valid whatever the frame of reference) but switches the displayed equity and cube verdict to those of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{evaluated} regime — the exact table being money by construction, it cannot answer the question asked at the score. The badge then becomes composite (“exact (win) · evaluated (cube)”) to say so explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{dice}, finally, are edited the same way, and they are what decides the question being asked: dice on the board make a checker decision (the list of candidate moves), no dice a cube decision. Left\sphinxhyphen{}clicking a die raises its value (6 wraps to 1), right\sphinxhyphen{}clicking lowers it (1 wraps to 6); clicking a die on a board that has none puts down two at once — a single die would be neither a checker decision nor a cube decision. Clicking a player’s rectangle removes the dice to ask a cube question, and the next click on a die puts them back as they were.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{BACKSPACE}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Clear the position} in the menu of a right click outside the board, clears the position: empty board, money score (\sphinxhyphen{}1, \sphinxhyphen{}1), no dice showing — values specific to the Eval panel, different from those used in edit mode (7 everywhere, dice 3\sphinxhyphen{}1), to stay consistent with what the panel shows by default. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Starting position}, in the same menu, sets up the checkers of a new game on those same values.


\subsubsection{Cube matrix}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:matrice-du-videau}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:eval-matrice-videau}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A cube decision is not a property of the board. The same checkers, the same pip count, are a double at 2\sphinxhyphen{}away/4\sphinxhyphen{}away and a no\sphinxhyphen{}double at 4\sphinxhyphen{}away/2\sphinxhyphen{}away; a player who has learnt the money answer has learnt one cell of a grid. The Eval panel shows the cell the position carries; the \sphinxstylestrong{cube matrix} shows the whole grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cm}} command opens it on the position on screen. Each cell gives the verdict at one score: the row is the number of points the player on roll still needs, the column the number the opponent still needs. The four verdicts read \sphinxstyleemphasis{ND} (no double), \sphinxstyleemphasis{DT} (double, take), \sphinxstyleemphasis{DP} (double, pass) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{TG} (too good); a cell the engine refuses carries a question mark and says why on hover, which also gives the cell’s three equities. Three match lengths are offered: 5, 7 and 9 points.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cell of the score the position actually carries is framed, and its row and column headers underlined: reading starts there, “my cell, and what surrounds it”. It is framed as soon as both of the position’s \sphinxstyleemphasis{away} scores fit in the displayed grid; changing the length moves the frame or removes it. A money position, the Crawford game, or an \sphinxstyleemphasis{away} beyond the grid designate none: there is no cell to show, and showing an approaching one would be false.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The position’s own score is replaced by each cell’s; its \sphinxstylestrong{cube} is kept. The grid answers “at what score would I turn \sphinxstyleemphasis{this} cube”, not what a centred position would do. It is post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford throughout: during the Crawford game the cube is not in play, and a column of “you may not double” would say nothing about the position.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every cell is its own search. The engine is match\sphinxhyphen{}aware — it does not play the same game at 2\sphinxhyphen{}away as at 7\sphinxhyphen{}away — so a single search read through different match equities would be wrong exactly where the score matters. The grid arrives at 0\sphinxhyphen{}ply first, then recomputes at the configured display depth once the window is at rest: the same escalation as the rest of the panel, for a 9\sphinxhyphen{}point grid costing about a second and a half.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The same grid is computed outside the interface, with the command line’s {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_analyse:cli-cubematrix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{cubematrix}}}}} command.


\subsubsection{Reference data panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-donnees-de-reference}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-reference}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Reference data} panel gathers the score tables. It opens with \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}SHIFT\sphinxhyphen{}R} or the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ref}} command, with no database open. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{met}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tp2}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tp4}} commands and their \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_live}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_last}} variants, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gv1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gv2}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gv4}} open it on the tab of the requested table (MET, Take points or Gammon values; the variants of one family open the same tab). Rows and columns are the points needed to win the match: the row is the player in question, the column is their opponent. Five tabs:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{MET} — the Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2 match equity table, from 1 to 15 points away, as a percentage chance of winning the match;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Take points} — at cube 2 (from 2 to 9 points away) and cube 4 (from 3 to 9), each in two side\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}side grids: long race (live cube) and last roll (dead cube);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Gammon values} — at cubes 1, 2 and 4;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Aggregated} — a grid from 2 to 9 points away with a legend at the top recalling how each cell is organised. Each cell has three lines: the take point at cube 2 (live / dead), at cube 4 (live / dead), then the gammon values at cubes 1, 2 and 4, in a muted colour. A dash marks a value that the table does not define at that score;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Neil’s numbers} — a mental shortcut for the MET, due to Neil Kazaross.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Neil’s numbers.} The leader’s equity is estimated by E ≃ 50\% + (score difference) × Neil(\sphinxstyleemphasis{n}), where \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} is the number of points the \sphinxstylestrong{trailer} needs. The tab gives the number for each \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} from 3 to 25, as an exact whole number and fraction (6½ at 7, 5⅔ at 9, 5⅓ at 10, 4¾ at 12; with no fraction glyph, “3 5⁄12”): the anchor points (10 at 3 away, 9 at 4, 8 at 5, 7 at 6, 6 at 8, 5 at 11, 4 at 15, 3½ at 19 and 3 at 25) are in upright type, the values in between, obtained by linear interpolation between two anchors, in italics. For example, at 3 away against 5 away, the estimate is 50 + 2 × 8 = 66\%, and the MET gives 64.8\%. The tab shows the row of numbers, then a leader × trailer grid, from 2 to 15 points away: each cell gives the estimate and, in small type, its difference from the Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2 MET, to show where the shortcut deviates. The shortcut does not hold when the leader is at 1 or 2 away: the row of the leader at 2 away shows the MET value, in a muted colour and with no difference.


\subsubsection{Bringing a position into the Eval panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:amener-une-position-dans-le-panneau-eval}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:eval-amener-position}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The panel opens by default on a bearoff position, but a study most often starts from a position already at hand. Four gestures bring it there:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Right click on the board}, in an analysis panel or while navigating a match, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{Evaluate this position}: the Eval panel opens directly on that position, as displayed; \sphinxstyleemphasis{Evaluate the mirror of this position} opens it there seen from the other side. The context menu does not appear in the Eval panel or in the Search panel, where the right button already serves to place checkers of the other colour.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Right\sphinxhyphen{}click on the board, then} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Evaluate in a new tab}: a new view, named \sphinxstyleemphasis{Variant of \#n} (n being the number of the original view), opens in the Eval panel on the displayed position, where variants can be set up freely. The original view keeps its position, its list and its analysis. This choice is not offered in the Transcription panel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}C then CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}V}: copy the position from the analysis panel, then paste it once in the Eval panel. Pasting also accepts an identifier from elsewhere — an XGID (eXtreme Gammon, GNU Backgammon, another blunderDB instance), an OGID (OpenGammon) or a GNUbg ID (GNU Backgammon): it only has to be on the clipboard.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The command} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import XGID=…}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import OGID=…}}) for when the identifier is not in the clipboard but in a message, on a forum read in a terminal, or produced by a script. It is the same verb as plain \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import}}: with no argument it opens a file picker, with one it reads the identifier. The path is then identical to pasting — same reading, same deduplication, same opening of the imported position.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An OGID carries a position and nothing else: no evaluation, no comment. The position therefore arrives without an analysis, exactly like a bare XGID, and the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator can fill the gap afterwards.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A GNUbg ID is pasted in the form GNU Backgammon copies: the position ID and the match ID joined by a colon (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4HPwATDgc/ABMA:cIkFAAAAAAAE}}), or the two lines \sphinxstyleemphasis{Position ID} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Match ID}. The position ID alone states neither the player on roll, nor the dice, nor the score: the position then arrives with the bottom player on roll, no dice, at money play, cube centred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In an OGID, the Crawford game is read from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} that follows the match length (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{7C}}): without it, a player one point from the goal is past the Crawford game.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A screenshot of the board} (eXtreme Gammon, default theme) can be read three ways: paste the image (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}V}), drag it onto the window, or open it with \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}I} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.png}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.jpg}}). No database is needed. The position read lands on the edit board and is only a proposal: the points and the cube the reading is unsure of are ringed in orange; a doubt that cannot be ringed (the board’s direction when the point numbers are outside the image, unreadable dice) and what a screenshot never shows (the score, the side to move when the dice are hidden) are named in the status bar. Correct the board as usual, then save with the usual gesture: nothing is saved before. An image in which no known board is recognised is refused, with the reason in the status bar. The same reading exists on the command line (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{capture}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Eval panel’s board is a draft: the position arrives there without its database identifier, so that no change made here can rewrite the record it came from. All the usual board edits remain available there (checkers, cube, dice, score), and the evaluation follows every change.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the other direction, \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}C} copies the Eval panel’s board to the clipboard, with an XGID recomputed from the checkers on the board — hence pasteable directly into eXtreme Gammon or into another instance of blunderDB. Only the position travels: the evaluation shown by the panel is not a database record and does not accompany the copy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On leaving the Eval panel, the position previously viewed is restored: the draft is never saved on its own.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the position is a pure bearoff (all checkers of both players in their home board) and no dice are showing, the cube decision shows, for the player on roll:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{exact} regime: the money equities (cubeless, no double, double/take, double/pass) and the \sphinxstylestrong{money cube verdict} (no double, double/take, double/pass or too good to double) — outside a match score, see above for the case of the score,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{evaluated} regime: the same equities and the same four\sphinxhyphen{}valued verdict, but \sphinxstylestrong{played out by gammonNet} (search + Janowski cube model) rather than read from a table — available \sphinxstylestrong{even at a match score}, which the estimated regime could never offer;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{estimated} regime: the cube verdict is then deliberately not shown — only the winning probability, in the facts table, along with its error margin, remains available.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As soon as dice are showing on a race position, this \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} cube decision disappears — the board then calls for a checker decision, not a cube one — but the winning probability, for its part, remains a fact of the position, not a decision: it joins the \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} row at the head of the move list, next to the EPC which, for its part, stays displayed just to the left.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A badge indicates the regime: \sphinxstylestrong{exact} (value read from a two\sphinxhyphen{}sided database), \sphinxstylestrong{evaluated · <depth>} (played out by gammonNet — the depth shown is the one that actually produced the figure shown), \sphinxstylestrong{estimated ± margin}, or, at a match score within the exact domain, \sphinxstylestrong{exact (win) · evaluated (cube)} — see above. The exact regime wins wherever it is available; otherwise the evaluated regime is displayed as soon as it has finished computing, replacing in place the estimated regime shown while waiting. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_eval:epc-methodologie}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel}}}}} for the precise definition of the three regimes and their assumptions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Widening the exact domain.} The table computed on first launch covers 6 chequers a side. Two ways to go further, in the configuration’s \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute a wider two\sphinxhyphen{}sided table — up to TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}15 if the machine has the memory for it. The tab states the size, the memory and the time on this machine before starting, and the computation pauses and resumes. A cancelled computation leaves a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.part}} file which is never read as a table;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
point to any two\sphinxhyphen{}sided gnubg \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.bd}} file. The database with the widest domain automatically wins.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The panel’s board is a scratch board, and it is remembered.} Leaving the Eval panel and coming back finds the position it was left on, not the default bearoff board: that one is only served the first time the panel is opened in a session. Sending a position from the database to the panel wins over that memory, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{BACKSPACE} hands back the default board at any time. Nothing is written to the database along the way — the scratch board has no position identity, and its evaluation is recomputed on arrival rather than carried over.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Challenge mode.} The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Challenge} box, in the header band, enables a training mode: on every change to the position, the values of three zones are masked (replaced by “···”); clicking a zone reveals that zone only. Without dice, these are the bottom player’s row, the top player’s row and the cube decision — the Δ row only appears once both player rows are revealed. The decision block then keeps its three rows: it is its values, its verdict and the highlighting of the best option that disappear, failing which the exercise would be solved by looking for the bold row. With dice showing on a race position, each player’s EPC row is masked as before, but the third zone then covers the \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll} row and the move list \sphinxstylestrong{together}: the list being sorted from best move to worst, revealing it partially would already give the answer away. With dice showing outside a race position, that same single zone alone covers everything the panel displays. One can thus practise estimating each side’s EPC, then deciding on the cube or on the move to play, before checking. The setting is remembered.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:eval-sans-base}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{No database open.} The Eval panel does not need a database: a position can be set up, pasted (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}V}) and edited there, evaluated, rolled out, and copied as text (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}C}) or as an image (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}X}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}X CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}X} with the evaluation). The right\sphinxhyphen{}click menu in the panel also offers \sphinxstyleemphasis{Save the image (SVG)…} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Save the image (PNG)…}. The board of the Search tab is a scratch board too: it can be edited and receives a paste without a database, and one moves from one to the other without losing anything; running the search, however, requires a database. Only \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add to database} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}S} require a database in the panel, and the status bar says so. No database is created behind the scenes. In the Eval panel as in the Search tab, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import XGID=…}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import OGID=…}}) command places the position on the scratch board, without a database. The \sphinxstylestrong{Training} tab also opens without a database: \sphinxstyleemphasis{Scores}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Checkers}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Evaluation} are available, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decision} is disabled with the reason shown, and the finished session is not recorded (the journal says so). Tournament Direction requires an open database.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To close the Eval panel, press \sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}E} or switch to another tab.


\subsubsection{Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:methodologie-et-hypotheses-du-panneau-eval}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_eval:epc-methodologie}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every value displayed by the panel rests on precise assumptions, stated here exhaustively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Domain.} The \sphinxstyleemphasis{race zone} — winning probability and cube verdict — covers pure bearoffs only: every remaining chequer of both players in their home board. The position is evaluated \sphinxstyleemphasis{before the roll}; any dice set on it are ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{EPC blocks}, on the other hand, go further: a side gets its EPC as soon as its farthest chequer fits in the loaded one\sphinxhyphen{}sided table. With the default table (six points) that is the old home\sphinxhyphen{}board rule; with an eight\sphinxhyphen{}point table, computed from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab, a side with a chequer on the 8\sphinxhyphen{}point is treated like any other. Nothing is extrapolated: a chequer one point too far simply has no EPC, exactly as a chequer on the 7\sphinxhyphen{}point had none before. When the table that answered is not the six\sphinxhyphen{}point one, its name appears in the corner of the race block (“OS\sphinxhyphen{}08”) — without it one would read “six” by default and believe the side entirely home.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{EPC blocks (always exact).} The EPC, the average number of rolls and the standard deviation come from the exact distribution of the number of rolls needed to bear every chequer off, read from GNUbg’s one\sphinxhyphen{}sided database (6 to 10 points, 15 chequers, computed on the machine). EPC = average rolls × 49/6 (49/6 ≈ 8.167 is the exact average of pips per roll, doubles counted four times); wastage = EPC − pip count. The only idealisation is \sphinxstyleemphasis{one\sphinxhyphen{}sided optimal play}: each player minimises their own rolls, ignoring the opponent — that is the standard definition of the EPC.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Winning probability, exact regime.} Direct lookup in the widest available two\sphinxhyphen{}sided database (TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}06 computed on first launch, an external file, or TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}11 computed from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab). These databases result from a complete retrograde analysis under optimal two\sphinxhyphen{}sided play by both sides: no additional assumption, error limited to quantisation (< 0.002\%).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Winning probability, estimated regime.} Outside the database’s domain: the probability is obtained by convolving the two one\sphinxhyphen{}sided distributions (the player on roll wins if their number of rolls is less than or equal to the opponent’s), then applying a frozen polynomial correction, calibrated offline against the TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}11 database. Three assumptions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{independence} of the two bearoff processes — structural in a race, with no contact there is no interaction whatsoever;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{optimal one\sphinxhyphen{}sided play by both sides} — this is \sphinxstyleemphasis{the approximation}: in reality the trailing player deviates to play for variance and the leader for safety. The measured effect is an antisymmetric bias (the convolution overstates the leader’s advantage) which the correction absorbs statistically;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{correction} was calibrated and validated on the oracle’s domain (up to 11 checkers per player). Measured residual error: standard deviation 0.05\%, 99th percentile 0.17\%, observed maximum 0.9\% (in winning\sphinxhyphen{}probability points). \sphinxstylestrong{Beyond 11 checkers per player, this bound is extrapolated} — the trend is monotonic but no oracle certifies it.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equities and cube verdict (exact regime only).} The displayed equities are those of the \sphinxstylestrong{money game, without Jacoby}, the reference framework of the bearoff literature. Within the ≤ 11 checkers per player domain, gammons are impossible (each side has already borne off at least 4 checkers): this is not an approximation. The verdict (no double / double, take / double, pass) is reconstructed exactly from the stored equities, following GNUbg’s rule, validated verdict for verdict against its analysis.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The cubeful equities assume \sphinxstylestrong{optimal cube play by both sides all the way to the end}: future recubes are fully valued (complete retrograde analysis). In the very volatile races at the end of the game, the cascade of recubes eats up almost all of the advantage of the side on roll — the “no double” and “double/take” equities can then be close to zero where an engine such as XG, whose cube model does not value this cascade, shows values close to the dead cube (for instance 2 checkers on the 3 point against 2 checkers on the 2 point: 62\% winning chances, exact D/T +0.006 versus +0.475 for XG). The displayed \sphinxstylestrong{decision}, however, coincides with the engines’.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Winning probability and verdict, evaluated regime.} Outside the exact domain, the winning probability comes from gammonNet’s raw output (0\sphinxhyphen{}ply search, then at the configured depth, never read from a table), and the verdict from a Janowski “Decide” applied to that output — the search \sphinxstyleemphasis{plays out} the trajectory instead of summarising a snapshot of it, which is precisely what the estimated regime could not do (see below) and allows, alone among the three regimes together with the exact one, a verdict \sphinxstylestrong{at the match score}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This regime was measured, not merely assumed, against the built\sphinxhyphen{}in two\sphinxhyphen{}sided table (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TestEvalMeasure}}, 4000 sampled money decisions, canonical parameters 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply k=12): money verdict agreement \sphinxstylestrong{93.4\%} (3735/4000), broken down by distance to gammonNet’s take point — 61.1\% within 1\% of the take point (the zone most sensitive to a coin toss), 88.3\% between 1 and 5\%, 91.5\% between 5 and 10\%, 94.0\% between 10 and 20\%, 94.4\% beyond. Winning\sphinxhyphen{}probability gap: mean 0.85\%, median 0.44\%, 95th percentile 3.21\%, maximum 8.30\%. Cubeful\sphinxhyphen{}equity gap: mean 0.039, median 0.018, 95th percentile 0.151, maximum 0.406. The shape is the expected one: most of the disagreement concentrates exactly at the take point, where two legitimately different methods diverge most on a close decision — not a diffuse error that would cost equity everywhere.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This measurement covers \sphinxstylestrong{money} decisions, in a race. The match\sphinxhyphen{}score verdict — which only this regime can render — and contact positions have no published measurement: none of the above carries over to those cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why not deeper than 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply?} Because the measurement says it buys nothing. A checker decision at 3\sphinxhyphen{}ply evaluates the network \sphinxstylestrong{14 times more} than at 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply (159,000 evaluations against 11,400, averaged over twenty real decisions) and takes about 14 times longer (3.9 s against 0.27 s on a single core of the same machine). Over forty real decisions replayed at both depths, the deeper search changed its mind \sphinxstylestrong{twice}, and both times the gain it claimed for itself was at most 0.0002 normalised equity: two orders of magnitude below 0.020, the threshold at which eXtreme Gammon calls a decision an error at all. Per decision, all cases together, the gain is 0.0000.

\sphinxAtStartPar
2\sphinxhyphen{}ply therefore remains the default; 3\sphinxhyphen{} and 4\sphinxhyphen{}ply are chosen in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gammonNet} tab of the settings. At 3 and 4 ply, as in GNUbg, only the root compares several plays: at every interior node, the reply kept is the best one at 0\sphinxhyphen{}ply, and it alone is searched deeper. This does not say 3\sphinxhyphen{}ply is worthless in general, only that on \sphinxstyleemphasis{this} network, with this filter, it does not pay for the wait of someone sitting in front of a panel. The measurement is reproducible (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TestThreePlyMeasure}}) and the conclusion will be re\sphinxhyphen{}judged if the network changes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why is there no estimated verdict?} What follows targets specifically the \sphinxstyleemphasis{convolution} method (estimated regime), not the evaluated regime above: cubeful equity is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{trajectory} problem (when to double) that no statistical summary of the position captures — the best static model measured leaves a residual error (standard deviation 0.016 of equity, maximum 0.20) large enough to flip every close decision. Likewise, converting the verdict to the match score through a match\sphinxhyphen{}equity table was measured to be insufficient (12\% of disagreements with GNUbg’s 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply analysis, including genuine blunders). Since a wrong verdict displayed with confidence is worse than no verdict, the convolution was never allowed to display a verdict — it is a search that plays out the trajectory, not a statistical summary, that fills this hole.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The bearoff databases are immutable mathematical tables. blunderDB computes them itself, identically to GNUbg’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{makebearoff}} tool — byte for byte — in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab of the configuration or with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb bearoff generate}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Training, Anki and duel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:entrainement-anki-et-duel}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:manuel-entrainement}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement::doc}}

\subsection{Anki Panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-anki}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Anki} panel (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}K}) allows studying positions with spaced repetition using the FSRS algorithm. Users can create decks from collections or search results.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Creating decks:} Click \sphinxstylestrong{+ New deck} to create a deck from a collection or the current search results. Search\sphinxhyphen{}based decks sync automatically when the Anki tab is activated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A deck of score sheets.} The third source, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Score sheets}, asks for nothing but a name: blunderDB fills the deck with the 36 unordered scores from 2 to 9 away, and the card of a score is the sheet the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-entrainement}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Scores exercise}}}}} displays — take points and gammon values, both faces. That deck exists only if you create it: 36 cards due on the first day are a review debt, and it is contracted on purpose. The sync button regenerates it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two places do not do the same work. The Scores exercise makes you retrieve those numbers \sphinxstylestrong{against the clock} and measures the speed; the deck makes them \sphinxstylestrong{last over time} and measures none of it. The two histories stay apart: the Training journal ignores Anki reviews, and Anki’s statistics ignore Training sessions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A selected deck takes over the panel header}: its name, the number of its positions, which a click opens, and the number of due cards; on the right, the settings (⚙), the reset (↻), \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cram} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Study}. ← returns to the deck list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Export to Anki:} the ⤓ button of a row of the list writes the deck as an \sphinxstylestrong{.apkg} file, which the Anki application imports on a computer or a phone (AnkiDroid, AnkiMobile). Each position becomes a two\sphinxhyphen{}sided card: on the front the board, the score as seen by the player on roll (placed at the bottom), the cube and the dice; on the back the best move or right cube decision, its equity and the played move’s error. The labels follow the interface language. The deck is exported as it stands, without a sync, and the export writes nothing to the database. Re\sphinxhyphen{}importing a later export into Anki updates the cards instead of duplicating them. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb anki export}}, which also exports a collection (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reviewing:} Select a deck then click \sphinxstyleemphasis{Study} (or double\sphinxhyphen{}click a deck) to start reviewing due cards. A position card shows the position on the board; a score card announces the score and leaves the board as it is. Rate your recall with keys \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} (Again), \sphinxstyleemphasis{2} (Hard), \sphinxstyleemphasis{3} (Good), or \sphinxstyleemphasis{4} (Easy). Press \sphinxstyleemphasis{Esc} to stop and return to the deck list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Undoing a rating.} The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Undo} button, under the rating buttons, or the \sphinxstyleemphasis{u} key, takes back the session’s last rating: the card gets back exactly the state it had before (due date, interval, stability, difficulty, number of reviews and lapses), the rating leaves the review log, and the card returns to the screen to be rated again. Repeated, it works back through the session rating by rating. When the session ends, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Undo} stays in the deck strip until the next session: the last rating can be taken back too, and the review resumes on that card. Nothing forces you to reveal the answer in order to rate: if you are sure of yourself, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{4} keys stay active. A position without a recorded analysis says so directly, with no masked area.

The proposed grade is highlighted; you stay in control and grade what you want with \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{4}. A legal move the analysis does not rank proposes nothing. Cube cards, score cards and decks of score sheets stay self\sphinxhyphen{}graded. Revealing the answer without playing gives up the move.

\sphinxstylestrong{Limiting the session.} By default a review session runs through every card that is due. When the limit is reached the session stops and says so — the message tells “limit reached, so many cards still due” apart from a queue that is genuinely empty. \sphinxAtStartPar
A limit of \sphinxstylestrong{0} serves no card at all: it is a state in its own right, useful to freeze a deck while preparing for a tournament, and it is not the same thing as “no limit”. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Study} button is then disabled.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The limit applies to the \sphinxstylestrong{session}, not to the day. A daily cap would never bite, or else would build a backlog on a deck that fitted in a single session.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Free drill (cram):} The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cram} button, next to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Study}, starts a free\sphinxhyphen{}drill session: random positions from the deck are shown to you regardless of the FSRS schedule. A \sphinxstyleemphasis{Free} badge replaces the card state and a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Next} button (keys \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{4}) cycles through the positions. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Esc} returns to the list without saving an interrupted session.

\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Suspend} — the card keeps its schedule and never comes up again while suspended. It is how a card that is wrong, or not useful yet, is set aside without losing the history attached to it.

\item {}

\item {}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Review log.} In a deck’s Settings, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Review log} button shows what the scheduler was \sphinxstylestrong{told} — date, position, grade, state, granted interval — as opposed to what it plans. It cannot be corrected there: the schedule stays out of reach, and that rule is precisely what makes the log useful — the past cannot be rewritten, but it can be known.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pause/Resume:} You can interrupt a review session at any time with \sphinxstyleemphasis{Esc}. The button changes to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Resume} and shows your progress. Click it to pick up where you left off.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Deck management:} Use the action buttons to rename, synchronise, reset or delete decks (a confirmation is asked for the last two). The FSRS parameters (target retention, maximum interval, fuzz) can be set per deck in the Settings (gear icon).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Retention: the target and the measurement.} The \sphinxstyleemphasis{target retention} is your own choice on the trade\sphinxhyphen{}off between workload and quality of recall: the higher it is, the shorter the intervals and the more you review. \sphinxAtStartPar
Changing the retention \sphinxstylestrong{is not retroactive}: each card takes up the new pace at its next review, and the due dates already set do not move. The effect is therefore gradual, and invisible on the day itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{maximum interval} bounds the spacing. A recently created deck starts at one year: a position the algorithm would push back by several years has left the deck without you deciding so, and your own game changes faster than that. Older decks keep the value they had.

\subsubsection{The six exercises}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:les-six-exercices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Scores} draws one of the 36 unordered scores from 2 to 9 away and shows a \sphinxstylestrong{score card}: two columns — \sphinxstyleemphasis{Vous} (you) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{L’adversaire} (the opponent) — and seven rows — the take point at cube 2 then at cube 4, each for a long race and for the last roll, then the gammon value at cubes 1, 2 and 4.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Each column carries only the cells the reference tables — those of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-reference}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Reference data panel}}}}} — define for its face: three numbers at 2a\sphinxhyphen{}2a, fourteen at most, and a single column at a level score. A row neither face defines does not appear on the card — so there is no “n/a” cell to guess. Both faces are there because a cube decision at a score needs both: the corrected take point combines both players’ gammon values, and it is the opponent’s take point that says whether your double passes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pip count} asks for the pip count of \sphinxstylestrong{both} sides. It is a mask and not a setting: your own choice is not changed, and it takes over again at the next question. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Board} source asks one question about the position shown, and only one; the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Database} source draws a new position for every question and brings it onto the board.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bearoff} asks for the \sphinxstylestrong{EPC of both sides} — the effective pip count, the one that adds to the pip count the wastage of the chequers that come off with pips to spare. \sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
The exercise’s domain: \sphinxstylestrong{both sides entirely in their home board}, \sphinxstylestrong{4 to 15 chequers} a side and the rest borne off, cube centred, money play. A seed that does not fit is \sphinxstylestrong{refused by name}, and nothing starts — no silent adaptation: playing on until contact breaks would hand you a position you did not choose. An empty board is the exception: the question then comes from the pool, and the panel says why.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The exercise needs the one\sphinxhyphen{}sided bear\sphinxhyphen{}off table; while it is still being generated in the background (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_interface:configuration}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Configuration}}}}}), it says so rather than asking a question with no answer.

\sphinxstylestrong{Évaluation} asks what a position is worth: the \sphinxstylestrong{win chance of the player on roll}, as a percentage, and the \sphinxstylestrong{cube action} — \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pas de double}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Double, prend} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Double, passe}. These are the two numbers the Eval panel shows, asked before they are shown. The domain is \sphinxstylestrong{any position}: a race as well as a contact position, in \sphinxstylestrong{money play}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As for Bearoff, the question is \sphinxstylestrong{generated}: the seed comes from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Vivier} (a position where contact has just broken, then zero to ten plies played by the engine), from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Plateau} (the position displayed, then one to four plies; the question is asked in money play with the cube centred, whatever the seed’s score) or from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Base} (a position of the browsed list, as it is). A library position qualifies only if it is a money\sphinxhyphen{}play cube decision — no dice, the cube centred or held by the player on roll —; otherwise the draw moves on to the next one, and when none qualifies, the exercise says so. Scores are drawn by \sphinxstylestrong{category} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Money}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DMP}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Gammon save}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Gammon go}), because from 4\sphinxhyphen{}away to 7\sphinxhyphen{}away the best plays barely change from one score to the next, whereas these four situations play differently. While an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Évaluation}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Décision} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ouverture} question awaits its answer, the Analysis panel is masked: it carries the answer.

\subsubsection{The journal and the summary}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:le-journal-et-le-bilan}}

Finished sessions are kept in the database itself — so they travel with the file — and without any cap. At rest, the panel shows one line per exercise: the number of sessions, the fault rate, the median time and, from ten sessions on, the \sphinxstylestrong{trend}, that is the gap between the fault rate of the last ten sessions and that of all of them — negative, you are improving.

A training PR of 6 and a match PR of 6 measure the same thing on the same scale.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Clicking the exercise’s name unfolds the detail \sphinxstylestrong{by number type}: « Point de prise 4 · dernier lancer, 6 / 9 ». That detail is what makes the journal worth keeping, and it counts by type and not by face: the same cell of the same table, seen from either side, is one single weakness.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decision} question keeps in the log its position, the answer given and its cost in millipoints. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decision} detail therefore carries three buttons that act on all the missed positions, each once, most recently missed first — a question that timed out counts as missed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Retake my misses} — the missed positions become the list browsed and a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Decision} session restarts on them;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Anki deck of misses} — an Anki deck of these positions;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Collection of misses} — a collection of these positions.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The deck and the collection are named “Decision misses” followed by today’s date. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{training missed}} returns the same list and makes a deck (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}deck}}) or a collection (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}collection}}) of it, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{training sessions}} reads the log back (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_entrainement:cli-training}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{training — The training log}}}}}).


\subsection{Duel panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-duel}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:id3}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Duel} panel plays a whole match against the Bot, with blunderDB as Arbiter: it rolls the dice, enforces the rules, and keeps the score and the clocks. It opens with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}H}}, with the “Play” button of the toolbar, or with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duel}} command. A database must be open: the Duel is written to it after each decision.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With no Duel open, the panel shows the form, remembered from one Duel to the next, and, if there are any, the list of suspended Duels. The header band carries the \sphinxstylestrong{Start}, the choices the starting position calls for, the \sphinxstylestrong{time control}, and “Play” at its end:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Start}: the initial position, or the position on the board. Starting from the board, it is edited as in the Eval panel (same scratch board, same gestures): the checkers, the cube and its owner, the dice — placed on a player’s side, they give that player the turn — and the score.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dice} (start from a board carrying dice): “Board dice”, the default, plays the roll as set; “Reroll” has the Referee draw it again.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cube decision} (start from a board with no dice to play, when the player on roll can double or a double is offered on the board): “Before the cube”, the default, begins with that decision — the player on roll doubles or rolls, or the opponent answers the offered double; “After the cube” goes straight to the roll, an offered double then being taken.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Time control}: none, \sphinxstylestrong{Standard} (2 min per point + 12 s), \sphinxstylestrong{Speed} (0.4 min per point, i.e. 2 min for a 5\sphinxhyphen{}point match, + 10 s), or a saved time control.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The form, one setting per line:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Match} of 1 to 25 points, or \sphinxstylestrong{money session} (Jacoby optional).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Score}: what each player still needs, by default the match length (start of a match); “1 (Crawford)” is the Crawford game, “1 (post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford)” a game that follows it. Starting from the board, these fields and the board’s score are one and the same: changing one changes the other, and a money board makes a money session. \sphinxstylestrong{Single game} stops the Duel at the end of its first game, to practise a score: the Match written counts only that game.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Time control} (a time control chosen): \sphinxstylestrong{minutes per point} and \sphinxstylestrong{delay} in seconds. Each player has minutes per point × match length (less, from a starting score: the average length left to play); on each turn, the delay runs down first, then the reserve. An exhausted reserve stays at zero, and the elapsed time keeps being noted, or loses the match. A name and “Save” keep the two numbers as a time control of the menu, in the user’s settings; “Delete” removes the saved time control chosen. A money session is played without a time control.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Side played} (player 1 or 2) and \sphinxstylestrong{Bot level} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{instant}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{normal}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thorough}}, those of the analysis). The selector states each level’s depth, for example “instant (0\sphinxhyphen{}ply)” or “normal (2\sphinxhyphen{}ply, pruned)”; deeper plays stronger and slower.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Your name} and \sphinxstylestrong{Record the match}: when unchecked, the finished Duel is discarded instead of becoming a Match.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pipcount}: unchecked, the pipcount stays hidden during the Duel, even through the toolbar button or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}}; it returns when the Duel ends.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
“Resume” reopens a suspended Duel at the same point, with the same upcoming dice; its clocks were stopped.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A suspended Duel does not leave its database: exporting the database does not take it along, because its upcoming dice must leave by no route before the end. A finished Duel travels like any Match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Duel is played on the board. The panel shows the match sheet in two columns, like the Transcription, and the clocks when a time control is running; its header band names the players, says what is expected, and carries on the right “Forfeit match”, “Pause match”, “Cancel match”. A match in points is recorded only whole: no stop keeps an unfinished match. The score and the cube are those of the board; the score and the clocks stay in the status bar when the tab is collapsed. The SHA\sphinxhyphen{}256 fingerprint of the dice seed, published by the Referee at creation, can be read in the tooltip of the header band’s prompt, then with the seed in the origin of the finished Match. The board switches to \sphinxstylestrong{DUEL} mode: the library can no longer be browsed, editing, the Eval panel and the other tabs do not open, except the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_eval:panneau-reference}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Reference data panel}}}}}, and the engine falls silent — no evaluation, no candidate. Only the Pile (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}}), the pipcount (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P}}, unless it is hidden for the Duel) and help remain.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before the roll, a click on the board, on the dice or on a checker rolls them; only a click on the cube offers to double, and the board asks “Double” or “Cancel”. When the cube is not available, the roll is automatic.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Facing a double from the Bot, the board asks “Take” or “Pass”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A click on a checker plays it at once with the left die that is still free, or with the other one when the left die cannot play it; a checker on the bar enters, a double is played in four clicks. A checker can also be dragged to its destination. Only the steps of a legal move go through.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A die greys out when it is played; on a double, each die stands for two steps and is half veiled after the first. A complete move greys out every die, including those the rules do not allow to be played.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As long as the move is not complete, a click on the dice swaps the dice still to be played. A right\sphinxhyphen{}click on the board takes back all the checkers played (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BACKSPACE}} too); with no checker played, it opens the Duel menu.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The complete move is validated by a click on the dice, by “Validate” on the board, or by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ENTER}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SPACE}}. Nothing can be taken back afterwards.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Bot answers immediately; its moves are replayed on the board, slowly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A right\sphinxhyphen{}click outside the board, or on the board outside its move or with no checker played, opens the Duel menu: put the position on the Pile or take it off, resign the game for a single game, a gammon or a backgammon (on one’s turn, after confirmation), forfeit the match, pause it, cancel it. This menu offers neither evaluation nor editing.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“Forfeit match” gives the whole match up, at any moment and after confirmation: the game in progress goes to the opponent for the points that bring them to the length, and the Match is written as won by them. In money play, the game in progress is lost as a single game at the cube’s value (Jacoby rule or not) and the session ends. Under a time control that loses the match, a reserve that runs out counts as that player forfeiting the match.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“Pause match” puts the Duel on hold, clocks stopped; it resumes where it stopped. “Cancel match” discards it, after confirmation: nothing of it is written.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A double\sphinxhyphen{}click outside the board puts the position on the Pile, or takes it off, like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}}; only the bookmark in the corner of the board shows it.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each decision carries its duration, with or without a time control. A resignation has no duration recorded in the Match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the end, the Match is written, its analysis starts and the Matches tab opens on it. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb duel}} drives the same Duel (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli_matchs:cli-duel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{duel — Play a Duel}}}}}).
