\section{Import, origin and sharing}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-origine-et-partage}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:manuel-partage}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage::doc}}

\subsection{Import: what is written, what never is}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-ce-qui-est-ecrit-ce-qui-ne-l-est-jamais}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-regles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Importing a match, a position or another database adds what is missing; it does not replace what is already there.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A position is never duplicated.} It is its identity — checkers, cube, dice, score — that recognises it, never the file it came from: the same position met in two matches stays a single row.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Importing a database reads back everything an export writes.} Positions, with their analyses and comments, but also matches (games and moves included), tournaments with their Direction and their Encounter, transcription drafts, aliases, collections, lessons and Anki decks: see {\hyperref[\detokenize{guide_utilisateur:guide-fusionner-base}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Merge a database}}}}}. Nothing is overwritten: a match already present is not copied again, a tournament of the same name receives the matches without changing the event’s date (its last\sphinxhyphen{}modified date advances, since it receives new matches), a tournament that already has its Direction keeps it and stays outside the imported Encounter, a match already filed in another tournament or another slot of the table stays there, and what the database already decided stays decided by it. The tournaments, Directions, Encounters, transcription drafts and aliases the import creates keep their original dates; the collections, lessons and Anki decks it creates do not.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{One analysis per engine.} eXtreme Gammon, GNUbg, BGBlitz and the embedded evaluator coexist on the same position, and the Analysis panel shows where each one came from. Importing one never erases another.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{An imported analysis is never recomputed.} blunderDB stores it as\sphinxhyphen{}is, with its level label (“3\sphinxhyphen{}ply”, “XG Roller++”, “Book”), its equities, its errors, its probabilities and the luck of the roll. The rule is “an evaluation only fills a hole”: the auto\sphinxhyphen{}analysis after import only visits the positions with \sphinxstylestrong{no} analysis, and the re\sphinxhyphen{}analysis of stale gammonNet analyses leaves untouched any position carrying an imported analysis (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_interface:configuration}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Configuration}}}}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Re\sphinxhyphen{}importing a match already stored only brings what is deeper.} The match is recognised by its play (players, length, dice, moves, cube), not by its analysis: no match, game or move is rewritten. Marks set in the source software are added, and an analysis deeper than the stored one replaces it, position by position — a Roller++ version of the same match replaces the 3\sphinxhyphen{}ply version, whatever the import order; at equal or lower depth, the stored analysis stays. Re\sphinxhyphen{}importing the same file therefore rewrites nothing. The import report tells duplicates that brought nothing from those that deepened analyses. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}skip\sphinxhyphen{}duplicates}} skips a duplicate, taking nothing from it but the marks. A truncated match later completed (more games) is not the same match: it is imported as a second match.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{An unreadable analysis does not stop the match from being imported.} A decision whose analysis holds a value that is not a finite number (NaN or infinity, which some XG files carry) is imported without that analysis; the rest of the match comes in as usual, and the import report counts the decisions concerned.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A match already present under other names is reported, never merged.} The two match fingerprints carry the player names: “Martin A.” and “Alice Martin” make two matches. The import also compares the dice (length, initial score, dice of each game) and reports, under the file’s line and in the report, the match already in the database under other names whose dice it has. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb repair \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}duplicates}} lists these pairs in an existing database, along with truncated matches and their longer version.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A name known under another spelling is recorded under its canonical name.} An \sphinxstyleemphasis{alias} says that “Martin A.” is another spelling of “Alice Martin” (or that one event name is another spelling of a different one). On import, the player and event names are replaced by their canonical name, and the match is filed in the tournament of the canonical event. The match’s fingerprints keep the names of the file: a file imported before its alias existed is therefore still recognised. A match whose dice are those of a match in the database, and whose names differ only by known aliases, is not a second match: its analyses enrich the one that is stored.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Aliases are managed in the \sphinxstylestrong{Corpus} tab of the settings: choose \sphinxstylestrong{Players} or \sphinxstylestrong{Events}, enter the alias and the canonical name, or remove an alias from the list. \sphinxstylestrong{Suggest} lists the names that differ only by case, accents, punctuation or word order; nothing is applied without a click on \sphinxstylestrong{Apply}. The same tab holds the \sphinxstylestrong{Skip duplicates on import} checkbox (the equivalent of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}skip\sphinxhyphen{}duplicates}}, for the session) and the search for the \sphinxstylestrong{probable duplicates} of an existing database, that of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb repair \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}duplicates}}: each pair is given by its match numbers, nothing is merged. Under a pair with the same dice, \sphinxstylestrong{Create these aliases} records in one click the player aliases that would make the two matches name the same players, the spelling of the most recent match becoming the alias: a single proposal when a name is common to both, otherwise two — seat for seat, then crossed — from which one chooses the one that says who is who. On the command line: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb players alias}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb events alias}}.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A folder is imported in parallel.} Files are read on several cores at once and written in groups, always in folder order: match numbers do not depend on the machine. A file identical, byte for byte, to a file already read from the same folder is not read again: it counts as a duplicate. Cancelling stops the import at the current group; what was already written stays.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Progress reads in positions per second.} The import window gives the percentage read, the throughput, the estimated time left and the running counts (imported, duplicates, failed). \sphinxstylestrong{Minimize} tucks it into the status bar, where a chip reopens it: the import goes on while you work, and the window comes back by itself with the report at the end. The first hundred errors are listed; the rest are counted, and the application log names them all. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb import \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}type batch}} shows the same progress on standard error, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}format json}} returns it in the final object (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{progress}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Each file of an import is logged, and an interrupted import can be resumed.} For each file, the batch log keeps the path, the size, the modification date, the SHA\sphinxhyphen{}256 fingerprint and the result: new match (with its number), duplicate (with the match that covers it), enriched match, or error (with the message). A cancelled or cut import continues without redoing what is already decided: a file with the same path, size and date is skipped without being read; a file with the same content is read but not analysed; a file in error is retried. In the application, the end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}import window lists the log (one file per line, with its result and the message of an error; a retried file shows its latest outcome), and a line that produced a match opens it. A \sphinxstylestrong{cancelled} import leaves the window open with the \sphinxstylestrong{Resume} button. On the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb import \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}type batch \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dir <folder> \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}resume <batch>}} resumes the batch whose number was shown when the import started, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}format json}} returns the log in the final object (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{journal}}). The server accepts \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{resume}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{imports.batch}} request and returns the log through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{imports.files}}. The log is data of the import: opening or reading a database writes nothing to it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{An import cut short by the application stopping resumes from the window.} The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{:resume}} command lists the imports nothing has finished; pick the one to continue, then point at the folder or files again, as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dir}} does on the command line. The batch’s journal decides what is not read again.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A large folder is imported in bulk mode.} From 200 files on, blunderDB writes with a larger cache and fewer checkpoints. If the database holds no position yet, it goes further: search indexes are rebuilt only at the end, and writes are no longer synced to disk. A power cut during such an import can then damage the database: recreate it and run the import again. A program crash, on the other hand, only leaves missing indexes, which the next opening rebuilds (the log says so).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What blunderDB never writes}: a recomputed luck value — it is read from the source file, or stays unknown — and a rollout it did not run itself: the rollout data held in a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.xg}} file is not opened. Only the rollouts blunderDB produces ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:rollouts}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Rollouts}}}}}) are stored, next to the analysis.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Metadata Panel}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:panneau-metadonnees}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:panneau-metadata}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Metadata} panel (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}M}) displays the general information of the current database: \sphinxstyleemphasis{User}, creation date (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Created}), schema \sphinxstyleemphasis{Version} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Description}. The user, the date and the description are edited in place and saved when leaving the field; the version is read\sphinxhyphen{}only. Also accessible via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{meta}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It also shows the database’s origin \sphinxstylestrong{when there is one} — see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:diffusion-controlee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Handing out a database: origin and password}}}}}. An ordinary database does not show that section.


\subsection{Handing out a database: origin and password}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:diffuser-une-base-origine-et-mot-de-passe}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:diffusion-controlee}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A teacher handing out a database of positions has two mechanisms, independent of each other, both optional and both chosen \sphinxstylestrong{at export time}: marking the file with its origin, and protecting it with a password.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Neither tracks what becomes of the file. blunderDB \sphinxstylestrong{records nothing on the recipient’s side}: opening a marked database is exactly like opening any other, and nothing anywhere logs who opened it, when, or where its contents came from.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Marking a database with its origin}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:marquer-une-base-de-son-origine}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The export window fits on a single screen: a header strip — the number of positions exported, \sphinxstylestrong{Cancel} and \sphinxstylestrong{Export…} — then a grid, one row per family with its count. These counts are exact: they are read from the server at every change of a box, on the same selection as the export, and are what the file will hold. The file is chosen last, after \sphinxstylestrong{Export…}; closing that choice without a name returns to the grid. A progress indicator then overlays for the duration of the write, the window closes by itself and the result appears in the status bar.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nine points deserve attention:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The scope}: from a list — a search, a collection — the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Scope} row chooses between the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Current list} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Whole library}. The current list exports its positions, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Matches} row offers only those in which these positions were played; each ticked match leaves with all its positions. From the library, the scope is the library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Whole library} is the export of the server and of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{export \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}type database}}: all families are ticked from the start, the Anki decks with their review history, and the transcriptions in progress leave with the rest.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Synchronisation}: with \sphinxstyleemphasis{Whole library}, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Synchronisation} row offers \sphinxstyleemphasis{Only what is new since the last export to this folder} and the \sphinxstylestrong{Choose the folder…} button. The file is then no longer asked for: it is written in that folder under a new name, and the counts are those of what is new (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_interface:synchroniser-deux-machines}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Synchronising two machines}}}}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A match leaves with its transcription draft}, under the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Transcriptions} box of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Matches} row, ticked from the start; the matches that a tournament also carries. A draft that has not yet produced a match leaves only with the entire library. A match or transcription linked to a local video carries only the file name, without its folder, which the recipient relocates on their own copy; a web link leaves as is. The file from which a match was imported likewise leaves only by its name.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A match leaves with the aliases of its players and of its event}: the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Aliases} box, ticked from the start, makes the player merge follow, and the recipient reads a merged player as one. An alias that names no one from the exported matches stays with you.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A collection whose positions are not all in the list arrives truncated.} The collection list shows, for each one, the share covered (“12/40”) and flags it in red when it is partial. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{+ their positions} box carries the positions of the ticked collections: those of a hand\sphinxhyphen{}made list, those that the query of a living collection selects. A living collection whose query names rows the file does not hold \sphinxstylestrong{leaves frozen}: it arrives as the list its query selects today, and the list marks it “frozen” in red with a note; ticking \sphinxstyleemphasis{+ their positions} keeps it living.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A tournament always leaves with its matches}: without them, the tournament–match link does not exist and the tournament would arrive empty. Ticking a tournament takes its matches along, even if the matches box is unticked or restricted to others. It also leaves with its Direction — journal, pairs, tables and attachment of the exported matches — and its Encounter leaves as soon as one of its tournaments does; the Direction’s output folder stays with you. The Direction is found again by opening the file, or by importing it into another database.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{An Anki deck leaves with its positions}, as a fresh study copy. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{with my history} box also carries the state of each card and the log of its reviews: a backup, or your decks moved to another machine. It is unticked for a list, ticked for the library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Saved filters} export not content but your own searches, useless in someone else’s database; the box is unticked for a list. A filter that designates a position, a match or a tournament by its number is renumbered for the file; if it designates one that does not leave, it stays with you.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Collections, lessons, transcriptions, Anki decks, aliases and tournaments leave with the creation and addition dates they bear on your side, not with the export date.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{User}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Description} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Creation date} fields describe the \sphinxstylestrong{produced file}; they are prefilled from the source database.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Ticking \sphinxstylestrong{Watermark} reveals two fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Origin} — what this file is and where it comes from, in your own words: “Jean Dupont’s course — 12 March 2026”. This field is \sphinxstylestrong{mandatory}: as long as it is empty, it is outlined in red and the export button stays inactive.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note}, optional — terms of use, a contact address, a request not to pass the file on.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The mark is signed with your issuer identity. It is therefore \sphinxstylestrong{tamper\sphinxhyphen{}evident and unforgeable}: nobody can alter it, nor fabricate one in your name. It is however \sphinxstylestrong{not unremovable} — the distributed file is an ordinary SQLite database, and blunderDB is free software. It prevents nothing: it says where the file came from.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The comments you have written are signed with the same identity: the recipient sees that they come from you, and whether they were altered along the way (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-commentaires}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Comments Panel}}}}}). A comment that already carries another issuer’s signature keeps it. The status bar says, at the end of the export, how many of your comments were signed; an export without a mark signs none.


\subsubsection{Issuer identity}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:identite-d-emetteur}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Marks are signed with your \sphinxstylestrong{issuer identity}, created by itself the first time you mark a file; there is nothing to set up. It belongs to a person rather than to a database: every file you mark carries the same public fingerprint, of the form \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A3F1\sphinxhyphen{}9C24\sphinxhyphen{}7B05\sphinxhyphen{}E1D8}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can give that fingerprint to your recipients so they can check that a file really comes from you. The identity moves from one machine to another as a single file (extension \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.bdbid}}), optionally protected by a passphrase. \sphinxstylestrong{That file lets anyone holding it sign in your name: do not share it.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the preferences (the gear icon in the toolbar), the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Issuer identity} tab shows your name and fingerprint, and offers \sphinxstyleemphasis{Save identity…}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Load identity…} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Regenerate…}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Regenerating revokes nothing.} A watermark embeds the public key that signed it, so it verifies for ever, on its own. If your identity file has leaked, whoever holds it can keep signing under your old fingerprint, and those marks stay valid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
What protects you after a leak is not software: it is publishing your new fingerprint and disowning the old one to your recipients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Regenerating overwrites the current key; blunderDB offers to save it before replacing it.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Protecting a database with a password}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:proteger-une-base-par-un-mot-de-passe}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The password is typed masked, here as when opening a protected file; the eye icon reveals it \sphinxstylestrong{while it is held down}, and masks it again as soon as it is released.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Ticking \sphinxstylestrong{Password} produces a file with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dbx}} extension — even if the name chosen in the save window ends in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}}. To open it, use the usual database opening: the selection window accepts \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dbx}} alike. blunderDB then asks for the password and installs an ordinary database alongside; after that nothing more is asked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dialog offers to \sphinxstylestrong{delete the protected file once opened}: without that you keep the same content under two names. The box is not ticked by default — the protected file is yours to keep if you mean to pass it on — and the deletion only happens after a successful open.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The password protects the file \sphinxstylestrong{in transit}, not the database. It stops a stranger opening a file left in a downloads folder or an attachment forwarded by mistake. It does not protect you from whoever you gave the password to.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The password is checked on \sphinxstylestrong{every} open, including when the file has already been opened on this machine before.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Technically, the database is encrypted with \sphinxstylestrong{AES\sphinxhyphen{}256 in GCM mode}, with the key derived from the password by \sphinxstylestrong{Argon2id} (64 MiB of memory, 3 passes, 4 lanes) and a random salt unique to each file. GCM authenticates the whole payload: a wrong password is detected as such, and so is any tampering with the encrypted file — you never silently end up with a corrupt database.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The protected file’s header stays \sphinxstylestrong{in the clear}: its origin remains readable without the password.


\subsubsection{Reading a file’s origin}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:lire-l-origine-d-un-fichier}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the application, open the file and show the \sphinxstylestrong{Metadata} panel (the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{meta}} command). An \sphinxstylestrong{Origin} section appears at the top of the panel, read\sphinxhyphen{}only, stating what was written, by whom, when, and how the signature checks out:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“\(\checkmark\) marked by you”: the file carries your mark, intact;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“\(\checkmark\) signature verified”: the mark is intact and comes from another key — compare its fingerprint with the one the producer gave you;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“⚠ invalid signature”: the document has been altered or forged.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section does not appear on an ordinary database.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From the command line, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb info \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}db file.db}} shows the origin and the state of the signature, \sphinxstylestrong{without ever writing to the file}. It works on a protected file too, without the password. See \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CLI\_USAGE.md}} for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{export}}’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}watermark}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}password}} options, and for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{identity}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}}.


\subsubsection{Publishing a database for others}
\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:publier-une-base-pour-d-autres}}\label{\detokenize{manuel_partage:partager-une-base}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A marked database is distributed like any other file — email, a personal site, a USB stick. blunderDB \sphinxstylestrong{provides no service}: no repository, no hosted catalogue, no account. That follows directly from its design: nothing is ever recorded on the side of whoever receives a file, so there would be nothing to report to a service even if one existed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
What makes a published database usable by someone else comes down to four fields, all of them already there:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{User} — who built it, under the name you want cited.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Description} — what the database holds, in one sentence that fits in a list: “240 cube decisions at a score, commented, intermediate level”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Origin} (of the watermark) — what this file is and who it was produced for. It is the first thing the recipient reads in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Metadata} panel.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Issuer fingerprint} — publish it beside the file, not inside it: comparing it is how the recipient checks the file comes from you and not from someone who took your name.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A database published without a watermark stays perfectly usable; it is simply anonymous, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Metadata} panel then shows no \sphinxstyleemphasis{Origin} section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To make a database known, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Show and tell} category of the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/discussions}{repository discussions} serves as a directory: it is a list kept by those who publish, not a service blunderDB renders. Announcing one there takes the link, the four fields above and the fingerprint.

\sphinxstepscope

\section{The error and the loss of a decision}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:l-erreur-et-la-perte-d-une-decision}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-erreur}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All measurements start from two quantities per decision.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The error e} is what the decision played cost in equity, compared with the best decision of the imported analysis (XG or gnuBG; blunderDB does not re\sphinxhyphen{}analyse matches for its statistics). It is expressed in \sphinxstylestrong{normalised equity}: ±1 is the current cube, in money play as at a match score (EMG at the score). It is rounded to the thousandth (the millipoint, mpt).
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Checker play: equity of the best candidate minus equity of the move played.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
No double: the “no double” error given by the analysis.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Double: the smaller of the “double, take” and “double, pass” errors — the doubler is judged against the best opposing response.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Take or pass: the gap between the response played and the better of the two.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The error is that of \sphinxstylestrong{the move played in this match}. A position reached in two matches and played differently carries two errors; neither overrides the other. A move played that the analysis does not name among any of its candidates has no error: it is not rated, and it drops out of all counts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The MWC loss ℓ} is the same error expressed in chances of winning the match (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Match Winning Chances}). At the score and at the cube v of the decision:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\ell = e \times \frac{\mathrm{MWC}_{+v} - \mathrm{MWC}_{-v}}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathrm{MWC}_{+v}\) and \(\mathrm{MWC}_{-v}\) are the chances of winning the match if the player wins, or loses, v points at this score. The match equity table (MET) is Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2, extended beyond 25 points by Zadeh’s formula; a post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford score is read as such. A take or pass is converted at the cube \sphinxstylestrong{before} the double, like the doubler and like XG: converted at the doubled cube, a response error would cost twice too much. A money game has no MWC: ℓ does not exist there.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These two quantities are additive. All the metrics below are sums of them, divided by different denominators, or compared with a reference.


\section{PR (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Performance Rating})}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:pr-performance-rating}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-pr}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} What is my level, on the scale everyone knows? PR is the figure of rankings, forums and clubs; it lets you place yourself and compare two matches analysed by XG.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} Over the player’s counted decisions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{PR} = 500 \times \frac{\sum_i e_i}{N_\text{compté}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The factor 500 is XG’s convention: a PR of 5.0 is an average error of 0.010, i.e. 10 mpt per counted decision. PR is an average, without unit; the lower it is, the better you played.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What counts as a decision.} The rules are XG’s, verified match by match against its figures ({\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}):


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxstyletheadfamily \sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%

\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A checker play is \sphinxstylestrong{forced} when the roll offers only one legal move, or when the analysis covers all legal moves (counted by blunderDB’s move generator) and all are worth the same equity to the thousandth: a choice that costs nothing whichever move is played is not a decision. This is XG’s rule for “non\sphinxhyphen{}forced but inconsequential” moves (a decided race ending, a bear\sphinxhyphen{}off where everything is equal). When the legal moves cannot be counted, only a single candidate makes the move forced.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{no double} is counted when the player was close to doubling: their equity without doubling (ND) is positive and exceeds by less than 0.200 the best outcome of the double for the opponent, min(D/T, D/P). Measuring against this minimum rather than against D/T alone keeps a “too good” position as a decision as long as it stays within 0.200 of the pass.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The condition \sphinxstylestrong{ND > 0} rules out positions where the player on roll is behind: they have no double to consider. XG rules them out too, which its manual does not say; the reference matches show it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A cube decision without a cube analysis is never a counted no double.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} The level bands of the Stats panel ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stats Panel}}}}}) are a blunderDB\sphinxhyphen{}specific landmark, not a published standard. A PR is compared first with your own PRs: same analyser, same kind of opponents, same lengths.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty.} The PR of one match is very noisy: the standard error of a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match is of the order of 1.5 PR. blunderDB gives a 95\% interval ({\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-intervalles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{95\% intervals}}}}}) by resampling the games of a match, and the matches of an aggregate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The PR of a tournament.} The tournament list gives the PR of a single player, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{reference player}, on that player’s decisions only: a PR of both seats would mix the errors of all his or her opponents with his or her own. It is the database’s main player, read under all of his or her aliases, as soon as he or she played in the tournament, even on a single match; otherwise, the player of the greatest number of matches, in a tie the one with the greatest number of decisions, then the name that comes first in character order. This fallback often designates the opponent in a one\sphinxhyphen{}match tournament, where both players are tied: designating the main player avoids it ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_tournois:panneau-tournois}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Tournaments Panel}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} The numerator depends on nothing, but the denominator depends on what is counted: the thresholds of 0.001 and 0.200 are arbitrary. You can lower your PR without playing better, by taking a close pass to add decisions to a race, or by choosing in a bear\sphinxhyphen{}off a move that creates one more decision. PR weighs an error at cube 8 like an error at cube 1 (equity is normalised to the cube), and an error at DMP like an error at 0\sphinxhyphen{}0. It inherits the engine’s imperfections, and the opponent who creates difficult positions raises the other’s PR. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-l7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{MWC loss}}}}} and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-difficulte}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{difficulty}}}}} answer these three flaws.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} On an XG file, blunderDB’s PR is XG’s, to the display precision, apart from the deviations explained in {\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}. gnuBG divides the same sum by another number: each move having more than one legal move, and the cube decisions it judges close according to its own window. Its per\sphinxhyphen{}decision rate therefore cannot be compared with XG’s PR, even on the same analysis. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Snowie Error Rate} ({\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}) divides by all the moves of both players: it depends on no counting rule, but is worth about half the PR.


\section{MWC loss per decision and match chart}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:perte-de-mwc-par-decision-et-graphique-du-match}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-perte-mwc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Which decisions cost me this match? PR puts all errors on the same scale; ℓ weighs them at the score where they were made. An error of 0.040 at 4\sphinxhyphen{}4 in a 5\sphinxhyphen{}point match does not cost what it costs at 0\sphinxhyphen{}0 in a 17\sphinxhyphen{}point match. For study, the column and the chart point out the few decisions that decided the match, and the cumulative curve shows where it turned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} ℓ ({\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-erreur}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{The error and the loss of a decision}}}}}) for each decision counted in PR; a player’s loss over the match is Σℓ over these decisions. A decision outside the count (forced move, no double outside the window) has no ℓ: it would have cost nothing anyway, or nearly so.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} A percentage of chances of winning the match: 2.5 means 2.5\% of MWC lost.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} The \sphinxstylestrong{MWC} column of the transcript, the per\sphinxhyphen{}decision bar and each player’s cumulative curve are described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_matchs:panneau-matchs}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Matches Panel}}}}}. A single tall bar is a decision to review; a curve that climbs steadily tells of a match of average errors, not of accidents.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty.} ℓ is exact with respect to the analysis: its uncertainty is that of the analysis itself (depth, rollout or not) and of the MET.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} ℓ depends on the MET: two programs that do not use the same table do not give the same loss. A money game has none, and an analysis computed with a different MET than the database’s stays out of the statistics. An unrated decision carries a dash, never zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} The sum is the MWC loss that XG displays for the match: checker plays, doubles and responses agree on the reference matches to XG’s display precision (deviation bounded to 0.06 percentage points by the test suite), except for the players with the known residual deviations of {\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}, up to 0.45 points. gnuBG does the same conversion, with its own equities: on a match it analysed, its figures differ from XG’s through the analysis, not through the formula.


\section{Match winning chances curve}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:courbe-des-chances-de-gagner-le-match}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-trace-mwc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Where did the match turn, and whose fault was it, the player’s or the dice’s? The cumulated loss tells what each player gave away; the curve tells where the match stood at each decision, and separates what the errors cost from what the dice did.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} For each decision, two values, always from the first player’s point of view. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Before}: his chances of winning the match if the decision is made optimally, read from the analysis: the equity of the best move for a checker play, max(no double, min(double/take, double/pass)) for the player who doubles, min(double/take, double/pass) for the player who responds, seen from the doubler and then flipped. \sphinxstyleemphasis{After}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} minus the loss ℓ of the player who played ({\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-perte-mwc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{MWC loss per decision and match chart}}}}}), or plus ℓ when it is the opponent.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{MWC} = \frac{\mathrm{MWC}_{+v} + \mathrm{MWC}_{-v}}{2}
+ e \times \frac{\mathrm{MWC}_{+v} - \mathrm{MWC}_{-v}}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxstyleemphasis{e} is the normalised equity of the option (±1 = winning or losing the cube), \sphinxstyleemphasis{v} the value of the cube (before the double, for a double and its response) and \(\mathrm{MWC}_{\pm v}\) the chances of the player who decides if he wins or loses \sphinxstyleemphasis{v} points, read from the database’s MET. This is the conversion of ℓ, to which the midpoint is added: the gap between \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} is therefore exactly ℓ, decision by decision.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} A fraction from 0 to 1, displayed as a percentage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} A drop on a decision is an error; a step between two decisions is the dice. A curve that stays high and then falls at once on a decision points to the error that lost the match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty.} That of the analysis and of the MET, as for ℓ; the rounding of the analysis can carry a won position slightly beyond 100\%.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} A decision without analysis has no value, never an estimated one: the curve breaks. An analysed decision without ℓ (outside the count, or a move played that no candidate names) leaves the chances where they were: \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} equals \sphinxstyleemphasis{before}. A money game has no match winning chances: the trace then carries no value, and says so (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{money}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} The formula is the inverse of gnuBG’s conversion between normalised equity and MWC (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mwc2eq}}); on the same position, two programs differ by their analysis and their MET, not by the formula.


\section{MWC loss (7\sphinxhyphen{}pt eq.) L₇ and Elo against the engine}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:perte-mwc-eq-7-pts-l7-et-elo-face-au-moteur}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-l7}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} How much of the match did I lose through my errors, whatever the way of counting decisions, and how do I compare a 5\sphinxhyphen{}point match with an 11\sphinxhyphen{}point one? L₇ divides by no number of decisions: it cannot be manipulated by adding easy decisions, and it weighs each error at what it cost.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} Under perfect play, the chances of winning the match evolve without bias: against a perfect opponent, a player who loses L of MWC over the match keeps q = 0.5 − L chances. The FIBS formula model says that at equal strength the loss grows as the square root of the length N. L is therefore brought back to a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match, the most common tournament length:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}L_7 = L \times \sqrt{7 / N}
\qquad
L_7^\text{agrégat} = \sqrt{7} \times \frac{\sum L}{\sum \sqrt{N}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The aggregate (several matches, one player, one tournament) adds up the losses and the square roots of the lengths before taking the ratio: a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match weighs more than a 1\sphinxhyphen{}point match, and a single match returns its own value. Without a player filter, the two seats of a match each weigh √N, but form a single unit of the interval.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Elo against the engine} inverts the FIBS formula at 7 points:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D = \frac{2000}{\sqrt{7}} \log_{10} \frac{q}{1 - q}, \qquad q = 0{,}5 - L_7\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Linearised, D ≈ −3474 × L / √N. At L₇ ≥ 50\%, q has no finite inverse; from L₇ > 49\%, q is floored at 1\% (D ≥ −1509) and the Elo is displayed “≤”. L₇ itself has no floor. Both rank players in the same order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} L₇: a percentage of MWC. D: Elo points, negative, the expected gap between the player and the engine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} 12.3\%: instead of 50\% chances against the engine, the player had only 37.7\% in a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match. The badge, the detail, the statistics, the tournament and the progression display it ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:perte-mwc-7pts}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{MWC loss (7\sphinxhyphen{}pt eq.)}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty.} 95\% interval by games for a match, by matches for an aggregate ({\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-intervalles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{95\% intervals}}}}}), then the same transformation as the value. A per\sphinxhyphen{}match row of the statistics has none: it is a single unit; the match review carries the by\sphinxhyphen{}games interval.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} The √N model is approximate below 7 points and around the Crawford game. L₇ depends on the MET. A money game has no length, hence no L₇: the screen says so instead of displaying a number. Real players lose more than half a match, because errors made after a swing of luck add up: the Elo then reaches its floor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} For a 7\sphinxhyphen{}point match, L₇ is exactly the MWC loss that XG displays. Neither program brings the loss back to a reference length or converts it to Elo. This Elo measures the gap to the engine, not a FIBS or BMAB rating between human players.


\section{Difficulty, avoidable errors, excess and ratio}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:difficulte-erreurs-evitables-exces-et-ratio}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-difficulte}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Was this error forgivable? The same loss of 2\% is a lapse in an obvious position, and a mistake any good player would make in a position where four moves are within a few thousandths. For study, difficulty sorts the mistakes: avoidable errors (lapse, rule poorly known) are fixed quickly and come first; losses on difficult decisions belong to the long\sphinxhyphen{}term work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} The difficulty d is the loss that a \sphinxstylestrong{reference player} would have suffered on average in the same position, choosing each option i with a probability that is lower the more it costs:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\pi(i) = \frac{e^{-\Delta_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{-\Delta_j/\tau}},
\qquad d = \sum_i \pi(i)\,\Delta_i,
\qquad \tau = 0{,}025\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Δᵢ is the cost of option i relative to the best one, in normalised equity. The options are the analysis candidates for a checker play; no double and double (against the best response) for the player who owns the cube; take and pass for the one receiving the double. d is converted to MWC like ℓ: both are in the same unit, and the option played has cost exactly ℓ.

\sphinxAtStartPar
τ = 0.025 is a strong\sphinxhyphen{}player prior: with two options separated by Δ, d = Δ / (1 + e\textasciicircum{}\{Δ/τ\}) is maximal around Δ ≈ 0.032, between “doubtful” and “error”; a gap of 0.1 costs only 0.002; five candidates spaced 0.01 apart give d ≈ 0.012, the average error of a player with a PR of about 6.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Avoidable error}: the loss reaches the database’s Error threshold and d ≤ ℓ / 10 — with two options, the reference player would not make it one time in ten.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Excess} of a player over a match: Σ(ℓ − d), what they lost beyond the reference (negative when they did better).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ratio}: Σℓ / Σd; 1 means “plays like the reference”, 2 “loses twice as much”. It is not given when Σd < 0.5\% of MWC: on a match that is too easy it measures only noise, the excess remains.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What counts.} The decisions counted in PR whose loss is rated and converted to MWC; elsewhere difficulty is absent, never zero. A forced move or a no\sphinxhyphen{}double outside the PR window therefore has neither loss nor difficulty. Among the counted decisions, no additional threshold sets apart an obvious decision: its difficulty is close to zero on its own.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} d and the excess: a percentage of MWC. The ratio: no unit.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} A loss well above its difficulty is a mistake the position did not excuse; a loss close to its difficulty, a shared mistake. Excess and ratio correct PR for the difficulty of the positions met, hence partly for the opponent’s style ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_matchs:panneau-matchs}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Matches Panel}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty.} Over one match, excess and ratio rest on few decisions and vary a lot: a trend, not a ranking.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} Difficulty depends on a player model and on τ, fixed once: changing them changes all the figures. It knows only the candidates the analysis kept (a few for XG, according to its filters for gnuBG): absent options weigh nothing, and d is then a lower bound. It inherits the analysis error, especially at low depth.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} Neither computes a difficulty. The idea comes from the likelihood indices of chess (Regan); τ is not calibrated on a population of players.


\section{95\% intervals}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:intervalles-a-95}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-intervalles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Does this figure say anything, or is it noise? A PR of 4.2 over one match and a PR of 4.2 over forty matches are not worth the same. The interval avoids building a work plan on a cell that rests on nothing, and reading a rank into an isolated match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} The interval resamples the largest independent unit: the \sphinxstylestrong{games} of a match, the \sphinxstylestrong{matches} of an aggregate (overall PR, phase cells, game plan, label and score, L₇ of an aggregate). Games of the same match share opponent, session and fatigue: resampling them separately in an aggregate would wrongly shrink the interval. Without a player filter, the two seats of a match form a single unit, because they play the same positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} For a ratio R = Σeᵤ / Σnᵤ over G units (eᵤ the sum of errors, nᵤ the number of decisions of the unit), the bootstrap variance is computed, without drawing:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(R) = \frac{G}{G-1} \cdot
\frac{\sum_u (e_u - R\,n_u)^2}{\left(\sum_u n_u\right)^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the interval is R ± 1.96 × √Var, the lower bound never below 0, then the same transformation as the value (× 500 for PR). The L₇ of an aggregate follows the same rule, L in place of e and √N in place of n; that of a match is a sum over its G games, with variance G/(G−1) × Σ(l\_g − l̄)², l\_g the loss of game g. The computation is deterministic: the same database always gives the same interval, on both storage engines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What is required.} At least \sphinxstylestrong{three units} and a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero width. With two, the dispersion rests on a single degree of freedom and the interval would be several times too narrow; units all at the same ratio say that they agree, not that the value is exact. Without an interval, the cell is greyed out, its sample size visible ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stats Panel}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} Two intervals that overlap widely settle nothing. A family whose interval stays above your overall PR is an established weakness.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} The normal approximation is rough on few units, and errors have a skewed distribution (a few big mistakes): with three or four units, the interval is indicative.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} Neither gives an interval.


\section{Match review}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:bilan-du-match}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-bilan-match}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} After a match: what do I review, did I lose because of the dice or the play, and do my errors come from haste or from a gap in knowledge? The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_matchs:bilan-match}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{match review}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Three decisions to review.} Among the player’s errors (database threshold) whose loss is quantified, the three with the greatest \sphinxstylestrong{avoidable part} ℓ − d = ℓ × (1 − d/ℓ), positive: the loss multiplied by how avoidable it is. An unknown difficulty counts zero; on a tie, the larger loss, then match order. An error the reference player would also make is not worth a session.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Luck\sphinxhyphen{}adjusted result}, for a finished match, in MWC points of the player:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A = R - C, \quad R = \text{issue} - \mathrm{MWC}_\text{départ}, \quad
C = \sum \text{chance de ses jets} - \sum \text{chance des jets adverses}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The outcome is 1 for a win, 0 for a loss; the starting MWC is that of the initial score (50\% at 0\sphinxhyphen{}0). Each roll is converted to MWC like a loss, at the score and cube of its position. Under perfect play, the expectation of A is the opponent’s loss minus yours: the review gives the \sphinxstyleemphasis{error gap} alongside for cross\sphinxhyphen{}checking. A > 0 on a lost match: lost by the dice; A < 0: lost by the play. The luck is the one the analyser wrote ({\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}): without luck, no row, and the coverage (rolls measured over rolls played) is displayed, because partial luck biases A. No row either for a money game or an unfinished match.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Hasty and considered errors.} Per player and per type (checker, cube), the threshold is the median of the known durations of their quantified decisions of that type in the match: an error played faster is hasty, the others considered. The median is their own, in this match: it does not depend on the pace, and with no link between speed and error the errors split half and half. A hasty majority calls for discipline; a considered majority, for knowledge.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} A match is a small sample: PR and L₇ carry their by\sphinxhyphen{}games interval there (three games at least). The adjusted result depends on the MET and on the luck in the file. Duration exists only for a match that kept it (a match played against a bot).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} XG and gnuBG display each player’s total luck, but neither an MWC\sphinxhyphen{}adjusted result, nor a selection of decisions to review, nor a split by duration.


\section{Study plan}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:plan-d-etude}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-plan-etude}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} What should I work on now? Ranking one’s errors by cost says where one lost the most, not where study pays the most: a family of really difficult positions costs everyone, and three errors do not make a trend. The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:plan-etude}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Study plan}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} A \sphinxstylestrong{family} is a triplet (game plan, nature of the decision, theme) of recurring errors; its members are the errors of the filter, counted decisions that cost at least the Error threshold. An error without a theme enters no family. A member is \sphinxstylestrong{quantified} if it carries ℓ and d; an error in a money game is counted “unquantified” and enters no priority.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} The \sphinxstylestrong{recoverable MWC} and its interval:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R = \sum_i (\ell_i - d_i), \qquad
R \pm 1{,}96 \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_i (\ell_i - d_i)^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
R is the family’s frequency multiplied by its average loss beyond difficulty: what one would regain by playing these positions like the reference player. The sum is signed, without clipping. The interval treats the number of members as a Poisson count.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What enters the plan.} At least \sphinxstylestrong{5 quantified members} and a \sphinxstylestrong{strictly positive lower bound}. The plan is ranked by decreasing lower bound: at equal recoverable, the better\sphinxhyphen{}established family comes first. The others are “to be confirmed”, without rank.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} A percentage of MWC, cumulated over the filter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reading.} A family of avoidable errors rises; a family of positions where everyone errs falls. A new player first sees “to be confirmed” families: the plan does not push toward noise.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} The theme comes from blunderDB’s classifier: a misclassified error falls into the wrong family, an error without a theme is in none. R inherits the limits of ℓ and d (MET, truncation of candidates).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} Neither offers a study plan.


\section{Reference positions}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:positions-de-reference}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-positions-reference}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Which positions to put in a collection to work on the plan? The ten worst errors often give ten variants of the same problem. A good reference position is at the centre of many of your avoidable errors, carries a clear lesson and is not already studied. The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:positions-reference}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{reference positions}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} The candidates are the quantified, themed errors of the filter, grouped by position; the excess of a position is the sum of the positive excesses ℓ − d of its errors. Two candidates of the same family — and, for the cube, of the same score — are \sphinxstylestrong{neighbours} at a transport distance of at most ρ = 12 checker\sphinxhyphen{}steps (one dice roll is worth 8 to 16).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} The gain of a candidate p is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G(p) = c(p) \times \sum_{q \,\in\, \text{voisinage}(p),\ q\ \text{non couverte}} \text{excès}(q)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as a fraction of MWC: representativeness, frequency and avoidable cost in a single quantity. c(p) starts at 1 and is multiplied by ½ if the lesson is \sphinxstylestrong{tight} (the second choice costs less than half the Error threshold), and again by ½ if it is \sphinxstylestrong{unstable} (another cube analysis depth or a rollout gives another verdict): ¼ when both combine. A rollout that confirms raises nothing: it breaks ties at equal gain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Selection.} Greedy by marginal gain: each position kept covers its neighbours, which no longer bring anything to the next ones, and its near\sphinxhyphen{}duplicates are discarded even outside its family. A position already dealt with (comment, Anki card, collection, “studied” mark) is never proposed and counts as already kept.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} The MWC covered, as a percentage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} The radius and the factors are fixed, not learned. The transport distance compares checker structures, not ideas: two positions with the same lesson but distant structure do not cover each other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} No equivalent.


\section{Before/after study}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:avant-apres-l-etude}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-avant-apres}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Does what I worked on cost me less in real matches? Without measurement, study is judged by impression; a family that does not move despite the work says that the method must change. The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:avant-apres-etude}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Before/after study}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} Every themed family of the filter is measured, those of the plan as well as the “to be confirmed” ones. A family is \sphinxstylestrong{studied} on the day (UTC) of the first study action on one of its positions: “studied” mark, Anki review whatever the grade, quiz answer. Creating a card or filing a position in a collection is not one. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Before} window: the matches dated strictly before that day; \sphinxstyleemphasis{after}: strictly after; the day itself and undated matches are discarded.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} In each window, the loss rate r = Σℓ / N: ℓ the losses of the family’s errors, N the decisions counted in matches of the same game plan and the same nature (the theme exists only for an error). The gain and its interval:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta = r_\text{avant} - r_\text{après}, \qquad
\Delta \pm 1{,}96 \sqrt{\frac{\sum \ell^2_\text{avant}}{N^2_\text{avant}}
+ \frac{\sum \ell^2_\text{après}}{N^2_\text{après}}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Verdict.} At least \sphinxstylestrong{30 decisions} in each window, otherwise “insufficient”. “Improving” if the lower bound of Δ is positive, “declining” if the upper bound is negative, “indeterminate” otherwise.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} MWC points per 100 decisions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} A change, not an effect. A family is studied \sphinxstyleemphasis{because} it was costing: regression to the mean inflates the gain. Nothing controls for opponents, format or dice.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} No equivalent.


\section{Signed biases}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:biais-signes}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-biais}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} In which direction am I wrong? “You take too much” is easier to correct than a PR: the rule to review is named. The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:biais-signes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Signed biases}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} Each counted decision carries x = +1 (error by excess of boldness), −1 (by excess of caution) or 0. With P and M the two counts over N decisions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}B = \frac{P - M}{N}, \qquad
B \pm 1{,}96 \sqrt{\frac{(P + M)/N - B^2}{N}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At least \sphinxstylestrong{20 decisions}; “too much” if the lower bound is positive, “not enough” if the upper bound is negative, “balanced” otherwise. The cost of P and M (in mpt) accompanies the counts. The sign and the cost are those of the move played in its match.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Take / pass}: over cube responses; P = faulty takes, M = faulty passes. B is exactly your take rate minus the bot’s on the same positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Doubles}: over the cube decisions of the cube owner counted in PR; P = premature doubles (no double, or too good), M = missed doubles. The bias is also given per score cell (your points to go, the opponent’s; post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford counted as 1; money game apart).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Blots}: over checker plays with contact; x is the sign of (your blots after the move played − your blots after the best move). A move is recognised by the board it leaves; a move that cannot be found drops out of the count, and its share is displayed.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unit.} A difference of proportions, no unit.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} Most score cells stay silent: that is the honest answer. The blot bias counts blots without weighing their exposure, and the discarded moves are not a neutral draw.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} No equivalent; XG and gnuBG count cube errors by type (missed double, faulty take…) without interval or verdict.


\section{Tournament review}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:bilan-du-tournoi}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-bilan-tournoi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} Did I play at my level, and if not, where did it give way: the last rounds, the long match endings, the scores where one point decides, the clock? The screens: {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_tournois:bilan-tournoi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{tournament review}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} The player defaults to the main player if he or she played in the tournament, otherwise the one most present in its matches. The \sphinxstylestrong{usual level} is the player over their point matches of the \sphinxstylestrong{365 days} preceding the tournament (its date, failing that the date of its first match), those of the tournament excluded; at least \sphinxstylestrong{5 matches} are needed. The tournament and the usual level each have their PR and their L₇, with the by\sphinxhyphen{}matches interval ({\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-intervalles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{95\% intervals}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} Δ = tournament − usual, with standard deviation √(σₜ² + σₕ²), each σ read from the upper half\sphinxhyphen{}width of its interval. “Worse” if the lower bound of Δ is positive, “better” if its upper bound is negative, “in line with usual” otherwise. The verdict requires an interval and at least \sphinxstylestrong{20 decisions} on each side; otherwise “insufficient”, figures visible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Breakdowns}, in PR: by round, each match against the overall usual PR; then each cell against the same cell of the usual level, by rank of the decision in the match (slices of 30: fatigue); by score (DMP, Crawford game, post\sphinxhyphen{}Crawford, others); by pace (either side of the median of your durations in the match). At most three families of the study plan restricted to the tournament.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Limits.} A three\sphinxhyphen{}match tournament almost never says “worse”: that is intended. The two sides are treated as independent, which widens the interval: the rule is cautious. The clock reserve is not recorded move by move: the pressure of the remaining time cannot be measured.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} No equivalent.


\section{Opening book: gap, 95 \% CI and tie}
\label{\detokenize{metriques:livre-d-ouverture-ecart-ic-95-et-egalite}}\label{\detokenize{metriques:metrique-livre-ouverture}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The question.} At this score, which move to play with this opening roll, and which reply? And is my move really worse, or only indistinguishable from the best? The screen: the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Opening} exercise of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-entrainement}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Training panel}}}}}. It serves to learn how the score shifts the first moves — which no money\sphinxhyphen{}play table teaches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition.} For every position and every score, the book stores the best candidates of a blunderDB cubeful rollout, with their equity and the standard error σ of that equity. A move’s \sphinxstylestrong{gap} is the equity of the best minus its own, in \sphinxstylestrong{score\sphinxhyphen{}normalised equity} (±1 = the centred cube; points in money play): the book shows only gaps, never an absolute equity, because the rollout’s cube model weighs on both moves the same way.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The formula.} σ(gap) = √(σ²best + σ²move), the two estimates taken as independent; the \sphinxstylestrong{95 \% CI} of the gap is ± 1.96·σ(gap). A move is \sphinxstylestrong{tied} with the best if gap < 1.96·σ(gap) + 0.005, the 0.005 being the measured bias of a truncated rollout against a full 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply rollout. The best is tied with itself. What counts as a decision: every move played, the opening and the reply apart.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{How to read it.} « Tied » does not claim that two moves are worth the same; it says the book cannot tell them apart — every move of the leading group is therefore a good answer. A gap beyond its CI is a real difference.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty and limits.} The rollout’s common dice correlate the two estimates positively: assuming them independent overestimates σ(gap), and the rule is cautious. A book computed with a fast setting (few games, truncated rollout) has wider σ: the leading group widens by itself, and the screen shows the number of games and the setting under the analysis. A move outside the book’s candidates is counted wrong with no quantified gap. The book only covers the scores of its grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG and gnuBG.} The published opening tables (bkgm.com) are money\sphinxhyphen{}play rollouts; XG and gnuBG roll out a position on demand but deliver no table per score. blunderDB computes its own and embeds it.

\section{Search Filters}
\label{\detokenize{cmd_mode:filtres-de-recherche}}\label{\detokenize{cmd_mode:cmd-filter}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This table is the reference for the search grammar: the command line, the filter library and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}query}} flag of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb search}} all read the same tokens. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{CLI Equivalent} column gives, when one exists, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search}} flag that does the same thing (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}); a dash marks a filter that only the grammar expresses.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Six tokens do not carry their value: they read it from the search board. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cube}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{score}} take up the cube and the score set there, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{d}} the decision type, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D1}} the dice, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x}} the structure drawn in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Except} tab. A roll is therefore never written into the token: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{D65}} does not exist, only the exclusion form carries its digits (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xD65}}). On the command line, where there is no board, these tokens compare against an empty board; it is the flags of the third column that must be used there instead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A single token \sphinxstylestrong{ranks} instead of narrowing: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{like}} orders the result by ascending distance to a target position, and every other token narrows the set it ranks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Errors and equities are counted in \sphinxstylestrong{thousandths of equity} — the \sphinxstyleemphasis{millipoints} of the table below: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E>100}} keeps the moves that cost at least a tenth of a point, one point being worth 1000 millipoints.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two full searches:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s p>30 w40,60 xco}} — more than 30 pips behind, between 40\% and 60\% winning chances, no comment.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s ph:race E>50 co:xg}} — in a race, a move that cost at least 50 millipoints, and a comment coming from eXtreme Gammon.

\end{itemize}

Depths: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3ply}} (exactly 3 plies), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3ply+}} (at least 3 plies), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{book}} (opening book), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rollout}} (rollout, including XG Roller and Roller++). Beyond two rolls the search is refused, as is a starred form (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{like42*}}), which no longer exists. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-recherche}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Search Panel}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pl}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pl!}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{op}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tn}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{au}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t}} values open with a double quote or an apostrophe and close with either. A token that keeps a quote without forming a complete value is ignored, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb search \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}query}} reports it. A tag may contain an apostrophe (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#l'ouverture}}), never a double quote. The semicolon is the separator of identifier and tag lists: it appears in no value, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ma1;2}} is not a token (write \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ma1 ma2}}).


\section{Transcribing from a terminal}
\label{\detokenize{cmd_mode:transcrire-depuis-un-terminal}}\label{\detokenize{cmd_mode:cmd-transcription-call}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command line has no transcription command: moves are entered in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Transcription} tab. Outside the application, they go through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb call}} ({\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-transcription}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Transcribing through the API}}}}}), for example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb call transcriptions.apply \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}db base.db \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}if\sphinxhyphen{}match 3 \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}json '\{"id":1,"gesture":\{"Kind":"validate"\}\}'}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}if\sphinxhyphen{}match}} names the revision returned by the previous call; every call is its own session, with no \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}} and no undo from one call to the next.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While a question of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-entrainement}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Training panel}}}}} is set on the board, the keys that browse the list do not scroll it: the question keeps the board. With a checker decision or an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ouverture} question and the panel focused: BACKSPACE undoes the last step and ESC restarts the move. ENTER, wherever the focus is except on a button, validates the move once it is complete, as a click on the dice does; in the notation field, ENTER validates the typed move (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{13/7 8/7}}). Once the answer is shown, ENTER does “Next”, or “Finish” if there is no next question.

\section{Direction page}
\label{\detokenize{raccourcis:page-direction}}\label{\detokenize{raccourcis:raccourcis-direction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the Direction page, \sphinxstyleemphasis{J}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{UP}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{DOWN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ENTER} go to the proposal queue, except when the focus is on a cell of the table grid, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{UP} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{DOWN} change cell. The context menus are described in the manual ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_tournois:direction-menus}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{context menus}}}}}).

Enter a die. On a game’s first play: player 1’s die, then player 2’s (the higher one starts and plays both dice).

1 … 6 (roll entered)

\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth

\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Type another opening roll: player 1’s die then player 2’s. The higher one wins — the big die first, the play goes to player 1 at the bottom; the small die first, to player 2 at the top; the first candidate is preselected. The same roll typed again changes nothing; \sphinxstyleemphasis{s} gives the play to the other player.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}

DOWN, j
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\

\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Double\sphinxhyphen{}click (on a row)

\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Validate that candidate.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Click (on the roll triangle)
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enter the roll in a single gesture: the cell carries both dice, doubles on the diagonal. On a game’s first play the triangle gives way to a row of six dice, one click giving one side’s die.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Click, drag (roll entered)
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Play the move on the board, constrained to the legal plays of that roll: a click plays the checker with the left die, a drag puts it on its destination, and each step keeps in the list only the candidates that contain it. With no dice entered, the board plays nothing.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Drag outside the rules (roll entered)
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Put the checker down where it is released, even from a point no legal play leaves from, to transcribe an illegal move. The rest of the move is played freely, by click as by drag, and the candidate list gives way to a line that says so.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
