\chapter{Glossary}
\label{\detokenize{glossaire:glossaire}}\label{\detokenize{glossaire:id1}}\label{\detokenize{glossaire::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The terms below recur throughout the rest of the documentation — manual, user guide, FAQ, CLI. This page gathers them in one place rather than redefining them in every section.
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Position}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A backgammon decision point: board, cube, dice, score and match flags. A position imported twice counts only once — it is its identity, computed automatically, that recognises it, never the file it came from.

\sphinxlineitem{Individually imported position}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A position entered into the database on its own — written from the board, or read from a position file — rather than brought in by a match. This property is durable: a position imported this way stays so even if a match containing it is imported afterwards.

\sphinxlineitem{Flagged position}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A position the user flagged as worth studying \sphinxstyleemphasis{in the software the match came from} — today only eXtreme Gammon records this mark, move by move. A flagged cube decision marks both positions it produces: the double and the take/pass.

\sphinxlineitem{Analysis}
\sphinxAtStartPar
What an engine (eXtreme Gammon, GNUbg, BGBlitz or the embedded gammonNet evaluator) concluded about a position, stored and read back later. A position carries one analysis per engine; importing an analysis never overwrites another engine’s, nor an analysis already present (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-regles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Import: what is written, what never is}}}}}).

\sphinxlineitem{Evaluation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The result of a computation the embedded evaluator performs on the position currently on the board, whether stored or not. An evaluation is valid only for as long as the position does not change; if stored, it becomes an Analysis.

\sphinxlineitem{Referential}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The scale a figure about a position is expressed in. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Money} answers “how many points is this worth”, a gammon always being worth two points. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Match} answers “how much of the match is this worth”, on a normalised scale where a gammon is worth whatever the score makes it — almost everything at 2\sphinxhyphen{}away/4\sphinxhyphen{}away, nothing to a leader at 1\sphinxhyphen{}away. The referential is a property of the position, never a display preference: it is the away score that sets it.

\sphinxlineitem{Normalised equity}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Match equity, expressed on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2 × MWC − 1}} scale, where ±1 represents the current cube won or lost. It is the scale blunderDB displays and stores at a match score, never the raw win probabilities.

\sphinxlineitem{EMG}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The acronym under which eXtreme Gammon and GNUbg name the normalised equity above, and under which blunderDB’s statistics count errors: “an error of 0.100 EMG” is an error of 0.100 on this scale. Both terms name the same quantity.

\sphinxlineitem{Error / blunder (\sphinxstyleemphasis{error}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{blunder})}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A decision whose cost reaches the library’s \sphinxstylestrong{error threshold} is an \sphinxstyleemphasis{error}; an error whose cost reaches its \sphinxstylestrong{blunder threshold} is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{blunder}. Every blunder is therefore an error. Both thresholds are set in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Library} tab of the settings, are 0.050 and 0.100 EMG by default, and follow the file rather than the machine — they do not travel in an export.

\sphinxlineitem{Away score}
\sphinxAtStartPar
How many points a player still needs to win the match, from that player’s own side. Two values are sentinels rather than counts: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}1}} means there is no match — the referential is \sphinxstyleemphasis{money} — and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}}/\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}} distinguish the game after Crawford (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}}) from the Crawford game itself (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}}), for the same distance to victory.

\sphinxlineitem{Regime}
\sphinxAtStartPar
What kind of answer the panel gives about a race, always stated on screen rather than left for the reader to guess:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{exact} — read from a two\sphinxhyphen{}sided bearoff database, never estimated;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{evaluated} — computed by the embedded evaluator, which plays the trajectory out;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{estimated} — a calibrated summary of a trajectory, valid for a win probability, never for a cube verdict.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Bearoff database}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A table of race answers, two\sphinxhyphen{}sided (the cube verdict) or one\sphinxhyphen{}sided (the EPC). blunderDB generates part of it itself on first launch (up to 6 checkers per player); wider domains are generated from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab of the settings or the CLI. A generated database is said to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{verified} when its fingerprint exactly matches the one GNUbg produces.

\sphinxlineitem{EPC (Effective Pip Count)}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A classic, one\sphinxhyphen{}sided estimate of the number of rolls needed to bear off all of a player’s checkers — corrected for wastage against the plain pip count.

\sphinxlineitem{Position fact}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A quantity that belongs to the board itself, independent of any choice a player might make: pip count, EPC, win/gammon/backgammon chances, cubeless equity. True before the roll.

\sphinxlineitem{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}roll baseline}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector of win/gammon/backgammon chances and cubeless equity, shown above the list of candidate moves once the dice are rolled. The gap between this line and a play measures the luck of the roll, never the merit of the move played.

\sphinxlineitem{Decision}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The answer to the question the board is asking: the ranking of candidate moves when dice are rolled, or the three cube options and their verdict otherwise. A position never asks both questions at once.

\sphinxlineitem{Verdict}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which option of a cube decision is the right one: \sphinxstyleemphasis{no double}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double/take}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{double/pass} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{too good (to double)}. Two special cases are never left blank: \sphinxstyleemphasis{no decision} (the regime is not entitled to one) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{refused} (the engine declined the position, typically a score beyond its table’s reach).

\sphinxlineitem{Too good}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The verdict saying the position is so favourable that doubling would prompt the opponent to pass, whereas playing on without doubling pays more — a cube best kept.

\sphinxlineitem{Luck}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The dice roll’s contribution to a move’s equity, read from the source file at import (eXtreme Gammon, GNUbg) and never recomputed by blunderDB. Formats that do not carry it (BGF, Jellyfish \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.mat}}) never provide it, and the import is not retroactive.

\sphinxlineitem{Blunder}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A move or cube decision whose error (the equity gap with the best choice) exceeds a threshold; the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bl}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunders}}) command directly loads the worst errors retained by the statistics filter.

\sphinxlineitem{Millipoint (mpt)}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A thousandth of an equity point: an equity error of 0.100 is worth 100 mpt. It is the unit a position’s own figures are read in — the blunder threshold, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{e>}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E>}} search filters, the error\sphinxhyphen{}magnitude histogram, the average luck per roll. PR is not read on this scale: its factor is 500, not 1000, so a PR of 5.0 is worth 10 mpt of average error per decision.

\sphinxlineitem{PR (Performance Rating)}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A player’s average error cost, in thousandths of an equity point per counted decision, checker play and cube combined. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}} for the exact counting rules (parity with eXtreme Gammon and GNUbg).

\sphinxlineitem{Snowie Error Rate}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same numerator as the PR (the sum of errors), but divided by the number of moves played rather than the number of counted decisions — more stable from one tool to another. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}}.

\sphinxlineitem{MWC cost}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A cube error expressed in percentage points of Match Winning Chance, rather than in equity — the natural quantity to compare the same player across different match scores.

\sphinxlineitem{Collection}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A named, ordered set of positions the user assembles by hand, drag\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}drop included. Collection membership is an explicit gesture, unlike an individually imported position (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-collections}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Collections Panel}}}}}).

\sphinxlineitem{Anki deck}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A set of positions turned into cards reviewed by spaced repetition (the FSRS algorithm). See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-anki}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Anki Panel}}}}}.

\sphinxlineitem{Review card}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A position from an Anki deck, presented as a question: the board is the question, the stored analysis is the answer, hidden until the gesture that reveals it.

\sphinxlineitem{Comment}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Free text attached to a position, typed by the user or taken from an imported file. A position can carry several, each signed by its author; an imported comment keeps its origin (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{XG}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GNU BG}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BGF}}). A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#word}} in a comment is a tag, which the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#word}} filter finds (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-commentaires}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Comments Panel}}}}}).

\sphinxlineitem{Player}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A name exactly as it appears in an imported match. blunderDB does not guess the person behind the name: the same human signing under two spellings is two distinct players, until an explicit merge (“Manage players”).

\sphinxlineitem{Watermark}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The signed statement, applied by whoever exports a database, of what it is and where it comes from. Unforgeable but not unremovable, it never records anything on the recipient’s side. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:diffusion-controlee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Handing out a database: origin and password}}}}}.

\sphinxlineitem{Issuer identity}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The key that signs one person’s watermarks — created on its own at the first watermark applied, and movable from one machine to another as a single file.

\sphinxlineitem{Protected file (.dbx)}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A database exported and encrypted with a password, opened once and then ordinary. It protects the file in transit, not its content: whoever receives the password can open it.

\sphinxlineitem{Tenant}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In server mode, the owner of a set of positions, matches and collections. Nothing one tenant stores is ever visible to another. On the desktop there is only one, implicit: the person whose file it is. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Headless mode (server)}}}}}.

\end{description}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)}
\label{\detokenize{faq:foire-aux-questions}}\label{\detokenize{faq:faq}}\label{\detokenize{faq::doc}}

\section{What is the purpose of blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quelle-est-l-utilite-de-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB lets you build a personalised database of positions. Its strength is that it assumes no classification \sphinxstyleemphasis{a priori}. Users are free to query positions with great flexibility by combining criteria of their choosing (race, structure, cube, score, back checkers, checkers in the zone, win/gammon/backgammon chances, …).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another convenient use of blunderDB is the creation of reference position catalogs. With the ability to tag positions, users can organize all their reference positions in a structured way using a single file. I hope that blunderDB facilitates the sharing of positions between players.


\section{What motivated the creation of blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:qu-est-ce-qui-a-motive-la-creation-de-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
I used to store interesting positions or blunders in various folders. However, I ran into trouble finding positions by criteria not initially anticipated by my choice of thematic categories. For example, if positions were sorted by game type (race, holding game, blitz, backgame, …), how do you retrieve every position at a given score, or at a given cube level? Lastly, some old positions tended to fall into oblivion. I wanted a tool that aggregates all my positions and does not presuppose \sphinxstyleemphasis{a priori} thematic categories, and then lets me ask questions of the database. With this flexible approach, new filters can be added without breaking the organisation of positions. This kind of software is quite common in chess, such as ChessBase.


\section{How to save the state of the current database?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:comment-sauvegarder-la-base-de-donnees-courante}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The database is updated immediately upon validation of the request. No explicit saving operation is necessary.


\section{Should I create different databases for different categories of positions?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:dois-je-creer-differentes-bases-de-donnees-pour-differentes-categories-de-positions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Barring well\sphinxhyphen{}identified reasons, it is essential not to split positions across separate databases, at the risk of not being able to relate them in future searches. blunderDB’s philosophy is not to presuppose position categories \sphinxstyleemphasis{a priori} and to let users query them flexibly. When positions were encountered under particular conditions or for specific reasons, it can be worth storing them in distinct databases. For example, one might build separate position databases for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
reference positions,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunders from live tournaments,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunders from online play.

\end{itemize}


\section{How to merge multiple databases?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:comment-fusionner-plusieurs-bases-de-donnees}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have several blunderDB databases you want to bring together, use the \sphinxstylestrong{Merge a database} button (\sphinxstyleemphasis{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}SHIFT\sphinxhyphen{}I}):
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the main database (the one that will receive the positions)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Click \sphinxstylestrong{Merge a database} in the toolbar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pick the database to merge

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB merges the positions

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
During the merge, blunderDB avoids duplicates: a position already present is not duplicated, and the analyses from different engines coexist instead of overwriting each other (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-regles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Import: what is written, what never is}}}}}).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is recommended to make a backup copy of your main database before importing another database.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Which match file formats are supported?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quels-formats-de-fichiers-de-match-sont-supportes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB supports the following match formats:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{eXtreme Gammon (XG)}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{.xg} files, with complete move analysis, cube decisions, played moves, and multi\sphinxhyphen{}engine support. \sphinxstyleemphasis{.xgp} files for importing individual positions with analysis.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{GNUbg}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{.sgf} files (Smart Game Format), with analysis.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jellyfish}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{.mat} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{.txt} files.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{BGBlitz}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{.bgf} files and text positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{HedgeHog} (OpenGammon): \sphinxstyleemphasis{.ogxm} files, with analysis.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Import can be done via a single file, multiple selection, recursive folder, paste from clipboard, or drag and drop.

\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB automatically detects duplicates and prevents importing a match already present in the database.


\section{Can I import the matches I played online?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:mes-matchs-joues-en-ligne-sont-ils-importables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Yes, by a detour: \sphinxstylestrong{Backgammon Studio (Heroes)}, \sphinxstylestrong{Backgammon Galaxy} and \sphinxstylestrong{GammonSpace} all three produce files eXtreme Gammon can read — Studio even ships an integration pack that drops into the XG folder. Those matches therefore reach blunderDB through the existing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.xg}} path, with no dedicated reader needed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exactly what survives that detour — analyses, roll luck, marks, comments — \sphinxstylestrong{has not been measured}: it would take a match exported from each of the three platforms. If you have one and something is lost on import, open an issue with the file: the measurement is what will decide whether a reader of their own is needed, not a guess.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The older text formats GNU Backgammon already reads — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.sgg}} (GridGammon), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.tmg}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.gam}}, Snowie’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.txt}} — are in the same case: going through GNU Backgammon makes them importable today.


\section{Can I synchronise my database across several machines?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:puis-je-synchroniser-ma-base-entre-plusieurs-machines}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A blunderDB database is \sphinxstylestrong{a single file}. That makes backup and copying trivial, and it settles the answer:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dropbox, Syncthing, iCloud, OneDrive}: these work, on one condition — do not open the database \sphinxstylestrong{on both sides at once}. They synchronise files, not concurrent writes: two instances writing in parallel produce a conflict the service resolves by keeping one version and renaming the other. blunderDB takes a write lock on the open file, which protects one machine, but no lock crosses a synchronisation service.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Several machines at the same time}: this is what \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} mode answers (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Headless mode (server)}}}}). A daemon holds the database, the machines connect to it, and there is only ever one writer.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Two databases that have diverged}: they are \sphinxstylestrong{merged} rather than synchronised — see “How do I merge several databases?” above. Deduplication by Zobrist hash does the work: shared positions are not duplicated and their analyses and comments are combined. It is a merge, not a reconciliation: nothing is deleted on one side because the other deleted it.

\end{itemize}


\section{Do I need eXtreme Gammon to use blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:ai-je-besoin-d-extreme-gammon-pour-utiliser-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No. blunderDB also reads GNUbg, BGBlitz, Jellyfish and HedgeHog files, and its embedded evaluator (gammonNet) analyses any position without depending on third\sphinxhyphen{}party software — see “What is the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator worth?” below. An XG import does, however, bring the most complete analysis (plays, cube decisions, flags, roll luck): it is the format the statistics draw on most richly.


\section{I already use eXtreme Gammon: what use is blunderDB to me?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:j-utilise-deja-extreme-gammon-a-quoi-me-sert-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB does not replay your matches, it brings them together. Three concrete differences:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{aggregating} into a single file matches coming from XG, GNUbg, BGBlitz and Jellyfish, deduplicated position by position;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{searching} by checker structure and by error: “the takes at this score where I lost more than 50 millipoints” is written as a single command line (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cmd_mode:cmd-mode}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{List of commands}}}}});

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{reviewing} the positions kept, by spaced repetition, in Anki decks (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_entrainement:panneau-anki}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Anki Panel}}}}}).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Your XG analyses remain XG’s: blunderDB imports them as they are and never recomputes them (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:import-regles}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Import: what is written, what never is}}}}}).


\section{Are XG rollouts imported? Does blunderDB do rollouts?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:les-rollouts-xg-sont-ils-importes-blunderdb-fait-il-des-rollouts}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From an XG analysis, the import keeps the level label (“3\sphinxhyphen{}ply”, “XG Roller++”, “Book”), the equities, the errors and the probabilities; it does not open the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.xg}} file’s rollout data, and therefore keeps neither the number of trials nor the standard deviation. An XG analysis pasted as text, on the other hand, keeps its label literally, “Rollout” included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB does, however, run its own rollouts, with the embedded evaluator: the Analysis panel rolls out the displayed position or the whole displayed list, and the result is stored next to the analysis, never in its place (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:rollouts}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Rollouts}}}}}).


\section{What has been measured of the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator, and what has not?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:qu-a-t-on-mesure-de-l-evaluateur-integre-et-que-n-a-t-on-pas-mesure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A measurement is published, on the Eval panel’s \sphinxstyleemphasis{evaluated} regime: 4000 money race decisions, compared against the exact bearoff table — 93.4\% verdict agreement (3735/4000), but only 61.1\% within 1\% of the take point against 94.4\% beyond 20\%; average winning\sphinxhyphen{}probability gap 0.85\%, maximum 8.30\%. What is not measured: the cube verdict \sphinxstylestrong{at a match score} and \sphinxstylestrong{contact positions}, for which no figure is published. The details of the assumptions are in {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_eval:epc-methodologie}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel}}}}}.


\section{What is a collection?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:qu-est-ce-qu-une-collection}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A collection is a custom grouping of positions. Unlike a filter search which is dynamic, a collection is a fixed set of positions manually chosen by the user. Collections allow, for example, grouping reference positions for a particular topic.


\section{What is EPC?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:qu-est-ce-que-l-epc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
EPC (Effective Pip Count) is a more accurate measure than the simple pip count for evaluating bearoff positions. blunderDB’s Eval panel uses a 6\sphinxhyphen{}point bearoff table identical to GNUbg’s, computed on the machine on first launch, and computes in real time the EPC, average number of rolls, standard deviation, pip count, and wastage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On pure bearoff positions, the panel also shows the winning probability of the player on roll and, when the position is covered by a two\sphinxhyphen{}sided database (TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}06 table computed on first launch, or extended TS\sphinxhyphen{}06\sphinxhyphen{}11 table computed from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bearoff} tab of the configuration), the exact money cube verdict. Outside that domain, the probability is estimated with its error margin and the verdict is deliberately not shown. See the manual section “Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel” for the details of the assumptions.


\section{What is the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator (gammonNet) worth?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:que-vaut-l-evaluateur-integre-gammonnet}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
gammonNet is a neural network trained by a third party (see Credits), ported to Go and compiled into blunderDB: no external software, no network connection. It plays the role of XG or GNUbg for positions that were not imported — search from 0 to 4 plies ahead (2 by default), cube decisions per Janowski and the database’s match equity table (the built\sphinxhyphen{}in Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2, or a table imported from GNUbg), honouring the match score. It is neither the only nor necessarily the best engine on the market: it is the one that works offline, without an account or subscription, on the position you are looking at. Nothing stops you from also importing XG or GNUbg analyses where they exist — the two sources coexist, and a column shows the origin of each analysis. See the “Eval Panel” section and “Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel” in the manual.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What that is worth, in figures.} On the bear\sphinxhyphen{}off positions the embedded exact table covers — the only place an oracle exists — gammonNet at 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply gives the \sphinxstylestrong{same cube verdict in 93.4 \% of cases}, and the disagreement concentrates exactly at the take point (61 \% agreement within 1 \% of the take point, 94 \% beyond 10 \%): that is where two legitimate methods diverge most on a close decision, not a diffuse error. The detail and the method are in “Methodology and assumptions of the Eval panel”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the same question asked of \sphinxstylestrong{your} library rather than of a reference corpus, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb analyze \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}compare}} compares the embedded engine with the analyses that came in your XG or GNUbg files — agreement on the best answer, cost of the disagreements, breakdown by game phase — \sphinxstylestrong{writing nothing}.


\section{What is the difference between PR and the Snowie Error Rate?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quelle-est-la-difference-entre-le-pr-et-le-snowie-error-rate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PR (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Performance Rating}) is the average equity error per counted decision, multiplied by 500 as eXtreme Gammon and GNUbg do; the lower it is, the better you are playing. The Snowie Error Rate reports that same average against the number of \sphinxstyleemphasis{plays} rather than the number of \sphinxstyleemphasis{decisions} — a longer match therefore does not mechanically worsen the SER. blunderDB shows both in the Stats panel, aligned with eXtreme Gammon’s and GNUbg’s conventions (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{stats_parity:stats-parity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Statistics model — XG / gnuBG / blunderDB alignment}}}}} for the counting rules in detail).


\section{Does blunderDB have a command\sphinxhyphen{}line interface?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:blunderdb-dispose-t-il-d-une-interface-en-ligne-de-commande}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Yes, blunderDB has a command\sphinxhyphen{}line interface (CLI) that allows performing without a graphical interface operations such as creating databases, importing matches, exporting, searching positions, displaying statistics, etc. Refer to the CLI documentation for more details.


\section{Does blunderDB offer a server mode?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:blunderdb-propose-t-il-un-mode-serveur}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Yes, an optional “headless” mode: the same binary, launched with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}}, exposes blunderDB’s engine over HTTP + JSON behind an authenticating reverse proxy (blunderDB itself performs no authentication). It can run on SQLite or on multi\sphinxhyphen{}tenant PostgreSQL, and is used to drive blunderDB from your own scripts or a homegrown application, over HTTP + JSON, or to share a database between several players. With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}web}}, it also serves a deliberately limited consultation page (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:page-web}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{The web page}}}}}). The normal use remains the desktop application; see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Headless mode (server)}}}}} for the details (including the ready\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}use Docker image) and the “Deploying server mode behind a proxy” tutorial in the user guide.


\section{Can I modify, copy, share blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:puis-je-modifier-copier-partager-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Yes, absolutely. blunderDB is licensed under the MIT license.


\section{Where is my data stored?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:ou-sont-stockees-mes-donnees}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
On your disk, in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}} file you chose when creating the database: no account, no server, no synchronisation by default. The desktop application opens that file directly; only the optional server mode (see above) runs blunderDB remotely, and in that case you are the one hosting that server.


\section{Can I share a database with another player?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:puis-je-partager-une-base-avec-un-autre-joueur}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Yes: a blunderDB database is a plain file, so copying or sending it is enough. To distribute a database to a third party, two optional mechanisms, chosen at export time, turn it into a \sphinxstyleemphasis{controlled} release rather than a plain copy: an \sphinxstylestrong{origin watermark} signs the file with your issuer identity (unforgeable, readable in the Metadata panel or via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb info}}, and never recording anything on the recipient’s side), and \sphinxstylestrong{password protection} produces an encrypted \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dbx}} file. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_partage:diffusion-controlee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Handing out a database: origin and password}}}}} in the manual.


\section{What data format does blunderDB use?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quel-format-de-donnees-utilise-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The database is a simple SQLite file. In the absence of blunderDB, it can thus be opened with any SQLite file editor.


\section{What were the design principles of blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quels-ont-ete-les-principes-de-conception-de-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
I wanted an interface that stays approachable, but designed above all for advanced, sustained use, where one moves from position to position and from search to search. The command line, opened by pressing the \sphinxstyleemphasis{SPACE} bar, and the keyboard shortcuts serve that use, without being mandatory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I also wanted blunderDB to be lightweight, self\sphinxhyphen{}contained, installation\sphinxhyphen{}free and available on different platforms, hence my choice of the Go language and the Svelte library. For serialising the database, the file format had to be cross\sphinxhyphen{}platform and suited to holding a database. The SQLite file format seemed the obvious fit.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I was also keen that a database should remain a single file, one that can be copied, backed up or sent to another player.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, blunderDB is not limited to the desktop application: the same binary provides a command\sphinxhyphen{}line interface and an optional server mode, which can rely on PostgreSQL for multi\sphinxhyphen{}user deployments. The normal way to use it nevertheless remains the desktop application. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Headless mode (server)}}}}}.


\section{What is the software architecture of blunderDB?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:quelle-est-l-architecture-logicielle-de-blunderdb}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The backend is coded in \sphinxhref{https://go.dev/}{Go}. It is responsible for all operations on the SQLite database that stores the positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The frontend is coded in \sphinxhref{https://svelte.dev/}{Svelte}. It is responsible for rendering the graphical interface and the Backgammon board.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The application is encapsulated with \sphinxhref{https://wails.io/}{Wails}, enabling the production of native desktop applications for Windows, Linux and macOS.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The database is managed by \sphinxhref{https://www.sqlite.org/}{SQLite}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional server mode can rely on \sphinxhref{https://www.postgresql.org/}{PostgreSQL} instead of SQLite for multi\sphinxhyphen{}user deployments.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The embedded evaluator (\sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/gammonNet}{gammonNet}, MIT) is a neural network ported to Go and compiled into blunderDB: it evaluates any position offline, without XG or GNUbg. See “What is the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator worth?” above.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more information, see the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB}{blunderDB GitHub repository}.


\section{Which platforms does blunderDB run on?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:sur-quelles-plateformes-blunderdb-fonctionne-t-il}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB runs on Windows, Linux and Mac.


\section{Where does the blunderDB icon come from?}
\label{\detokenize{faq:d-ou-vient-l-icone-de-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The blunderDB icon is the “goggling” emoticon from the  \sphinxhref{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/SMirC}{SMirC series}.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Headless mode (server)}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:mode-headless-serveur}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section describes an \sphinxstylestrong{advanced, optional mode} of blunderDB, intended for server deployments, multi\sphinxhyphen{}user setups and automation. \sphinxstylestrong{The normal and recommended use of blunderDB remains the desktop application} described in the previous chapters. If you use blunderDB on your own, on your computer, you do not need this mode: you can skip this chapter without losing any of the analysis features.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:vue-d-ensemble}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the desktop application and the command\sphinxhyphen{}line commands (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}), the same \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb}} binary can run in \sphinxstylestrong{headless mode}: without a graphical interface, driven entirely from the command line or over the network. This mode covers three use cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{the} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} \sphinxstylestrong{daemon} — exposes the blunderDB engine as an HTTP + JSON service, to run a shared database on a server and access it from several clients;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the generic \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} dispatcher — calls any storage operation directly, locally, for scripting and testing;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}} command — transfers a single\sphinxhyphen{}user SQLite database to a multi\sphinxhyphen{}user PostgreSQL backend.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These three use cases rely on a shared \sphinxstylestrong{storage layer} that can talk to two backends: \sphinxstylestrong{SQLite} (the usual \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}} file format of the desktop application) and \sphinxstylestrong{PostgreSQL} (for multi\sphinxhyphen{}user server deployments).


\section{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{serve}} daemon}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:le-demon-serve}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-serve}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb serve}} runs the engine as an HTTP service that responds in JSON. It lets you host a position database on one machine and access it from several clients.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} sqlite}
blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }serve\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}db\PYG{+w}{ }database.db\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}addr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{127}.0.0.1:8080

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} postgres}
blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }serve\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}backend\PYG{+w}{ }postgres\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dsn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}postgres://user:pass@host:5432/blunderdb?sslmode=disable\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}addr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{127}.0.0.1:8080
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sslmode=disable}} is only suitable for a trusted private network — a database in a neighbouring container, on a network with no route to either the host or the Internet. For a remote database, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sslmode=require}} encrypts the link, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{verify\sphinxhyphen{}full}} also checks the server’s certificate and hostname. The other connection strings on this page carry \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sslmode=disable}} for the same reason: they all describe a private network.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The daemon performs no authentication.} It trusts the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} request header and \sphinxstylestrong{must} run behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy…) responsible for authentication. \sphinxstylestrong{Never expose it directly to the public Internet.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} is the tenant’s \sphinxstylestrong{integer} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{42}}…): it is the reverse\sphinxhyphen{}proxy’s job to map the authenticated account to that integer. A name (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alice}}) is refused with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{400 invalid}}, never converted.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}User\sphinxhyphen{}Name}} header names the person behind the request: it signs the comments they write (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{comments.add}}, the MCP tool \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{comment\_position}}), and the daemon trusts it without checking, like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}}. Without it, the comment has no author — never the tenant, which would leave with an export. An import does not sign in the name of whoever imports: the notes of an XG file are signed “XG”, those of another file by its transcriber, those of a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}} database by their original author.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Options:}

All options except \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}db}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}transcription\sphinxhyphen{}ttl}} can also be given through an environment variable (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_BACKEND}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_DSN}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_ADDR}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_LOG\_LEVEL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_METRICS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_WEB}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_DIRECTION}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_MCP\_WRITE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_TRANSCRIPTION}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_DUEL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_CORS\_ALLOW\_ORIGIN}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_RATE\_LIMIT\_RPS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_RATE\_LIMIT\_BURST}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_QUOTA\_POSITIONS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_QUOTA\_BYTES}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_QUOTA\_ANALYSIS\_SECONDS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_QUOTA\_IMPORTS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_ANALYSIS\_WORKERS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_HEAVY\_SLOTS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_ANALYSIS\_WEIGHTS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_RLS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_READ\_TENANTS}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_TS\_PATH}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_IDENTITY\_DIR}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_IDENTITY\_NAME}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_IMPORT\_DIR}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_OPS\_ADDR}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_PPROF\_ADDR}}): an explicit flag still wins over the matching variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The daemon has \sphinxstylestrong{no} data\sphinxhyphen{}directory option: it writes its bearoff tables to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$XDG\_DATA\_HOME/blunderdb}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textasciitilde{}/.local/share/blunderdb}} otherwise. So it is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{XDG\_DATA\_HOME}} that moves them — see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-bearoff}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{The bearoff databases}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rate limiter’s own bucket table carries a hard cap (10,000 distinct tenants): beyond it, each new tenant evicts the least\sphinxhyphen{}recently\sphinxhyphen{}used bucket rather than letting the table grow without bound — useful if a client sends many distinct \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} values, whether by accident or not, between two periodic sweeps of idle buckets.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb serve}} rejects any unexpected positional argument (beyond the single leading \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} that an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ENTRYPOINT}} already reduced to the bare binary lets through): without this check, a flag placed after such an argument was silently ignored — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker run image serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}addr :9090}}, a natural reflex since the image’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ENTRYPOINT}} is already \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}}, used to start on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{:8080}} without a word.


\subsection{Endpoints}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:points-d-acces}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The service exposes operational endpoints, always present:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /healthz}} — liveness (the process is running);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /readyz}} — readiness (storage responds and its schema is at the expected version);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /metrics}} — Prometheus metrics (if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}metrics}} is enabled);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /app/}} — the read\sphinxhyphen{}mostly web page (if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}web}} is enabled).

\end{itemize}


\subsection{The web page}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:la-page-web-de-consultation}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:page-web}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}web}} serves a page under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/app/}}: a library you can consult from a tablet or a phone, with nothing to install.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can do \sphinxstylestrong{four things}, and that list is the decision, not a stage:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{consult} a position, its analysis and its board;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{search}, with the same token grammar as the application’s command line;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{review} an Anki deck — answer revealed and grade given;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{display a tournament}, read\sphinxhyphen{}only: the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tournoi} tab shows a Direction’s display page (bracket, pairings, results, standings), the same one the desktop writes to its display folder, and refreshes it every ten seconds by conditional read (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}None\sphinxhyphen{}Match}}: a 304 as long as nothing has changed). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/app/?tournoi=<id>}} shows only that tournament, with no menu — the address to project or share.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It cannot edit a position, import, delete, manage collections, matches or the configuration, nor enter anything into a tournament, and it will not learn to. A feature missing here is not a gap: it is the perimeter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{It is off by default, and that default is the decision.} The daemon authenticates nobody: it trusts the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} header and must run behind a proxy that authenticates. Shipping a browser\sphinxhyphen{}reachable interface switched on out of the box would invite exactly the deployment that rule forbids.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The desktop itself serves a tournament’s display on the local network, without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}}: the Direction starts on demand a server that exposes only the web page and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.pageHtml}} for the single chosen tournament — any other address of the page redirects to that tournament’s display, never to the full application —, sets the tenant itself, and shows the address’s QR code (see the manual, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Displaying a tournament}). It authenticates no one either: anyone on the local network reads the page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The page \sphinxstylestrong{sends no tenant}: the proxy sets the header, as for any other client. In local development, and there only, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/app/?tenant=1}} names one — which changes nothing about the safety of a daemon that already accepts that header from anyone. Opened without a proxy, the page loads, but its data calls are refused: it says so in plain words (“cette page se sert derrière un mandataire…”) rather than staying blank, and the daemon recalls it in its log at startup.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The page’s files are served \sphinxstylestrong{without a tenant}, deliberately: a browser must be able to load the page before the proxy assigns it anything, and a page holds no data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Liveness and readiness answer two different questions. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/healthz}} always answers 200 as soon as the process serves requests, without ever querying the storage: an orchestrator restarts a container whose liveness fails, and a briefly unreachable database must not restart a healthy daemon in a loop. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/readyz}} answers 503 (with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{status}} set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{down}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{version\_mismatch}}) as long as the database does not answer or its schema is not the binary’s: traffic is simply routed away until it comes back.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb healthcheck}} subcommand (also present in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} binary of the container image) performs a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /readyz}} request on the local daemon and returns \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}} when it is ready, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}} otherwise; the address is that of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}addr}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_ADDR}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{:8080}} by default. It is the Docker image’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{HEALTHCHECK}}, and it works just as well from a script or a systemd unit:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }healthcheck\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}addr\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{127}.0.0.1:8080\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }ready
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The business surface follows the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST /v1/<family>.<method>}} shape (for example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/positions.save}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/matches.get}}). The families cover positions, analyses, matches, comments, collections, tournaments, Anki cards, filters, sessions, history (search and commands), search, metadata, library settings, statistics, import and export. Listing endpoints return an NDJSON stream (one JSON object per line). The server shuts down cleanly on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SIGINT}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SIGTERM}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An error returns the envelope \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"error":\{"code":…,"message":…\}\}}}. The code \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{not\_found}} says a named resource does not exist; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unknown\_route}}, also a 404, says the daemon does not serve the method called: a client and a daemon of different versions, or a family the daemon only serves behind a flag. A client concludes that data is missing only on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{not\_found}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions.save}} returns \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"id":…,"created":…\}}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{created}} is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} for the one call that inserted the position, and the write itself says so: a client that copies a position then its analysis, and must undo the copy after a failure, deletes the position only if it created it, without the race of a prior \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions.exists}}.


\subsubsection{What \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} promises}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:ce-que-v1-promet}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-versionnage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A client written against \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} must keep working. The rule fits in three lines, and it is more useful written down than guessed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What exists does not change meaning.} A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} route is never renamed, removed or re\sphinxhyphen{}purposed. A request or response field is never renamed, dropped or retyped.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What is added is added.} A new route, an \sphinxstylestrong{optional} request field, a new field in a response: a client that ignores them keeps working — that is the definition of “compatible” taken here. A client must therefore ignore the fields it does not know rather than refuse them.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Everything else is} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v2}}. Making a field mandatory that was not, changing a unit, changing the meaning of an error code: those are breaks, and they live under another prefix, beside \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}}, for as long as clients need to cross over.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two clarifications that matter. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/ops/}} routes are \sphinxstylestrong{not} covered: they operate a deployment, change with it, and are not an API for third\sphinxhyphen{}party programs. And the \sphinxstylestrong{contract itself is generated} from the daemon’s route table (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{openapi.yaml}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{api_reference:api-reference}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{API contract}}}}}): it cannot describe anything other than what the server serves.


\subsubsection{Lessons}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:les-lecons}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-lecons}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Lessons ({\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:lecons}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Lessons}}}}}) are read and written under the caller’s tenant through fourteen routes: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/lessons.list}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.get}} (the lesson and its steps, in order), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.create}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.update}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.delete}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.addStep}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.updateStep}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.removeStep}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.reorderSteps}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.setStepDone}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"id": <step>, "done": true|false\}}}, the reader’s “step done” gesture, written under their own tenant) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.doneSteps}} (the date of that gesture per step). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.html}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"id": <lesson>, "language": "en"\}}}) renders the lesson as one self\sphinxhyphen{}contained HTML page, boards included; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.markdown}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.importMarkdown}} exchange Markdown (see below). Deleting a lesson is permanent and leaves the collections and positions that its steps showed. The MCP tools \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list\_lessons}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lesson}} read them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.markdown}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"ids": {[}<leçon>, …{]}\}}}) renders lessons as one Markdown text (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{markdown}}): \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\# nom}}, the description, then one \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#\# titre}} section per step; an article is a lesson with no step. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lessons.importMarkdown}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"markdown": "…"\}}}) creates one lesson per document, in a single transaction, and returns their \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ids}}. The Markdown carries text only: an imported step shows neither board nor collection. A code block that no fence closes is refused.


\subsubsection{Transcribing through the API}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:transcrire-par-l-api}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-transcription}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcriptions.*}} family lets an external client transcribe a match move by move, with the same logic as the desktop. The reads (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exportMat}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{losses}}) are always served. The moves (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{editMatch}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apply}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{undo}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{redo}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{candidates}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{close}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{abandon}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{materialize}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import}}) are served only with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}transcription}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Config.Transcription}} for a host that embeds the engine): without this flag, these routes answer 404.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}} return the draft’s state, its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{revision}} and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apply}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{undo}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{redo}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{close}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}} name that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}}: missing → \sphinxstylestrong{400}, expired or unknown session → \sphinxstylestrong{410}; the client then reopens the draft (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}}), cursor at the end of the document. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{abandon}} names no session: it deletes the draft under the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} revision alone. Every move that writes carries the last revision seen in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} header and returns the next one:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} missing → \sphinxstylestrong{428};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
stale revision → \sphinxstylestrong{409}; the error envelope gives the current revision (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.revision}}) and the draft’s fresh state (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.state}}: document, revision, session and cursor), which the client displays before replaying its move if it still applies.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The revision advances only when the document changes (header and actions): moving the cursor or entering a die of the action in progress writes nothing and returns the same revision. A session belongs to the draft, not to a client: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}} returns the live session when there is one, and the tabs or workstations that share it also share the cursor and the undo stack.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The session keeps only the undo stack, the cursor and the entry in progress: the draft is written after every move that changes it, so a lost session (inactivity, restart, another instance) loses no move. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcriptions.get}} returns the revision as an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ETag}} and answers 304 to an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}None\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} that names it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The state returns the video tracking as the desktop shows it, with no recomputation on the client side: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{annotated.document.header.video\_source}} is the video the markers refer to; each \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{annotated.actions{[}i{]}}} carries its markers (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{roll\_tick\_ms}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tick\_ms}}, in milliseconds from the start of the video) and the durations they give (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_ms}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cube\_decision\_ms}}), with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_estimated}} when a play’s duration is an upper bound estimated up to the next action. An unknown key is absent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{candidates}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{id}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}}) returns the legal plays of the roll being entered, both dice typed (otherwise \sphinxstylestrong{400}): all of them, with no cap, ranked at 0\sphinxhyphen{}ply without pruning, from best to worst, as in the desktop’s transcription panel. Each play carries \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{index}} (the one \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{select\_candidate}} names), its notation, its steps, its rank and its evaluation (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analysis}}). If the ranking fails (score outside the match equity table), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unranked}} is true and the plays follow the generator’s order. This ranking neither counts against nor checks the analysis quota; it goes through the same workers as evaluations, taking its turn among tenants, and is not subject to the heavy\sphinxhyphen{}read gate (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}heavy\sphinxhyphen{}slots}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}} saves the Match and deletes the draft, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{abandon}} deletes it without a Match, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{close}} only releases the session. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{editMatch}} opens a draft on an existing Match and, for an imported match, returns the count of analyses and comments that the transcription does not keep (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{losses.lossy}}). The analysis of the saved match is started with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gammonnet.analyzeMissing}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{materialize}} writes a Match in a single call from an actions document (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{header}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{actions}}, dice included), without a draft or a session, under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Idempotency\sphinxhyphen{}Key}}. It applies the rules machine like the Duel referee: the first refused action stops everything, nothing is written, and the error (\sphinxstylestrong{400}) gives its rank from 0 (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.rank}}, \sphinxhyphen{}1 for the header), its kind (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.kind}}) and its reason (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.detail}}). The Match is the one that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}}, one \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apply}} per action and then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}} would give: same fingerprints, no “played here” origin. The decision duration of an action (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_ms}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cube\_decision\_ms}}) is carried over onto its move; when absent, it stays unknown. The response is that of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import}} opens a new draft on a document written elsewhere, under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Idempotency\sphinxhyphen{}Key}}: either the text of a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.mat}} file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mat}}) or the actions of a transcription document (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{actions}}, with optionally \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{header}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{format\_version}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{next\_score}}: a draft’s document is sent as it is) — one of the two, otherwise \sphinxstylestrong{400}. Unlike \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{materialize}}, nothing is refused for an inconsistency: it is kept and marked, and the client corrects it before \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{finish}}. Only what no replay can read is refused (\sphinxstylestrong{400}, nothing is written): a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.mat}} without a game, a newer document format, an unknown action kind, a player, die or point off the board; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{details.rank}} then gives the rank of the faulty action (\sphinxhyphen{}1 for the header). A document without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{format\_version}} is read in the current format. The response is that of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}}: the draft’s state, its revision and its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The daemon authenticates nobody: opening writes means entrusting them to the proxy ({\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-proxy-deployment}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Deployment behind an authenticating proxy}}}}}). A “transcriber” role is a proxy rule on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/transcriptions.}} prefix, not a notion of the daemon.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Playing a Duel through the API}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:jouer-un-duel-par-l-api}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-duel}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duels.*}} family drives a Duel one Action at a time, with the same logic as the desktop. The reads (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get}}) are always served. The gestures (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{open}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{act}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flag}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{suspend}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stop}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{forfeit}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{discard}}) are served only with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}duel}}: without this flag, these routes answer 404.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}} receives the match length (or a money session), the Start position, the two Sides (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"kind": "external"\}}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"kind": "bot", "level": "instant"\}}} — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{normal}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thorough}} exist too; an unknown Side or level is refused with a \sphinxstylestrong{400}), the Cadence and the names. Two Bots play the whole match in the call that creates the Duel; a money session between two Bots, which would never end, is refused with a \sphinxstylestrong{400}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{act}} plays an Action — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{roll}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{double}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pass}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{move}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{resign}} — and names its Side (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{play.side}}, 0 or 1, mandatory: absent → \sphinxstylestrong{400}): the daemon authenticates no one, so the client answers for who plays for whom. The response returns the state of the Duel at the next point where an external Side decides, with the Actions that happened in between (rolls, forced moves, Actions of a Bot). An Action the rules refuse is a \sphinxstylestrong{400} and writes nothing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An external Side may declare the Bot that plays behind it, a gammonNet Bot the client runs itself: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"kind": "external", "declared": \{"configuration": "normal", "engine": "v1.6.0"\}\}}}, two texts of at most 64 bytes. Without a given name, the player takes the Bot’s (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gammonNet normal}}). The Arbiter treats this Side as any external Side. The Match’s origin (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{matches.origin}}) carries the declaration apart, in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{declared\_bots}}, as declared by the client and not attested: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bot\_level}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bot\_engine}} only name the Bot the Arbiter played itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"combinedSeed": true}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create}} publishes the fingerprint and does no more: the Duel awaits each external Side’s contribution to its seed (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{awaitingContribution}}), with no roll and no clock, and a game Action before them is refused with \sphinxstylestrong{400}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duels.contribute}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{id}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{side}} 0 or 1, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{contribution}}, 1 to 64 bytes) brings it once per Side; a second contribution, one from a delegated Side or one without a combined seed are refused with \sphinxstylestrong{400}, and the last contribution starts the dice. The rolls then come from the effective seed, the HMAC\sphinxhyphen{}SHA256 of the sealed seed over each Side’s contribution, in player order, preceded by its length as 4 big\sphinxhyphen{}endian bytes. The Match’s origin carries the contributions (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{contributions}}) and the effective seed (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{roll\_seed}}): everything is recomputed from the revealed seed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every gesture on an existing Duel carries the revision last seen in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}Match}}: absent → \sphinxstylestrong{428}, stale → \sphinxstylestrong{409}, including for a second client that read the same revision as a first one that already got through. A tenant can have \sphinxstylestrong{several open Duels} at a time, each with its clocks running: opening one suspends none of the others, and a Bot’s computation holds up its own Duel only. A gesture on a suspended Duel opens it in the same write. “Open” is written in the draft: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}} reads it there, an open Duel stays open after a daemon restart, and two daemons on the same database see the same open Duels, the revision settling their gestures. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get}} returns the revision as an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ETag}} and answers 304 to an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}None\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} that names it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dice seed leaves through no route before the end: the state carries its fingerprint, and the seed is revealed only with the Match that the end of the Duel writes (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ended.diceSeed}}). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{discard}} throws the Duel away: nothing of it is written. The gestures are announced on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/events}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{duel}} filter). Under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb call}}, a Duel has no Cadence and no decision time: each call is its own process.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{forfeit}} gives the match up for a Side (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{side}}, 0 or 1, required): the game in progress goes to the other Side for the points that bring them to the match length — at money play, a single at the cube’s value — and the Match is written won by them. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stop}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep}} true writes a money session’s Match as it stands, the game in progress without a winner; on an unfinished match in points it is refused with \sphinxstylestrong{400} and the Duel stays open: the Match is written whole only, and the Duel is suspended, forfeited, or stopped with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{keep}} false, which throws it away. Stopping is not forfeiting. Under a Cadence whose overrun loses the match (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{timeOut}} set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lose\_match}}), losing on time counts as a forfeit by the Side whose time ran out: in points, the Match is written won by the other at the length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Export is no exception: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exports.sqlite}} carries no suspended Duel, even when it covers the whole tenant, since its seed is every roll to come. The Match of a finished Duel travels with its origin, seed revealed. Only \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}} carries the suspended Duels with their seed, so that they resume on PostgreSQL with the same dice.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The daemon authenticates no one: whoever reaches these routes plays for either Side. A proxy rule on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/duels.}} prefix decides who may ({\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-proxy-deployment}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Deployment behind an authenticating proxy}}}}}).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{A Python client}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:un-client-python}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-client-python}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clients/python/}} holds a minimal client with no dependency beyond the standard library — the daemon speaks POST and JSON, which \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{urllib}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{json}} cover entirely:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{blunderdb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{Client}

\PYG{n}{api} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{Client}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{http://127.0.0.1:8080}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{tenant}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{api}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{metadata\PYGZus{}counts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{api}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{positions\PYGZus{}list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{limit}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{position}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{id}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It comes in \sphinxstylestrong{two halves, on purpose}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_generated.py}} carries one method per route, generated from the daemon’s route table by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{go run ./cmd/openapi\sphinxhyphen{}gen}}: a hand\sphinxhyphen{}written surface would drift the day a route is added, and nobody would notice before a user did. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{client.py}} carries the transport — the session, the tenant header, the error envelope, the NDJSON decode — and is written by hand. What changes with the API is generated; what changes with judgement is not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Method names are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{family\_operation}} in snake\_case: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/positions.loadByIds}} becomes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions\_load\_by\_ids()}}. The family is kept because several families share an operation name (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delete}}), and a bare \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list()}} would collide.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{events()}} follows \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/events}} and returns one dictionary per message (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-events}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Being notified of gestures: /v1/events}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A failure raises \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{APIError}}, carrying the daemon’s envelope as it is: the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{code}} (what a program branches on), the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{message}} (what a person reads), the HTTP status and the details.


\subsubsection{Embedding the engine in a Go program}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:embarquer-le-moteur-dans-un-programme-go}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-bootstrap}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pkg/blunderdb/server.Bootstrap}} opens the storage and returns a set of handlers \sphinxstylestrong{in the calling process}, without listening on a port. It is the way in for a trusted parent — gammonGo — that wants the position library without running a daemon beside it or speaking HTTP to itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
What that assumes is explicit: the parent is \sphinxstylestrong{trusted}. There is no tenant to verify, no header to validate, no rate limiter — those belong to the daemon because it faces a network, and ADR\sphinxhyphen{}0005 says why. A program that embeds the engine chooses its own tenant and answers for its calls.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Config.EnableDirection}} opens the tournament direction gestures in the embedded engine, as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}direction}} does for the daemon; they are closed by default.


\subsection{Tournament direction and events}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:direction-de-tournoi-et-evenements}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-direction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tournaments directed at the workstation and the events that group them (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontre}} in the API and its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1/rencontres.*}} routes) are read through the API, under the caller’s tenant, with the same code as the workstation. Reading is always served; the gestures (entering a result, pairing, creating an event) are served only under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}direction}} ({\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-direction-gestures}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Direction gestures}}}}}).
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.list}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.directory}} read the whole tenant: the list of directed tournaments, the player directory.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The other \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.*}} take \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"tournamentId": N\}}}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.get}} (the full view: proposals, standings, matches in progress), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.participants}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.freeParticipants}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.tableGrid}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.freeSlots}} (the bye slots a latecomer can still take), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.brackets}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.standings}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.standingsCsv}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.history}} (optional \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{player}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{match}} filters), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.clock}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.slots}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.lastDecision}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.pageHtml}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.pairingSheetHtml}} (with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{round}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{directions.statuses}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tournamentId}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ids}} to read only some registrants) answers “am I playing?”: for each registrant, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kind}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{playing}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bye}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qualified}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{undecided}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{eliminated}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{winner}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{withdrawn}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{not\_entered}}), the phase, the section, the round and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{label}} in codes, never in sentences, the remaining lives (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lives}}) and, when a match is in progress, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{matchId}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{table}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{opponent}}. An identifier that is not registered is omitted.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontres.list}}, then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontres.get}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontres.pageHtml}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"id": N\}}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontres.pageHtml}} renders the room’s wall page, a self\sphinxhyphen{}contained HTML document in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{html}} field: a wall screen displays it and reloads it periodically.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontres.ranking}} returns the season ranking, like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb tournament ranking \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}season}}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontreId}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{from}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{to}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{points}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{participation}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{elo}}, all optional; without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rencontreId}} or a period, all the tenant’s directed tournaments count.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pages are rendered in French, the language of the direction engine. A tournament that is not directed, or that belongs to another tenant, answers \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{404}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Conditional reads.} Each of these routes returns an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ETag}} header.
