\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }blunderDB/deploy
cp\PYG{+w}{ }.env.example\PYG{+w}{ }.env\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} POSTGRES\PYGZus{}PASSWORD}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }compose\PYG{+w}{ }up\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 401}
curl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i\PYG{+w}{ }http://localhost:8080/v1/metadata.counts\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{}}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 200}
curl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{+w}{ }alice:demo\PYGZhy{}password\PYG{+w}{ }http://localhost:8080/v1/metadata.counts\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{}}
curl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{+w}{ }alice:demo\PYGZhy{}password\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}H\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}X\PYGZhy{}Tenant\PYGZhy{}ID: 999\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{     }http://localhost:8080/v1/metadata.counts\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}\PYGZsq{}}

docker\PYG{+w}{ }compose\PYG{+w}{ }logs\PYG{+w}{ }blunderdb\PYGZhy{}serve
docker\PYG{+w}{ }compose\PYG{+w}{ }down\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first request is rejected by Caddy, before it even reaches the daemon. The next two are authenticated as “alice”, whom the mapping table associates with tenant 1: they return the same body (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"positions":0,"analyses":0,"matches":0,…\}}}) and the daemon’s log carries \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tenant=1}} for both — the value 999 sent by the client did not survive the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Caddyfile}}’s guard. This scenario has been replayed as written.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To pull the published image instead of building it, replace the three \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build:}} lines of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb\sphinxhyphen{}serve}} service in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker\sphinxhyphen{}compose.yml}} with a single \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{image:}} line, then run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker compose up \sphinxhyphen{}d}} without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nt}{blunderdb\PYGZhy{}serve}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{image}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ghcr.io/kevung/blunderdb\PYGZhy{}serve:\PYGZlt{}version\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{restart}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{unless\PYGZhy{}stopped}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Compose file publishes Caddy’s port on every interface (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{8080:80}}): that is what one expects from a proxy, which is there to be reached. What must never be published is the daemon — and it is not, it has no \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ports:}} at all.


\subsection{Updating a deployment}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:mettre-a-jour-un-deploiement}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-mise-a-jour}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The schema is migrated automatically at startup, and this migration is \sphinxstylestrong{one\sphinxhyphen{}way}: a database migrated to a recent schema is no longer readable by an earlier version of blunderDB (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:annexe-db-migration}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Database Schema}}}}}). The order of the steps therefore matters.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Back up first}, before anything else: it is the only way back (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-sauvegarde}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Backup and restore}}}}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pull the tag of the intended version}, never \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{latest}} in production. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{latest}} follows the most recently published version: a deployment that pins it changes version at the whim of restarts, without anyone deciding to, and without the backup from step 1 necessarily being recent.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Restart the daemon} on the new image. It migrates the schema before serving a single request; if the migration fails, it stops on the error rather than serve a half\sphinxhyphen{}migrated database.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Check the readiness probe.} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GET /readyz}} answers \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{200}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"status":"ready","version":"…"\}}} when storage responds and its schema matches the binary’s; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{503}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"status":"down"\}}} when the database is unreachable; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{503}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"status":"version\_mismatch","version":"…","expected":"…"\}}} when the two schemas differ — the response names the database’s and the one the binary expects. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb healthcheck}} returns the same verdict as an exit code.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under row\sphinxhyphen{}level security (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}rls}}), the first start of a version that adds a derivation computed by the daemon, such as the provenance of analyses, walks once through the rows of every tenant: each batch briefly locks the tables it touches, and tenant requests wait for the batch to finish. If a table stays busy for more than five seconds, the daemon starts anyway and resumes the walk at the next start; once the walk is complete, later starts lock nothing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{version\_mismatch}} that persists after the restart means a rollback: an older binary facing an already\sphinxhyphen{}migrated database. There is no downward migration; it is the backup from step 1 that must be restored.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Before enabling} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}read\sphinxhyphen{}tenants}} \sphinxstylestrong{on an existing deployment}, update the proxy: a proxy configured before this header existed strips only \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} and would forward as is an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Read\sphinxhyphen{}Tenants}} sent by the client, which would then read other tenants. Without the option, the daemon refuses this header: a proxy that lets it through shows up in its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{400}} responses.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{PostgreSQL backend and multi\sphinxhyphen{}user}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:backend-postgresql-et-multi-utilisateurs}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-postgres}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a shared deployment, blunderDB can store data in \sphinxstylestrong{PostgreSQL} rather than in a SQLite file. The backend is selected with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}backend postgres}} and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dsn}} connection string. The schema is created and migrated automatically at startup.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Data is \sphinxstylestrong{partitioned per tenant}: each request carries its tenant’s identifier (the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} header, a positive decimal integer such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{42}}), which lets several users share the same instance without seeing each other’s data. An identifier that is not such an integer — a name like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{alice}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{default}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{007}} — is refused with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{400 invalid}}: the reverse\sphinxhyphen{}proxy maps an account to its integer, the daemon never guesses.


\subsection{Row\sphinxhyphen{}Level Security}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:row-level-security}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}rls}} option additionally enables PostgreSQL’s \sphinxstylestrong{Row\sphinxhyphen{}Level Security}. At every startup, the daemon installs on every table carrying a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tenant\_id}} a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tenant\_isolation}} policy that lets through only the rows of the tenant named by the session parameter \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{current\_setting('app.tenant\_id')}}, and enforces it down to the table’s owner (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY}}). This parameter is set on the connection when it leaves the pool and reset when it returns; a connection with no tenant sees no row and inserts none. This is an optional defence in depth, disabled by default: the application code’s tenant filtering stays in place either way.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The connection role must be ordinary}: neither superuser nor \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BYPASSRLS}}. PostgreSQL lets both of those sail through every policy without a word, and isolation falls back to the application code alone. That same role must, on the other hand, own the tables, since it is the one that runs the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ALTER TABLE}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CREATE POLICY}} statements.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{On an already\sphinxhyphen{}populated database, there is nothing to migrate}: applying the policies is idempotent DDL, replayed at every startup after the schema migration. No data is moved, no row rewritten; turning \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}rls}} on or off is just a restart.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The cost is measured}: on reading a position, 101.8 µs without, 177.0 µs with, i.e. \sphinxstylestrong{+73.8 \%} — same container, same rows, two pools differing only by this flag. It is paid on every connection borrowed from the pool (setting then resetting the parameter) and on the predicate every query crosses in addition, never on the volume of data.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Opening and closing a tenant}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:ouvrir-et-fermer-un-tenant}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There is \sphinxstylestrong{nothing to create} on the server side: a tenant is not a record, it is the integer its rows carry. The database has no table of tenants and the daemon keeps no list of them — opening an account means adding an entry to the proxy’s mapping table, and the member’s first write is what makes their tenant exist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An empty tenant answers like an empty database, with no error: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{metadata.counts}} returns zeros and the lists return nothing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a tenant is decommissioned, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST /ops/tenant.purge}} permanently deletes all its data (positions, matches, collections, history, etc.) for the current tenant (the one carried by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}}), \sphinxstylestrong{as well as its session state} (last search, last position, open tabs — the rows of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{session\_state}} table carrying that tenant): the operation runs in a single transaction, is idempotent (no error purging an already\sphinxhyphen{}empty tenant or repeating the call), and does not affect any other tenant. It erases this tenant’s rows in \sphinxstylestrong{every} table that carries one, leaving only what belongs to no one: the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{metadata}} table, including the global schema\sphinxhyphen{}version row, and the migration log. The purged tenant therefore becomes exactly an empty tenant again, and its integer can be reassigned. It is only available with the PostgreSQL backend — it returns an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{invalid}} error on a SQLite backend, which has no notion of tenant.


\subsection{Compaction and connection pool}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:compactage-et-pool-de-connexions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST /ops/maintenance.vacuum}} compacts the daemon’s SQLite file — the counterpart of the “Reclaimable space” line of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Maintenance} tab of the graphical interface and of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb vacuum}} command (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}), with the same disk\sphinxhyphen{}space guard — and returns the sizes before and after (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sizeBefore}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sizeAfter}}, in bytes). It is only available with the SQLite backend; on PostgreSQL, which has no file to compact, it returns an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{invalid}} error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The PostgreSQL connection pool is tuned via environment variable: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_MAX\_CONNS}} (50 by default), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_MIN\_CONNS}} (5), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_MAX\_CONN\_LIFETIME}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1h}}), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_HEALTH\_CHECK\_PERIOD}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{30s}}), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_CONNECT\_TIMEOUT}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5s}} — past it, an unreachable database fails fast instead of hanging on the operating system’s TCP timeout) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_MAX\_CONN\_IDLE\_TIME}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{30m}} — a connection opened for a burst of traffic does not sit in the pool forever once the burst is over). Each value is a Go\sphinxhyphen{}formatted duration (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{5s}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{30m}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1h}}); absent or malformed, it falls back to its default. When \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}metrics}} is on, the pool’s state is continuously exposed on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/metrics}}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb\_pg\_pool\_acquired}} (connections currently in use), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_idle}} (available ones), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_max}} (the configured ceiling) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_wait\_count}} (the cumulative count of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Acquire}} calls that had to wait for a free connection).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BLUNDERDB\_POSTGRES\_QUERY\_EXEC\_MODE}} selects the pool’s query execution mode: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cache\_describe}} (the default), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cache\_statement}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{describe\_exec}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exec}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{simple\_protocol}} (pgx’s names). By default the engine does not prepare named plans on the server: with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cache\_statement}}, every distinct SQL text (variable\sphinxhyphen{}length \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IN}} lists and multi\sphinxhyphen{}row inserts) leaves a plan in memory on the connection until it closes. An unknown value makes startup fail; a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{default\_query\_exec\_mode}} given in the connection URL takes precedence over the variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the SQLite backend, the daemon opens one connection per core, ten at least (the desktop keeps ten). Requests that scan the whole library (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats.*}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search.count}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search.find}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search.ids}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search.query}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search.indexOf}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{matches.list}}) run at most one per pair of cores, two at least, so that connections stay free for single\sphinxhyphen{}row reads; the next ones wait their turn, at most 20 s and eight per slot, then receive \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{503}} (code \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unavailable}}) with a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Retry\sphinxhyphen{}After}} header. A write that cannot get the database, held by another writer beyond its wait, receives the same answer: nothing was written, and the request can be retried as is. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}heavy\sphinxhyphen{}slots}} sets another number; on PostgreSQL these reads are bounded only when it is given.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At startup, a SQLite daemon computes in the background the missing per\sphinxhyphen{}match statistics (the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stats.matches}} line of the maintenance); a statistics read arriving during this computation waits for it, then reads the result.


\section{Migrating a SQLite database to PostgreSQL}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:migrer-une-base-sqlite-vers-postgresql}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-migrate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb migrate}} copies a single\sphinxhyphen{}user SQLite database to a PostgreSQL backend, under a chosen tenant — the integer the reverse\sphinxhyphen{}proxy will send in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} for that user — this is the path to “upload” a desktop library to a server deployment.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }migrate\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}from\PYG{+w}{ }sqlite:///path/to/database.db\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}to\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=disable\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}tenant\PYGZhy{}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{42}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dry\PYGZhy{}run}
blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }migrate\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}from\PYG{+w}{ }sqlite:///path/to/database.db\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}tenant\PYGZhy{}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{42}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}dry\PYGZhy{}run
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The migration copies the \sphinxstylestrong{positions, their analyses and comments, the matches (games + moves), the tournaments (with their match links) and the collections (with their composition)}, as well as the match equity tables (the current one and the one with which each analysis was valued), reassigning primary and foreign keys, all within a \sphinxstylestrong{single transaction} on the destination side: the operation is atomic (a failure leaves the destination intact, just run it again). Positions, their analyses and moves are written in batches. Progress and the final summary are emitted as NDJSON on standard output; each copied family also leaves one line in the log (standard error) with its row count and duration. If the source database is old enough to need its own in\sphinxhyphen{}place schema upgrade, that runs first and emits its own \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"schema\sphinxhyphen{}migration"}} events (phase/done/total) before the copy begins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
During the copy, the transaction holds a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE}} lock on the position, analysis, match, game and move tables: two simultaneous \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}} runs, even to different tenants, run one after the other and autovacuum skips those tables; the daemon’s reads and writes are not blocked. The DSN’s role must be allowed to run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ANALYZE}} on these tables — own them, be superuser or, from PostgreSQL 17, hold the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MAINTAIN}} privilege — otherwise \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}} stops before copying anything.

Application states are not migrated: Anki decks/cards, the filter library, search and command history, and session metadata; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}} announces their count at the end. The error and blunder thresholds, however, are copied (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-sauvegarde}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Backup and restore}}}}}).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\section{The generic \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{call}} dispatcher}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:le-dispatcher-generique-call}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-call}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the historical subcommands ({\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb call}} exposes \sphinxstylestrong{all} storage operations directly, locally. It goes through the same handlers as the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} daemon: the behaviour is therefore identical to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST /v1/<family>.<method>}}. This is useful for scripting and integration testing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}backend remote}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} reads no database: its handlers go through the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} API of the daemon named by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}dsn}} (an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{http://host:port}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{https://…}} URL), with the tenant of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}scope}} and the headers of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}header}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} is refused there: the tenant is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}scope}}). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}db}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}backend remote}} exclude each other. The daemon does not authenticate; the proxy in front of it decides: a refusal by the proxy (HTTP 401 or 403) reads “refused” and points to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}header}}, a limit (HTTP 429, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rate\_limited}}) reads as such, and only a daemon that is unreachable or silent beyond \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}timeout}} reads “daemon unavailable”. A daemon older than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{withPlayed}} ignores it and returns the analysis without the moves played: the answer is printed as is and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} reports it on standard error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A method whose storage has no \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} route (a transaction, a Direction, Rencontre, Duel, match equity table or transcription service) does not go through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}backend remote}}: the error says so, the process exits non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} prints on standard error the request to send to the daemon (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST <dsn>/v1/<method>}}). The same holds for exports (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exports.sqlite}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exports.json}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exports.plan}}, incremental ones included): call the daemon directly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} serves the transcription moves without any flag: it works on a local file, like the CLI. Every call is a fresh process, hence its own session: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sessionId}} can be omitted, and there is no undo from one call to the next.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The JSON response (or the NDJSON stream for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{*.list}} endpoints) is written to standard output. On error, the process exits with a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero code and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{"error":\{…\}\}}} envelope is printed to standard output so it stays parseable (for example with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{jq}}); so is an error that occurs in the middle of a stream. A response carrying a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Direction\sphinxhyphen{}Version}} header prints it on standard error: that is the value the next gesture passes to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}if\sphinxhyphen{}match}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}} serves direction gestures without a flag, like the CLI, since it runs locally.


\section{Tools for an AI assistant (MCP)}
\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:outils-pour-un-assistant-ia-mcp}}\label{\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-mcp}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB embeds no language model: it offers its tools to the assistant you already use (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, a local client), through the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Model Context Protocol}. The assistant searches, reads and explains; blunderDB answers with its own figures.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools go through the same handlers as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}}:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only these tools write — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{save\_position}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{comment\_position}} (which signs with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{author}} argument, otherwise with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}User\sphinxhyphen{}Name}} header), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create\_collection}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{add\_to\_collection}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anki\_review}}, which grades a card drawn by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anki\_next}}, and the transcription gestures \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_create}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_open}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_apply}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_undo}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_redo}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcribe\_finish}}, served only by a daemon launched with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}transcription}}; each gesture that changes the draft names its session and the last revision seen, and a stale revision is refused as for a direct client — and they are offered only on request: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}write}} locally, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}mcp\sphinxhyphen{}write}} on the daemon. All the others only read; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rollout}} nevertheless gains, when writing is offered, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{store}} argument, which records the rollout beside the position’s analysis. No tool deletes anything.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Locally}, the assistant launches \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb mcp}} on a file (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}). For Claude Code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
claude\PYG{+w}{ }mcp\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYG{+w}{ }blunderdb\PYG{+w}{ }mcp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}db\PYG{+w}{ }/chemin/vers/base.db
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{On the daemon}, the same tools answer over HTTP on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POST /mcp}} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{streamable HTTP} transport, sessionless). Like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mcp}} requires \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Tenant\sphinxhyphen{}ID}} and each tool works in that tenant; a program that embeds \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pkg/blunderdb/server}} serves it too. The daemon authenticates nobody (ADR\sphinxhyphen{}0005): \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mcp}} is protected at the proxy like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}mcp\sphinxhyphen{}write}} is decided there like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}direction}}. Every \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/v1}} call a tool makes goes through the daemon’s whole chain again: it is logged, counted in the metrics and charged to the tenant’s rate limit, on top of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mcp}} request that carries it. A tool call therefore costs several requests; none is exempted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{call}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb mcp}} migrates an older database’s schema when it opens it, even without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}write}}.

\sphinxstepscope

\section{Idempotency}
\label{\detokenize{api_reference:idempotence}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Most methods need no special mechanism: reads have no side effects, and the writes of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions.*}} are idempotent in effect thanks to the Zobrist hash of the content — saving the same position twice returns the same row, never a duplicate. 59 methods accept an optional \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Idempotency\sphinxhyphen{}Key}} header: those whose two calls are two distinct effects, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{positions.save}}, whose response says whether the call created the position (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{created}}) and would say so wrongly if replayed after a lost response. A call replayed with the same key returns the result of the first attempt instead of repeating its effect — see the “(Idempotency\sphinxhyphen{}Key)” mark in the table above. No other method needs or accepts this header.


\section{Conditional reads}
\label{\detokenize{api_reference:lectures-conditionnelles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Methods marked “(ETag)” return an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ETag}} header. Sending it back in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{If\sphinxhyphen{}None\sphinxhyphen{}Match}} gets a body\sphinxhyphen{}less \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{304}} response as long as nothing the method reads has changed — see {\hyperref[\detokenize{mode_headless:headless-direction}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Tournament direction and events}}}}}.


\section{Saving and reading an analysis}
\label{\detokenize{api_reference:enregistrer-et-lire-une-analyse}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analyses.save}} stores the analysis as given and replaces the one the position carried: nothing of the old one is kept. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analyses.merge}} folds it into the stored analysis, in one transaction, as the desktop and the command line do: the candidate moves of both (by notation), each engine’s cube analysis, the union of the moves played, the rollouts of both, the creation date of the stored analysis. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analyses.load}} returns the analysis as stored; with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{withPlayed}} set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}}, its played moves and cube actions are joined with those the matches played in the position, and its cube analyses come XG first, as the desktop reads them. Every \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analyses.load}} response carries the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{X\sphinxhyphen{}Blunderdb\sphinxhyphen{}With\sphinxhyphen{}Played}} header: a daemon that does not send it ignores \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{withPlayed}} and returns the analysis without the matches’ moves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{checkerAnalysis}} is the merged view of the candidate moves: for each move, the deepest evaluation. When several sources have evaluated the position (one engine at one depth, a rollout being a depth of its own), the analysis also carries \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{allCheckerAnalyses}}: one entry per source, with its engine (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analysisEngine}}), its depth (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analysisDepth}}) and its own moves (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{moves}}), XG first, like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{allCubeAnalyses}} for the cube. The field is absent when a single source has evaluated the position: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{checkerAnalysis}} is then that source, even when its moves carry several depths (XG rolls out its best moves and evaluates the others less deeply). A source imported again replaces its own entry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{allCheckerAnalyses}} is absent and the moves of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{checkerAnalysis}} carry several \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analysisEngine}}, the position was analysed by several engines under a schema older than 2.58.0: each move carries the deepest evaluation, and what each engine alone said is no longer known. No source is then available, and a new import does not rebuild it.


\section{Reading a match’s moves}
\label{\detokenize{api_reference:lire-les-coups-d-un-match}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every move that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{matches.moves}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{matches.movesByMatch}} return is judged by the stored analysis of its position, without the read starting any engine. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{error\_mp}} is the equity the played move lost, in millipoints. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{best\_move}}, on a checker move, is the analysis’s first candidate move, in its notation, from the point of view of the player on roll — the one who played the move; it is returned even when the played move is not among the candidates. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{best\_cube\_action}}, on a cube action, is the cheaper of the two decisions that player had: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Double}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{No Double}} for the player who could double (too good to double gives \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{No Double}}), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Take}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pass}} for the player who was offered the cube. It is ranked by the very errors \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{error\_mp}} is drawn from, never by the best\sphinxhyphen{}action label the analysis carries: once imported, that label can contradict the equities it comes with. At equal cost, it is the decision played.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Without an analysis of the right type, all three fields are absent. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{error\_mp}} is also absent when the played move is not among the candidates, whereas \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{best\_move}} is returned. A position reached by several matches names the same best move in each.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A client shows “better” only when \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{error\_mp}} is present and non\sphinxhyphen{}zero; it does not compare the played move with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{best\_move}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{best\_cube\_action}}: two notations of the same move can differ, and two moves of equal equity both cost 0.


\section{Timecodes of a transcription}
\label{\detokenize{api_reference:reperes-d-une-transcription}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transcriptions.apply}} gesture can carry the video instant at which it is made, in milliseconds from the start of the media: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TickMS}}, read only when \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{HasTick}} is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} (0 is an instant). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{enter\_die}} makes it the timecode of the roll (the first die key counts); \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{enter\_play}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{validate}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dance}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{double}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pass}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{resign}} make it the timecode of the action, on a new action only: an in\sphinxhyphen{}place correction keeps the timecodes it had. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_timecode}} gesture sets \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TickMS}} (with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{HasTick}}) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RollTickMS}} (with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{HasRollTick}}) on the cursor’s action; a negative value clears the timecode. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_video}} gesture attaches the video source named by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VideoSource}} (http(s) URL or local path), and an empty string detaches it; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_header}} also sets it when its header names one, but never clears it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{seek\_cursor}} gesture puts the cursor on the action of rank \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{At}}, the end of the document past the last one, without writing anything or stacking on the undo stack: this is how the cursor follows a playing video. A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_ms}} accompanied by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_estimated}} is an estimate: a play without an action timecode, measured from the roll to the next action’s first instant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rendered state carries the source in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{header.video\_source}}, the timecodes of each action in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{roll\_tick\_ms}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tick\_ms}}, and, on each annotated action, the durations \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decision\_ms}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cube\_decision\_ms}}: measured by the Arbiter when they are, otherwise deduced from the timecodes. A timecode earlier than the previous one is flagged by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{timecode\_backwards}} inconsistency and leaves the durations that depend on it unknown.

\chapter{Annex: Advanced Filter Usage}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_filtres:annexe-utilisation-avancee-des-filtres}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_filtres:annexe-filtres}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_filtres::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is for advanced users of blunderDB who wish to fully leverage the position search features.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Filters are at the heart of position analysis in blunderDB. Their use allows for searching specific positions with great precision. In this section, the use of filters through the command line is detailed. The command line can be accessed by pressing the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SPACE}} key. It allows users to quickly combine filters and use the filter library with ease.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The search grammar — the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s}} command, its tokens, searching within the current results with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ss}} — is described once, in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{cmd_mode:cmd-filter}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Search Filters}}}}} section of the command list; the search panel itself is described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-recherche}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{manual}}}}}. This annex keeps only the filter library and examples.


\section{Filter Library}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_filtres:bibliotheque-de-filtres}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The filter library allows the user to save search commands to facilitate their thematic studies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To add a filter to the library,
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Start the search you want to keep (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{s}} command followed by filters).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the search panel (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TAB}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}F}}) and select the \sphinxstyleemphasis{History} tab.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Click the bookmark icon of the search to save.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Give the filter a name and confirm.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use a filter saved in the library,
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open the search panel (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TAB}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CTRL\sphinxhyphen{}F}}) and select the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Saved} tab.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Search for the desired filter.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Double\sphinxhyphen{}click on the filter to start the search.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A filter used every day is pinned with one click on its star: it then runs with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ALT\sphinxhyphen{}1}} … \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ALT\sphinxhyphen{}9}} without opening the panel (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_bibliotheque:panneau-recherche}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Search Panel}}}}}).

\chapter{Windows Annex: what to do if Windows blocks the launch}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite:annexe-windows-que-faire-si-windows-bloque-le-lancement}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite:annexe-windows-malware}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following applies to Windows 10 and 11 operating systems.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows now requires software publishing companies or independent software developers to digitally certify their applications, or even distribute them via the Windows Store. It is therefore recommended to turn to external companies to obtain a digital certificate, which costs several hundred euros (see, for example, \sphinxurl{https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/ie\_fr/certificats-de-signature-de-code-ev-extended-validation-et-microsoft-smartscreen}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since I am offering blunderDB for free, I do not wish to pursue these costly options. A \sphinxstylestrong{free} avenue reserved for open\sphinxhyphen{}source software (the \sphinxstyleemphasis{SignPath Foundation}, \sphinxurl{https://signpath.org/}) was explored, but the application was unsuccessful; the Windows binaries are therefore not digitally signed. Consequently, it is very likely that Windows will warn you of a potential threat or even block the execution of blunderDB entirely. The following sections explain the steps to bypass Windows’ reluctance, and how to verify the integrity of the downloaded binary.


\section{Windows SmartScreen Warning}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite:avertissement-windows-smartscreen}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After downloading blunderDB, when you run it, Windows may display a warning such as:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{smartscreen_en}.png}
\end{figure}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This screenshot comes from an English\sphinxhyphen{}language Windows. On a French\sphinxhyphen{}language Windows, the same screen is titled \sphinxstyleemphasis{Windows a protégé votre ordinateur} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Windows protected your PC}); the link to click is \sphinxstyleemphasis{Informations supplémentaires} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{More info}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Informations complémentaires} depending on the Windows version), and the button that appears next is \sphinxstyleemphasis{Exécuter quand même} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Run anyway}).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Two clicks are enough in almost every case} — \sphinxstyleemphasis{More Info}, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run anyway} — and there is nothing else to do: no antivirus exclusion, no setting to change. The following section only covers the rare cases where the block did not come from SmartScreen.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to allow a specific executable blocked by SmartScreen:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Try running the executable}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you attempt to launch the executable, SmartScreen may block it and display a warning.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Click on “More Info”}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the SmartScreen warning window, click on \sphinxstylestrong{More Info}.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Select “Run anyway”}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you trust the executable, click \sphinxstylestrong{Run anyway} to bypass the SmartScreen warning for this instance.

\end{itemize}

\end{enumerate}


\section{Windows Defender Blocking}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite:blocage-windows-defender}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is a \sphinxstylestrong{last resort}, to be followed only if the block did not come from SmartScreen. For certain security settings, it does happen that despite the unblocking described above, Windows Defender still prevents blunderDB from running, with messages such as:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{blunderdb_potential_virus}.png}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or even:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{threat_found_action_needed}.png}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or even place it in quarantine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows Defender is known to trigger false positives. This issue is explicitly mentioned in the FAQ on the official Golang website ( \sphinxurl{https://go.dev/doc/faq\#virus} ) or in GitHub tickets for some projects programmed in Go ( \sphinxurl{https://github.com/golang/vscode-go/issues/3182} ).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Excluding a file from antivirus scanning is not a trivial action: the exclusion applies to a path, and any file later placed at that location will also escape scanning. First check the SHA\sphinxhyphen{}256 fingerprint of the downloaded file (next section): it is that fingerprint, not the exclusion, that proves you are running the published binary.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to prevent Windows Security from scanning blunderDB:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Open Windows Security}:

\section{Verify the download integrity (SHA256)}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_windows_securite:verifier-l-integrite-du-telechargement-sha256}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each binary published on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{releases} page comes with a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.sha256}} file containing its cryptographic fingerprint. Checking this fingerprint ensures that the downloaded file is authentic and has not been tampered with, which is a useful guarantee in the absence of code signing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On Windows (PowerShell), in the download folder:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{Get\PYGZhy{}FileHash} \PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{n}{blunderDB}\PYG{n}{\PYGZhy{}windows}\PYG{p}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{version}\PYG{p}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{exe} \PYG{n}{\PYGZhy{}Algorithm} \PYG{n}{SHA256}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare the displayed value with the one in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderDB\sphinxhyphen{}windows\sphinxhyphen{}<version>.exe.sha256}} file. The two must be identical.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On Linux or macOS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sha256sum\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }blunderDB\PYGZhy{}linux\PYGZhy{}\PYGZlt{}version\PYGZgt{}.sha256\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Linux}
shasum\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}a\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{256}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }blunderDB\PYGZhy{}macos\PYGZhy{}\PYGZlt{}version\PYGZgt{}.zip.sha256\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} macOS}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Mac Annex: Possible Blocking of blunderDB}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_mac_securite:annexe-mac-blocage-eventuel-de-blunderdb}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_mac_securite:annexe-mac-malware}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_mac_securite::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following concerns the macOS operating system.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Mac requires software publishing companies or independent software developers to digitally certify their applications. The developer must enroll in the Apple Developer Program by paying an annual membership fee (\sphinxurl{https://developer.apple.com/support/compare-memberships/}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since I am sharing blunderDB for free, I do not wish to pursue these costly options. As a result, Mac will likely warn you of a potential risk or even block the execution of blunderDB entirely. The following sections explain the steps to bypass Mac’s restrictions.


\section{Installation of blunderDB}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_mac_securite:installation-de-blunderdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After downloading \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderDB\sphinxhyphen{}macos\sphinxhyphen{}x.y.z.zip}}, unzip it, then drag \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderDB.app}} into the Applications section of your Finder. If you have already tried to run blunderDB and Mac warns you of a potential risk, follow the steps below.


\section{Authorization to Run blunderDB}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_mac_securite:autorisation-de-l-execution-de-blunderdb}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open Finder and go to the Applications section.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find blunderDB and right\sphinxhyphen{}click on it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select Open.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A warning window will appear. Click Open.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB will open, and you can start using it.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since macOS 15 (Sequoia), right\sphinxhyphen{}clicking no longer offers to bypass the warning:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Launch blunderDB once, then dismiss the warning.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open \sphinxstyleemphasis{System Settings}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Privacy \& Security} section.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under \sphinxstyleemphasis{Security}, click \sphinxstyleemphasis{Open Anyway} next to blunderDB, then confirm.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You only need to perform this operation once. Afterward, you can open blunderDB without having to go through these steps.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Annex: Database Schema}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:annexe-schema-de-la-base-de-donnees}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:annexe-db-migration}}\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A blunderDB database is a plain SQLite file (extension \sphinxstyleemphasis{.db}). Without blunderDB, it can therefore be opened and inspected with any SQLite editor or file browser.


\section{Versioning and migrations}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:versionnage-et-migrations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The database schema is \sphinxstylestrong{versioned}. The current schema version is \sphinxstylestrong{2.60.0}; it is independent of the application version and is only incremented when the internal structure changes. The schema version of an open database is shown in the \sphinxstylestrong{Metadata} panel (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{meta}} command).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Always back up your \sphinxstyleemphasis{.db} file before opening a database created with an earlier version of blunderDB.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since version 0.10.0, \sphinxstylestrong{all schema migrations are performed automatically} when a database is opened. No manual migration command is needed. The migration is done in place: a database migrated to a recent schema can no longer be opened by older versions of blunderDB, hence the importance of backing it up first.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A database also records in its metadata (key \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_reader\_version}}) the minimum schema version a blunderDB must read to open it. From this version on, blunderDB knows this key: if it reads a schema older than that minimum, it refuses to open the database, in the graphical interface, on the command line, with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{serve}} as with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{migrate}}, and shows both versions: the database is left untouched. Earlier versions ignore this key. A database read without being opened, the source of an import or a file compared with the open one, is refused in the same way.


\section{Main tables}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:principales-tables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The current schema is built around the following tables:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Positions and analyses}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{position}} (the positions, deduplicated), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{analysis}} (the associated analysis data) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{comment}} (the comments).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matches}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{match}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{game}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{move}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{move\_analysis}} store the imported matches, their games, their moves and the analysis of each move.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Collections}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{collection}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{collection\_position}} (link table) group together manually chosen positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tournaments}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tournament}} groups matches into tournaments.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spaced repetition (Anki)}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anki\_deck}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anki\_card}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{anki\_review\_log}} manage the decks, the cards and the review log (FSRS algorithm).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Change journal}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{change\_log}} dates the last write of each object, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{position\_part\_fact}} that of a position’s drawing and variant link, erasures included. Two libraries use them to synchronise.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Marks on a position}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{position\_drawing}} holds the drawing and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{position\_derivation}} the link from a variant to the position it comes from; the column \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{position.public\_id}} holds a label chosen by the caller.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{History and miscellaneous}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{command\_history}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{search\_history}} keep the history of commands and searches, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{filter\_library}} the filter library, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{metadata}} the database metadata (including the schema version).

\end{itemize}


\section{Design principles}
\label{\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:principes-de-conception}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From schema 2.0.0 onwards, several design choices speed up searches and reduce the file size:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Position deduplication}: each position carries a Zobrist hash and a unique index, so that the same position encountered across several imports is stored only once.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Denormalised filter columns}: frequently searched criteria (decision type, dice, race difference, checkers borne off, back checkers, checker\sphinxhyphen{}play or cube error, chances of winning, etc.) are precomputed into dedicated columns for fast filtering.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bitboard prefilter}: occupancy and point\sphinxhyphen{}mask columns enable a very fast integer prefilter when searching for structure patterns.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compact storage}: positions are encoded compactly and analysis data is stored in a compressed binary format (zstd with a shared dictionary; older analyses, in JSON, remain readable and are converted by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vacuum}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reencode}}), which greatly reduces the file size.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{WAL journaling}: WAL mode and tuned PRAGMAs improve read and write performance.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope

\section{Formal definitions}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:definitions-formelles}}

\subsection{PR (Performance Rating)}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:pr-performance-rating}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PR is the average equity error per counted decision, multiplied by 500 as eXtreme Gammon does:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{PR} = \frac{\sum_i |\mathrm{error}_i|}{\mathrm{N_{counted}}} \times 500\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The numerator is the sum of the errors in normalised equity (EMG at the score), each one being that of the move played in its match.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The denominator \(N_\text{compté}\) counts decisions according to XG’s rules: non\sphinxhyphen{}forced checker plays, doubles offered, takes and passes, and close “no double” decisions. These rules, their rationale and their limits are detailed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-pr}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{PR (Performance Rating)}}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The factor 500 is XG’s convention. It is not a conversion to millipoints: an average error of 0.010 of equity — i.e. 10 millipoints (mpt) — gives a PR of 5.0. The errors of a position, on the other hand, are properly read in millipoints, that is, in thousandths of equity: the blunder threshold below, the search filters \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{e>}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{E>}}, the magnitude histogram of the Stats panel.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Snowie Error Rate}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:snowie-error-rate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Snowie ER uses the \sphinxstylestrong{same numerator} as PR, but the denominator is the number of checker plays of both players, forced moves included, with no counting rule:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{SnowieER} = \frac{\sum_i |\mathrm{error}_i|}{N_\text{P1} + N_\text{P2}} \times 500\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reference: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/formatgs.c:415–424}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Snowie ER is more stable across tools because its denominator depends on no decision\sphinxhyphen{}counting rule. It serves as a cross\sphinxhyphen{}check metric XG ↔ gnuBG ↔ blunderDB.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The “Player” filter applies to the numerator only.} Selecting a player restricts the summed errors to that player’s own decisions, but the denominator stays the number of checker plays by \sphinxstylestrong{both} players, over the matches the filter retains. This is what sets the Snowie ER apart from the PR, and the reason for the following property: on a database holding only matches between two players, the sum of their two Snowie ERs is exactly the unfiltered Snowie ER.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A player’s Snowie ER is typically about half their PR, because the denominator includes moves from both players while PR only uses that player’s decisions.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{MWC loss (Match Winning Chance)}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:perte-mwc-match-winning-chance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
MWC loss expresses in percentage points of match\sphinxhyphen{}winning probability the cumulative effect of a player’s errors. For each decision, the EMG error is converted to MWC using the MET (Match Equity Table) at the current score:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{MWCLoss} = \sum_i \mathrm{eq2mwc}(\mathrm{erreur}_i, \mathrm{score}_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A take or pass is converted at the cube before the double, like the doubler’s decision and like XG does. The conversion and its limits are detailed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{metriques:metrique-perte-mwc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{MWC loss per decision and match chart}}}}}.


\subsection{Luck}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:chance-luck}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{luck} of a roll is the gap between what the dice gave and what they give on average:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{luck} = \mathrm{eq}(\text{best play with the roll obtained})
              - \frac{1}{36}\sum_{d} \mathrm{eq}(\text{best play with } d)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the sum running over the 36 outcomes of the roll (30 non\sphinxhyphen{}double rolls for the opening play of a game, which cannot be a double). A positive value means a favourable roll. Reference: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/analysis.c:199–269}} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LuckNormal}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LuckFirst}}, cubeful evaluation at 0 ply).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{important}{Important:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{blunderDB never recomputes luck}: the built\sphinxhyphen{}in evaluator is not used for that. It takes verbatim the value written by the tool that analysed the match — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ErrLuck}} for eXtreme Gammon, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LU}} property for gnuBG — having checked that both share the same convention (same unit, positive = lucky).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Practical consequences:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Formats that do not carry luck (\sphinxstylestrong{BGF}, \sphinxstylestrong{Jellyfish .mat}) produce no value at all.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Matches \sphinxstylestrong{already imported} have none either: luck was never stored before schema version 2.15.0, and nothing in the database allows it to be reconstructed. The source files must be \sphinxstylestrong{re\sphinxhyphen{}imported} to obtain it.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A missing value means \sphinxstyleemphasis{unknown}, never \sphinxstyleemphasis{zero} — zero is a genuinely neutral roll. Luck averages therefore divide only by the number of rolls whose luck is known.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A match in which \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} roll would have exactly zero luck is treated as unanalysed in that respect (eXtreme Gammon writes 0 both for “neutral” and for “not computed”): its rolls stay unknown. On the gnuBG side the distinction is explicit — an unevaluated roll carries \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LU{[}\sphinxhyphen{}inf{]}}} — and those rolls stay unknown as well, rather than being turned into a value.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Wins and losses}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:victoires-et-defaites}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB \sphinxstylestrong{stores no winner at match level}: only the points of each game are stored. The result is therefore derived at display time, by adding up the points per seat:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{N\sphinxhyphen{}point match} — winner = the player who reaches N. If nobody does, the match is \sphinxstylestrong{unfinished} (truncated log, resignation) and counts neither a win nor a loss, for anybody.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Money game} (no target) — winner = whoever took the most points; on a tie, neither a win nor a loss. This is gnuBG’s session\sphinxhyphen{}result convention (+1 / 0 / −1, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/relational.c}}).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A consequence to keep in mind when reading the Players tab: \sphinxstylestrong{wins + losses can be lower than the number of matches}. The gap is the unfinished matches.


\subsection{Errors and blunders}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:erreurs-et-blunders}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A decision counts as an \sphinxstylestrong{error} as soon as the associated equity error reaches the library’s \sphinxstylestrong{error threshold}, and as a \sphinxstylestrong{blunder} as soon as it reaches its \sphinxstylestrong{blunder threshold}. Both are set in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Library} tab of the settings and are \sphinxstylestrong{0.050} and \sphinxstylestrong{0.100 EMG} (50 and 100 millipoints) by default. The comparison is \sphinxstyleemphasis{inclusive}: an error of exactly 0.100 is a blunder at the default threshold, on every screen (breakdown by cube action, match detail, players table), and the same pair serves the status bar’s counter and the list offered after an import.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These thresholds belong to each library, and the default values are blunderDB’s own: gnuBG grades plays in three steps (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.03}} doubtful, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.06}} bad, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.12}} very bad — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/gnubg.c:281–286}}) rather than in a single category, and eXtreme Gammon draws its own at 0.020 and 0.080. The settings offer three presets: blunderDB (0.050 and 0.100), XG (0.020 and 0.080) and GNUbg (0.040 and 0.080).

\subsection{Known residual deviations}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:ecarts-residuels-connus}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Four players of the reference matches deviate more, each for a cause rooted in what the file does not carry:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Unanalysed move} (two players). For a move it did not rate, XG writes an error of −1000 and leaves it out of the count; this value is not read at import, and blunderDB rates the move from the stored candidates. blunderDB counts one more decision; PR deviates by up to 0.09, MWC loss by up to 0.45 point.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bear\sphinxhyphen{}off judged outside the file} (one player). XG counts as a decision a bear\sphinxhyphen{}off whose stored candidates cover all legal moves at the same equity: it judged it on evaluations the file does not keep. blunderDB counts one decision fewer; PR deviates by 0.02.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sum of checker\sphinxhyphen{}play errors} (one player). The counts and the cube agree; the sum of the errors of the stored moves exceeds XG’s checker\sphinxhyphen{}play total by a few millipoints (2.150 versus 2.147).

\end{itemize}

\section{Validating your own figures}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:valider-vos-propres-chiffres}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your PR or MWC values diverge from XG figures, check the following points:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Complete analyses} — PR can only be computed on positions that have an analysis. Positions without analysis count as zero error but are not included in \(N_\text{counted}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{XG version} — XG may change its calculations between versions. blunderDB is aligned with the behaviour observed in recent versions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Import format} — gnuBG SGF files produce larger gaps on cube metrics (see table above) because the file does not include complete analyses for all cube decisions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Database migration} — After updating blunderDB, existing databases are migrated automatically. Make a backup before opening a database with a new version.

\end{enumerate}


\section{gnuBG reference}
\label{\detokenize{stats_parity:reference-gnubg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The gnuBG formulas cited on this page are found in the following source files (gnuBG repository):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/formatgs.c:399–409}} — error rate per decision (“Error rate per decision”).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/formatgs.c:415–424}} — Snowie Error Rate.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/analysis.c:458–462}} — checker\sphinxhyphen{}play accumulation, exclusion of forced moves (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cMoves > 1}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/analysis.c:1430–1474}} — Per\sphinxhyphen{}decision EMG → MWC conversion.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/analysis.c:1449–1464}} — MWC loss accumulation (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{eq2mwc}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gnubg/eval.c:5088–5100}} — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isCloseCubedecision}} predicate.

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Version history}
\label{\detokenize{historique:historique-des-versions}}\label{\detokenize{historique:historique}}\label{\detokenize{historique::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Versions are listed from the most recent to the oldest, one bullet per change, and every version ends with references to the pages that describe in detail what it brought. A bullet that a later version has undone carries a note naming the one that replaced it: it tells the software’s history, it does not describe the installed version.


\section{After an update}
\label{\detokenize{historique:apres-une-mise-a-jour}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The database schema migration is \sphinxstylestrong{automatic} on opening, and \sphinxstylestrong{irreversible}: a migrated database is no longer readable by an earlier version of blunderDB, hence the backup beforehand ({\hyperref[\detokenize{annexe_db_scheme:annexe-db-migration}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Annex: Database Schema}}}}}). The rest does not happen by itself, because none of this data is retroactive:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Re\sphinxhyphen{}analyze stale positions} (0.38.0, 0.40.0, 0.46.0, 0.52.0). A gammonNet analysis written by an earlier version of the engine (gammonNet v1.9.0 today, network \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strehl\sphinxhyphen{}prob5\sphinxhyphen{}768\sphinxhyphen{}768\sphinxhyphen{}256\sphinxhyphen{}256\sphinxhyphen{}256}}) is stale: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb analyze \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}stale}}, or the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Stale gammonNet analyses} row of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Maintenance} tab, rewrites it. An imported analysis is never touched.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{0.34.0 (2026\sphinxhyphen{}09\sphinxhyphen{}02)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An \sphinxstylestrong{embedded evaluator}: gammonNet, ported to Go and compiled into blunderDB, evaluates any position offline, without XG or gnuBG — neural network, 0 to 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply search with pruning, cube decision per Janowski and blunderDB’s match\sphinxhyphen{}equity table, and a search that honours the match score.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluation is \sphinxstylestrong{progressive}: 0\sphinxhyphen{}ply immediately on the gesture, then 2\sphinxhyphen{}ply at rest, cancellable by any new gesture, the depth label always naming the one that produced the figure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{gammonNet} tab in settings separates the display depth from the analysis depth.

\item {}

After an import, a bounded, visible, cancellable, resumable \sphinxstylestrong{analysis batch} fills positions with no analysis at all, never overwriting an imported analysis; \sphinxstylestrong{catching up an existing library} starts from the interface, the new \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb analyze}} command, or server mode.

\section{0.33.0 (2026\sphinxhyphen{}08\sphinxhyphen{}26)}
\label{\detokenize{historique:id27}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Stats panel gains a \sphinxstylestrong{Players} tab: the three previous tabs describe one player, this one compares them all, one row per player in the database — matches, wins/losses, counted decisions, overall / checker / cube PR, Snowie Error Rate, blunders and luck. The table sorts by any column, narrows down to the dates of a competition through the usual filters, and clicking a row switches to that player’s detail. A dash marks a value that was never measured, never a zero. The table is also available from the command line (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb list \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}type players}}, as text, JSON or CSV) and in server mode.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{luck} of every roll is now stored in the database and displayed: average luck per roll, in thousandths of a point, signed. It is read on import from eXtreme Gammon files as well as from gnuBG. It is not retroactive — matches imported earlier show a dash, and the source files must be re\sphinxhyphen{}imported to recover it; formats that do not carry it (BGF, Jellyfish \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.mat}}) never will.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{Errors} tab now shows in which \sphinxstyleemphasis{direction} cube decisions go wrong, not just how much they cost: an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Offer} row (missed doubles, premature doubles) and an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Answer} row (wrong passes, wrong takes), deliberately kept apart since one and the same player can double late and take loosely. Each cell carries its count, the tooltip the equity lost, and clicking it loads the matching positions.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
New \sphinxstylestrong{Compact database} command, reclaiming the space left behind by deletions: a button in the settings and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb vacuum}} subcommand. It never runs on its own.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ergonomics: destructive actions ask for confirmation, a search in progress is signalled, an unknown command gets a message instead of silence, and tabs, docked panels and small dialogs are fully keyboard\sphinxhyphen{}operable. Search is also noticeably faster.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Notable fixes: non\sphinxhyphen{}doubles labelled “Double No” by gnuBG were counted as doubles, skewing the cube PR (an existing database can be repaired without re\sphinxhyphen{}importing, in server mode); the player filter wrongly narrowed the denominator of the Snowie Error Rate; exports wrote an outdated schema; and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{blunderdb vacuum}} opened the graphical interface instead of compacting the database.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{manuel_stats:stats}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stats Panel}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{cli:cli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Command Line Interface (CLI)}}}}}.

Importing single positions from new formats (eXtreme Gammon \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.xgp}}, BGBlitz text, native \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.db}} library) with enrichment of duplicates across formats.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Contact}
\label{\detokenize{a_propos:contacts}}\label{\detokenize{a_propos:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Author: Kévin Unger <\sphinxhref{mailto:blunderdb@proton.me}{blunderdb@proton.me}>. You can also find me on Heroes under the username postmanpat.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I initially developed blunderDB for my personal use to help detect patterns in my mistakes. However, it’s very rewarding to receive feedback, especially after spending a lot of time on design, coding, and debugging. So feel free to reach out to share your experiences. All (constructive) feedback is welcome.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are several ways to discuss:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Join the Discord server of blunderDB: \sphinxurl{https://discord.gg/DA5PpzM9En}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Email me at \sphinxhref{mailto:blunderdb@proton.me}{blunderdb@proton.me}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Discuss with me if we meet in a tournament.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
On GitHub.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Open an issue: \sphinxurl{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/issues}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For bug fixes or improvement suggestions, create a pull request.

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Open tickets are grouped by \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/milestones}{milestone} on GitHub. Ideas are discussed in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/discussions/categories/ideas}{Discussions — Ideas category}, and every published release is announced in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/discussions/categories/announcements}{Announcements category}.

\section{Credits}
\label{\detokenize{a_propos:credits}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
blunderDB embeds code, data and fonts written by other people. The full inventory, with the licence texts, is the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{THIRD\_PARTY.md}} file shipped with every package (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/share/doc/blunderdb/}}) and kept at the root of the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/blunderDB/blob/main/THIRD\_PARTY.md}{repository}. The essentials:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strehl\sphinxhyphen{}prob5\sphinxhyphen{}768\sphinxhyphen{}768\sphinxhyphen{}256\sphinxhyphen{}256\sphinxhyphen{}256}} neural network is the work of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Alexander Strehl} (\sphinxhref{https://github.com/alexstrehl/puretd}{alexstrehl/puretd}, MIT licence); the search, cube model and match equity table around it are \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/gammonNet}{gammonNet}’s own configuration (MIT);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the tournament engine \sphinxstylestrong{Nicomaque} is the work of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nicolas Harmand} (\sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/nicomaque}{kevung/nicomaque}): it holds the format, the pairings, the brackets and the standings of a tournament directed from blunderDB. Its \sphinxhref{https://kevung.github.io/nicomaque/}{documentation} is published online, in French and English;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the Kazaross\sphinxhyphen{}XG2 match equity table is the work of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Neil Kazaross}, as are Neil’s numbers, his mental shortcut, published by \sphinxstyleemphasis{Kit Woolsey} in \sphinxhref{https://bkgm.com/articles/GOL/demo/equity.htm}{Match Equity Table} (GammOnLine, 1999) and summarised by \sphinxhref{https://pion.ch/backgammon/mem-met.php}{pion.ch};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the take point and gammon value tables are taken from \sphinxstyleemphasis{The Theory of Backgammon} by \sphinxstyleemphasis{Dirk Schiemann};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the one\sphinxhyphen{}sided (6 points, 15 checkers, for EPC) and two\sphinxhyphen{}sided (6 points, 6 checkers, for cube verdicts in races) bearoff tables are computed by blunderDB itself, through a port of \sphinxhref{https://www.gnu.org/software/gnubg/}{GNU Backgammon}’s \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{makebearoff}} tool; the result is byte\sphinxhyphen{}identical to gnubg’s, whose SHA\sphinxhyphen{}256 fingerprint serves as the reference. GNUbg is free software under the GPL licence;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
match files are read by \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/xgparser}{xgparser}, \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/gnubgparser}{gnubgparser}, \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/bgfparser}{bgfparser} and \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kevung/ogxmparser}{ogxmparser} (MIT);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
on the Go side: \sphinxhref{https://gitlab.com/cznic/sqlite}{modernc.org/sqlite} (BSD\sphinxhyphen{}3\sphinxhyphen{}Clause), \sphinxhref{https://github.com/jackc/pgx}{pgx}, \sphinxhref{https://wails.io}{Wails} and \sphinxhref{https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/go-fsrs}{go\sphinxhyphen{}fsrs} (MIT);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
on the interface side: \sphinxhref{https://svelte.dev}{Svelte}, \sphinxhref{https://two.js.org}{two.js} and \sphinxhref{https://www.chartjs.org}{Chart.js} (MIT);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/googlefonts/nunito}{Nunito} and \sphinxhref{https://fonts.google.com/noto/specimen/Noto+Sans+JP}{Noto Sans JP} fonts (SIL Open Font License 1.1).

\end{itemize}
